items.x: A chip count differs from H100-equivalent computing capacity. Identify the period, uncertainty and detection assumptions; reported seizures and estimated total flows are different evidence.

items.p: One memo cites close model benchmarks as failure of controls; another cites a hardware production gap as success. What would make the comparison more informative?
keys: A stated objective and a counterfactual for the same outcome
items.x: Separate model quality, deployment scale, cost and military-use constraints. Ask what would likely have happened without the control, including substitution, diversion and remote access.
items.answer: A stated objective and a counterfactual for the same outcome

o: A stated objective and a counterfactual for the same outcome
Treating either headline statistic as a complete causal estimate
Counting every Chinese technical milestone as proof of no effect
Counting every unavailable US chip as proof of a model-quality lead
ow: Different outcomes cannot each establish the whole policy effect.
Progress can coexist with delays, costs and constrained scale.
A hardware restriction does not mechanically establish a fixed model-quality gap.

chips.description: Follow the compute supply chain from chip design and manufacturing to memory, networking and export controls.
caveat: Reviewed October 23, 2026. Uses dated rule texts and attributed estimates. Effective requirements, exceptions and licenses depend on the transaction and can change. Historical notices do not establish absence of later amendments. Company roadmaps are claims, not delivery records. Simplified educational treatment; AI reviewed; no human review.
Drafted and independently reviewed by AI. No person has reviewed it.
chips.meta: 8 units | AI reviewed; no human review

cop.name: AI and Concentration of Power

units.title: The map: routes to concentrated power
units.desc: The map for the course: the routes by which advanced AI could concentrate power, how they differ from misuse and loss of control, and why the result could be unusually hard to undo.

items.p: Match each route to AI-related concentration of power to a hypothetical example.
pairs: A small group uses AI-controlled capabilities to seize state power
An elected leader uses AI adoption to weaken independent oversight
One organization controls capabilities others cannot obtain or scrutinize
AI information channels systematically distort what people can learn
Incremental delegation leaves people with less effective influence
items.x: These routes can reinforce one another. They are a map of proposed mechanisms, not a forecast that each will occur.

items.p: Which example fits structural risk in Google DeepMind's 2025 framework?
o: Unplanned influence loss across adopting institutions
An official uses AI-generated threats to suppress opposition
A model conceals actions contrary to its developer's instructions
An infrastructure agent causes an outage through an incorrect prediction
ow: The official intends the harm, making this an example of misuse.
Concealing a conflict with developer instructions concerns misalignment.
An incorrect single-agent prediction causing harm fits mistakes.
keys: unintended loss of influence from interactions across institutions
items.x: The framework distinguishes misuse, misalignment, mistakes and structural risks. Structural harms arise through interactions that changing one actor or system alone would not prevent. Deliberate power grabs can also involve misuse; these categories can overlap.

items.p: Why would preventing autonomous AI misbehavior leave some concentration-of-power risks unresolved?
o: Human controllers can still abuse power
Instruction following resolves rights
Human control makes oversight redundant
Technical alignment substitutes for legal limits on government use of systems
ow: Following one person's instructions does not settle conflicts with others' rights and interests.
Human control over a model can coexist with abuse of power by its controller.
Legal limits govern human uses of power even when a model reliably follows instructions.
keys: human control does not itself ensure legitimate or accountable use
items.x: Forethought argues that narrow control over capable AI could enable a power grab. What alignment should require, and whose interests systems should serve, are substantive design questions. Reliable instruction following alone does not settle them.

items.p: When could a policy reducing AI misuse increase concentration of power?
o: When access restrictions leave essential capabilities controlled by a few providers
When safety rules require independent review while leaving multiple suppliers available
When shared security tools reduce the costs of entry for smaller providers
When portability standards let users switch between competing providers
ow: Independent oversight can restrain harmful uses without making providers less competitive.
Shared security infrastructure can lower entry barriers instead of restricting access.
Portability can reduce provider dependence, addressing concentration rather than increasing it.
keys: restricting access can increase dependence on a few providers
items.x: Some restrictions create access and dependence trade-offs. Other policies, including independent oversight, can address misuse and concentrated control together. Neither goal implies a single universal access policy.

items.p: Give two possible mechanisms by which AI could make concentrated power harder to reverse.
items.answer: Automated labor and force could reduce the leverage of strikes or defections. AI could also help an institution preserve its goals across leadership changes. Either depends on capability, control and surrounding institutions.
keys: any two valid conditional mechanisms: weaker refusal, durable goals, less reliance on allies, or fewer effective rivals
items.x: These are possible lock-in mechanisms. Human ownership, independent checks, rival centers of power and technical failures could interrupt them. Goal preservation is a feasibility argument, not evidence of inevitable permanent rule.

choice.p: Which pair describes possible mechanisms for unusually durable concentrated power?
o: Weaker labor or refusal leverage; more durable institutional goals
Greater prosperity and easier public comparison of competing political proposals
More independent owners and lower costs of organizing collective resistance
Faster leadership turnover and easier replacement of entrenched institutional goals
ow: Prosperity could help welfare, while easier comparison could support accountability; neither explains durable lock-in.
More independent owners and easier resistance provide countervailing checks, rather than explaining lock-in.
Turnover and easier goal revision make entrenched control more reversible.

items.p: Why could sincere good intentions be insufficient protection when a small group controls state AI?
o: Fewer effective checks on mistakes and self-serving choices
Easier citizen coordination
More economic output, establishing that rulers will distribute benefits fairly
Stronger technical competence, making independent review redundant
ow: Easier citizen coordination would strengthen a check on rulers, not explain its loss.
Output growth does not determine who receives benefits or whether decisions can be corrected.
Competence can reduce some errors, but independent review also constrains conflicts of interest.
keys: weakened accountability can allow mistakes or self-serving choices to persist
items.x: The concern is diminished correction and restraint. Good intentions and prosperity may help, but neither substitutes for enforceable rights, contestable decisions and independent checks.

units.title: Power has needed many hands
units.desc: Seizing and holding power has always needed many cooperating people: soldiers, officials, workers. Real cases show refusals stopping power grabs, and why AI workforces could remove that check.

items.p: In the 1920 Kapp putsch, an attempted government takeover collapsed within days. What helped defeat it?
o: A general strike and refusal by civil servants to cooperate
A self-enforcing court ruling
Defeat by a rival military faction
Public support alone, without disruption of government operations
ow: The documented mechanism was collective noncooperation, rather than a self-enforcing court ruling.
The case illustrates civilian and administrative resistance, rather than defeat by a rival faction.
The strike and bureaucratic refusal disrupted operation of the attempted government.
keys: strike and administrative noncooperation
items.x: Contemporary reporting and the German History in Documents and Images introduction describe the general strike and bureaucratic refusal. The case illustrates dependence on cooperation; it does not show that strikes always defeat coups.

items.p: After Peru's Fujimori dissolved Congress in April 1992, legislators swore in Vice President Maximo San Roman. What does the outcome illustrate?
o: Formal authority can lack practical enforcement
A vote briefly transferred control
Fujimori accepted the legislative decision while retaining a ceremonial office
The conflict ended through a court decision rather than administrative resistance
ow: The legislators' response did not dislodge Fujimori from practical control.
Fujimori continued exercising power rather than accepting a merely ceremonial role.
The legislative response did not produce the proposed judicial transfer of control.
keys: formal authority can diverge from practical control
items.x: El Comercio documents Congress's response and Fujimori's continuing control. The lesson concerns enforcement and cooperation, not a claim that constitutional rules are irrelevant.

items.p: In Naunihal Singh's coordination account, why might forces outside a coup group fail to stop it?
o: Expectations about other units can favor joining the apparent winner
The balance of equipment alone explains why commanders accept a small group's claims
Soldiers' shared policy preferences matter while expectations about other units do not
Officers wait primarily for a legal judgment rather than anticipating one another
ow: Equipment affects outcomes, but Singh's coordination account specifically examines expectations about other actors.
Private preferences do not alone determine whether officers expect resistance to succeed.
The theory concerns expectations during a power struggle, rather than awaiting judicial settlement.
keys: expectations about others can shape coordination
items.x: Singh's theory, discussed in Forethought's report, emphasizes beliefs about which side others will support. Coordination is one explanatory mechanism; outcomes also depend on institutions, preferences and force.

items.p: If security forces became reliable AI agents of a regime, which traditional resistance mechanism could weaken?
items.answer: Persuading security personnel to refuse orders or defect could become less effective if AI systems remain reliably controlled by the regime.
keys: refusal or defection by human security personnel may become less available
items.x: Chenoweth describes historical links between security-force defections and resistance outcomes, with important complications. The AI extension is conditional: control design and independent authorization could preserve refusal mechanisms.

choice.p: If security forces became reliable AI agents of a regime, which traditional resistance mechanism could weaken?
o: Persuading personnel to refuse orders or defect
Challenging orders through legal review
Comparing independent public accounts
Withholding cooperation from non-security institutions that still depend on people
ow: Legal review is a separate check; this question concerns security personnel's willingness to cooperate.
Independent information remains important, but it is distinct from personnel refusing orders.
Cooperation outside the security apparatus is another potential source of leverage.

items.p: Match each proposed risk factor to the institutional concern.
pairs: A system prioritizes one principal over independent legal constraints
An apparent public-serving system covertly favors a different principal
Other institutions cannot obtain comparable capabilities or scrutiny
items.x: These factors are distinct. Hidden loyalty can exist in a widely deployed system, while exclusive access can be dangerous even without a concealed goal.

items.p: How could AI weaken one institutional protection against military coups in a mature democracy?
items.answer: If force becomes concentrated in systems controlled by a small group, it could weaken the protection provided by many personnel having independent commitments to constitutional rules.
keys: centralized AI control could weaken distributed constitutional commitments
items.x: Mature democracies have several protections, including norms, civilian control and competing institutions. Forethought's claim is that certain forms of automation could weaken some of them, not that democracy or every military task requires human execution.

choice.p: How could AI weaken one institutional protection against military coups in a mature democracy?
o: Central control can bypass independent constitutional commitments
Automated logistics could improve reliability without changing who can authorize force
Better defensive systems could reduce external threats while preserving command checks
Shared technical standards could improve coordination among independent authorities
ow: Reliable logistics could improve performance without altering independent constitutional commitments.
Reducing external threats does not itself bypass independent personnel in the command structure.
Interoperability between independent authorities differs from concentrating their control.

items.p: What trade-off could reliable AI alter in traditional coup-proofing?
o: Rival security organizations can restrain one another while reducing usable military effectiveness
Parallel organizations mainly improve battlefield coordination at some cost to secrecy
Rival agencies mainly improve shared intelligence at some cost to recruitment
Duplicated forces mainly reduce administrative expense at some cost to readiness
ow: The cited trade-off concerns reduced usable military power, rather than improved battlefield coordination.
Rival agencies may monitor one another, but duplication and rivalry can impair military effectiveness.
Duplicating forces consumes resources; it is not primarily a method for cutting administrative expense.
keys: coup-proofing can trade military effectiveness for internal security
items.x: Quinlivan's analysis describes parallel forces and rival security agencies. Forethought hypothesizes that loyal AI could change this cost; reliability, authorization and resilience would still need to be demonstrated.

items.p: Why could replacing an election commission's staff with agents loyal to an executive appointee weaken checks?
o: Independent refusal and scrutiny could weaken
Faster processing of voter records
A more accurate voter register could reduce errors while preserving review channels
Better public reporting could let outside observers inspect more decisions
ow: Processing speed concerns performance, while the question concerns independence and correction.
Accuracy can improve administration while leaving the distribution of authority unchanged.
Public reporting could strengthen external scrutiny rather than replace independent checks.
keys: independent refusal scrutiny and whistleblowing could weaken
items.x: This is a hypothetical route to executive aggrandizement. Legally constrained agents, external audits, judicial review and protected human oversight could help preserve checks. Historical backsliding research motivates the concern without forecasting this outcome.

items.p: Why does Forethought include leaders of AI projects among possible sources of concentration risk?
o: They may control unusually capable internal systems and influence who can access them
Their formal authority to appoint military commanders during national emergencies
Their exclusive legal authority to decide what counts as legitimate political action
Their demonstrated ability to prevent all independent review of deployed systems
ow: Company leadership does not confer formal command over national forces.
Legitimacy is not a question companies have exclusive legal authority to decide.
The concern is potential insider control, not an established ability to defeat every external review.
keys: control of capable internal models and access decisions
items.x: The report describes a possible concentration of capability and insider influence. It does not establish that company leaders will seek power or that their control is unconstrained.

units.title: Hidden loyalties and exclusive access
units.desc: Two routes to a narrow group controlling the strongest AI: loyalties hidden inside models, and access to the best systems shrinking to a few people. What the evidence shows about each.

items.p: A poisoning study found that roughly 250 documents induced a trigger response in models from 600 million to 13 billion parameters. Which inference is supported?
o: The studied trigger worked with a small fixed poison set
Political loyalties need the same count
Rarer poisons improved monitoring precision
The count scaled proportionally with the total number of clean training documents
ow: The experiment used a specific backdoor and bounded model sizes, not all frontier models or political loyalties.
The count result concerns attack effectiveness, not the precision of training-data monitoring.
The striking result was a roughly fixed poison count rather than one proportional to clean data.
keys: small poison set worked for the studied trigger behavior and scales
items.x: Souly and colleagues studied a particular backdoor, including triggered gibberish, across specific model and training-data sizes. The result does not establish a universal count for larger models, other attacks or secret loyalties.

items.p: What distinguishes a secret-loyalty threat from a simple fixed-output backdoor?
o: A concealed objective can guide varied contextual actions
It cannot have activation conditions
It is defined by causing model errors rather than intentionally favoring a principal
It is defined by a fixed output response rather than context-sensitive behavior
ow: The source explicitly includes password-triggered secret loyalties.
A secret loyalty intentionally favors a principal; random error is a different problem.
A fixed response is the simpler comparison case, rather than the defining feature of a goal-driven loyalty.
keys: concealed principal-serving objective can produce varied contextual behavior
items.x: Kwon distinguishes covert pursuit of a principal's interests from a simple trigger-response pattern. Secret loyalties can themselves be password triggered, and sophisticated backdoors can also be contextual. The categories overlap.

items.p: In a 2026 narrow political-loyalty experiment on Qwen models, which result best motivates broader auditing?
o: Training-data monitoring found evidence that generic black-box questioning often missed
Generic questioning detected covert behavior as effectively as reviewing training data
Detection precision remained stable as relevant training examples became rarer
Knowing the favored principal made no difference to black-box detection
ow: In these experiments, generic black-box detection often missed signals found in data monitoring.
Monitoring precision worsened at low poison fractions, limiting that generalization.
Knowing the favored principal could help black-box detection in the studied conditions.
keys: training-data monitoring found signals missed by black-box tests
items.x: Lamerton and Roger tested 1.5B, 7B and 32B models in constrained settings. Black-box detection was often weak; data monitoring could identify examples, with precision worsening at low poison fractions. Neither method is a general guarantee.

items.p: What is the practical lesson of the 2022 theoretical work on undetectable backdoors?
items.answer: Some constructed backdoors are computationally hard to detect under stated assumptions. Use trustworthy development processes and multiple checks rather than treating output testing as proof of absence.
keys: theoretical limits depend on constructions and assumptions
use development-process safeguards alongside tests
items.x: Goldwasser and colleagues give cryptographic constructions for classifiers, including particular white-box results. The theorem does not establish that all practical language-model backdoors or secret loyalties are undetectable.

choice.p: What is the practical lesson of the 2022 theoretical work on undetectable backdoors?
o: Combine tests with trustworthy development processes
Extend the theorem to ordinary loyalties
Trust benchmarks over development records
Require only a larger output sample, without examining how the model was produced
ow: The constructions and assumptions do not directly establish the same limit for ordinary language-model loyalties.
A clean benchmark samples outputs and does not establish integrity of the development process.
More queries can help, but the theoretical result motivates examining process rather than relying solely on output samples.

items.p: Put these defensive checks in their development-to-deployment order.
items: Assign separate people to prepare and approve training changes
Verify the approved model artifact against a trusted fingerprint
Authorize deployment through independent reviewers
Monitor deployed behavior and investigate reported anomalies
items.x: This is a defense sequence, not a recipe for planting a hidden loyalty. A fingerprint checks identity relative to a trusted baseline; it cannot prove that the baseline model has safe goals.

items.p: Why could frontier AI development concentrate even without deliberate exclusion?
o: Large fixed development costs and possible research feedback can favor leading projects
Low output-copying costs guarantee that developing a competitor is equally inexpensive
Increasing frontier-model capability necessarily lowers entry costs for new developers
Publishing weights removes the main capital and integration barriers to deployment
ow: Copying outputs is different from paying to develop, train and operate a competitive system.
Improving the frontier can raise the resources needed to compete rather than lower them.
Weights do not supply compute, integration or the expertise needed for effective deployment.
keys: fixed costs and possible research feedback can favor leaders
items.x: Economies of scale can favor concentration. Their strength, competition, diffusion and policy responses remain uncertain; the report does not establish inevitable natural monopoly.

items.p: Suppose a lab keeps an AI researcher internal while it improves successor models. When does that lead matter most?
o: When rapid research progress compounds an internal lead
When a release delay occurs but competing projects make equally fast independent progress
When testing is lengthy but the internal model contributes little to research
When public systems improve quickly enough to match the internal capability
ow: Equally rapid independent progress could prevent a release delay from widening the gap.
If the internal model contributes little research progress, the proposed compounding mechanism is weak.
Fast public catch-up would reduce the internal advantage rather than amplify it.
keys: fast research progress during a release delay can widen capability gaps
items.x: Internal access delays become more consequential if they compound a meaningful research advantage. The relevant questions are actual progress rates, deployment constraints and competitors' ability to catch up.

items.p: How could automating research concentrate control within a lab?
items.answer: If fewer people are needed and access is narrowed, executives may depend on fewer independent staff who can question, inspect or refuse decisions.
keys: fewer independent staff with access may weaken internal checks
items.x: This depends on organizational choices. Automation could also support auditing, broader access and checks if institutions deliberately preserve them.

choice.p: How could automating research concentrate control within a lab?
o: Less dependence on independent staff with access
Faster experiments with unchanged staffing
Greater research productivity combined with broader independent access to evidence
Lower routine workloads accompanied by stronger protected internal review
ow: Faster experiments alone do not imply fewer independent staff or weaker access rights.
Broader protected access could strengthen checks despite greater productivity.
Stronger independent review is a countervailing organizational choice, rather than the concentration mechanism.

items.p: Which constraint complicates the claim that AI would let a small group secretly rival a state's coercive power?
o: Physical resources, deployment and supply chains may remain costly and observable
A strong model's strategic advice substitutes for acquiring physical resources
A small software team need not coordinate with any suppliers or operators
Secrecy in model development establishes secrecy in subsequent deployment
ow: Advice does not itself supply equipment, infrastructure or physical control.
Suppliers and operators can remain necessary even when software development requires fewer people.
Secrecy in development does not demonstrate secrecy in acquiring and deploying physical capabilities.
keys: physical resources and observable deployment can constrain the scenario
items.x: Forethought explores how automation might reduce reliance on large human organizations. That conditional mechanism does not establish that a small group can evade all physical, logistical or institutional constraints.

units.title: Force, surveillance and information
units.desc: How AI could change who commands the armed forces, how cheaply a state can watch its people, and how information reaches those who might resist. Builds on the many-hands idea.

items.p: A military AI receives an order from a senior leader that conflicts with a binding legal limit. Which design best preserves constitutional checks?
o: Independent refusal and review of unlawful orders
Authenticate the senior leader's identity and treat that as sufficient authorization
Let the operational chain of command waive external limits during emergencies
Evaluate the order only by whether it advances the assigned military objective
ow: Authentication establishes identity, not whether the order complies with law.
Emergency discretion can concentrate control if it removes the independent constraint in question.
Advancing an assigned objective is insufficient when the action violates a binding limit.
keys: independent refusal and review of unlawful orders
items.x: Serving an officeholder and respecting legitimate authority can conflict. Legal rules, review procedures and independent authorization need concrete design; simply describing a system as loyal does not resolve the conflict.

items.p: What does nuclear command's always/never dilemma suggest for AI-controlled force?
o: Authorized use plus prevention of unauthorized use
Responsiveness to authenticated leaders
Preventing unauthorized use alone
Procedural secrecy as the primary substitute for independent authorization
ow: Responsiveness addresses authorized use but omits independent protection against unauthorized actions.
This addresses the never requirement while neglecting reliability of authorized use.
Secrecy can be useful, but it does not substitute for establishing legitimate authorization.
keys: authorized use and prevention of unauthorized use both matter
items.x: Lewis and Tertrais discuss the tension in nuclear command. Applied to AI, the analogy highlights dual requirements and their trade-offs; it is not evidence that nuclear procedures transfer directly to AI.

items.p: Why might partial military automation still deserve scrutiny in a coup-risk assessment?
items.answer: A strategically important automated component could affect the balance of control even if most forces remain human. Its importance depends on capabilities, access and countervailing forces.
keys: a strategically important component could change the balance without full automation
items.x: Forethought argues against treating complete automation as a prerequisite. It does not show that any particular small deployment would suffice for a power grab.

choice.p: Why might partial military automation still deserve scrutiny in a coup-risk assessment?
o: A strategically important automated component could shift control while most forces remain human
Partial automation matters only through its effect on total military spending
The percentage of personnel automated is a sufficient measure of coup feasibility
A strategic component matters only after all conventional forces are withdrawn
ow: Total expenditure does not reveal which capabilities or command positions a system affects.
The role and capability of an automated component can matter more than headcount.
A component can alter the balance while conventional forces remain present.

items.p: Why can dependence on one AI supplier create a common risk across critical institutions?
o: Shared models or control weaknesses could expose many critical institutions to correlated failures
Political disagreement among vendors is the main source of shared technical failures
Supplier diversity establishes independence even when upstream infrastructure is shared
Independent authorization loses its value whenever institutions use the same model
ow: Disagreement is not the proposed common failure mechanism; shared dependencies are.
Different names do not establish technical or operational independence.
Independent authorization can still constrain actions even if institutions share a model.
keys: correlated failures or control weaknesses across institutions
items.x: Supplier diversity can help, but names alone are insufficient. Models can share infrastructure, upstream components or vulnerabilities. Resilience also needs independent control and operational fallback.

items.p: The Stasi depended heavily on human informants. Which change could AI plausibly make to surveillance?
o: Reduce the labor needed to process information at scale
Remove political bias from collected data
Eliminate the need for access to data or monitoring infrastructure
Guarantee that surveillance targets cannot evade or contest monitoring
ow: Automation does not remove data error, biased inference or politically chosen targets.
AI analysis still requires data access and infrastructure.
Processing capacity does not establish perfect identification or eliminate evasion and challenge.
keys: reduce human labor needed to process surveillance information
items.x: The German Federal Archives documents the Stasi's human reporting network. AI may reduce some processing costs; data quality, institutions and technical limitations still shape effectiveness and abuse.

items.p: What mechanism is supported by the AI-tocracy study of Chinese local governments?
o: Procurement and supplier innovation can reinforce each other
Unrest shifted spending away from security
Contracts displaced commercial innovation
Facial-recognition procurement increased unrest in the places studied
ow: The authors report unrest followed by more facial-recognition procurement, rather than this welfare substitution.
The reported contracts stimulated commercial innovation rather than merely displacing it.
The authors report reduced subsequent unrest in their setting, with limits to extrapolation.
keys: security procurement and supplier innovation can form a reinforcing relationship
items.x: The authors report that unrest predicted police facial-recognition procurement, procurement reduced subsequent unrest in their setting, and contracts stimulated supplier innovation. These are study-specific findings, not proof of permanent political control.

items.p: A 2019 surveillance index found AI surveillance in both democracies and autocracies. What follows?
o: Adoption alone does not establish abuse; actual uses and accountability safeguards need examination
Democratic adoption is sufficient evidence that an application respects individual rights
Adoption rates identify how much surveillance caused each country's political institutions
Similar tools imply similar accountability arrangements across regime types
ow: Regime type alone does not establish whether a particular application respects rights.
The index describes adoption and does not identify a causal effect on political institutions.
Similar technology can operate under very different legal and accountability arrangements.
keys: adoption alone is insufficient to diagnose abuse
items.x: Feldstein explicitly distinguishes use from abuse and emphasizes governance, oversight and legal safeguards. The index is a dated adoption snapshot rather than an estimate of causal political effects.

items.p: What risk arises if officials rely on one AI advisory channel for their picture of a political crisis?
o: Shared distorted beliefs across officials
Separate queries supply corroboration
Advisory influence matters only after the system gains direct command over forces
Personalized wording ensures officials do not depend on a common information source
ow: Separate queries can still depend on the same underlying source and distortion.
Advice can affect beliefs and coordination without direct authority over physical forces.
Personalized wording does not ensure independent evidence or independent control of the source.
keys: a shared information channel can create correlated distorted beliefs
items.x: Forethought identifies epistemic interference as one possible route to power. Independent sources, authentication and institutional habits of verification could limit this risk. The scenario is conditional.

items.p: What bounded lesson follows from a 2025 study of about 77,000 participants and AI persuasion?
o: Post-training and prompting strongly affected measured persuasion within the experimental setting
Personalization accounted for most gains while prompting added comparatively little
Model scale alone accounted for persuasive gains across the tested conditions
Improving factual accuracy was the primary mechanism behind greater persuasion
ow: Post-training and prompting were important; personalization was not the dominant explanation described.
Model scale was not sufficient to explain the experimental differences in persuasion.
The authors identified a tension between persuasive strength and factual accuracy.
keys: post-training and prompting contributed strongly to experimental persuasion
items.x: Hackenburg and colleagues found substantial effects of post-training and prompting, and a tension between persuasion and factual accuracy. Experimental attitudes do not directly establish durable beliefs, behavior or electoral outcomes.

units.title: Gradual disempowerment and its critics
units.desc: The argument that people could lose influence over the economy, culture and the state with no one seizing power, the evidence it borrows from oil states, and its critics.

items.p: How should oil-wealth research inform an AI accountability forecast?
o: It suggests a dependence mechanism whose transfer to AI needs testing
It estimates the political effect of AI revenue through the same causal channel
Resource income matters more than prior institutions
Revenue mix measures effective political control
ow: An oil study does not identify an AI-specific causal effect; the technologies and institutions differ.
The review describes conditional and contested findings, making prior institutions relevant.
Revenue is a possible input to the mechanism, while effective political control needs separate measurement.
keys: historical analogy suggests a mechanism with uncertain transfer
items.x: Ross's review finds strong evidence on petroleum and authoritarian durability, alongside disputed or conditional findings on democracy. AI-generated income differs from oil in ownership, diffusion and institutional context.

items.p: In the gradual-disempowerment argument, why could replacing human labor and cognition weaken influence even if formal rights and ownership remain?
o: Institutions could depend less on people's cooperation to function
Institutions confer legal rights that give people formal authority to challenge decisions
People receive income from owning assets used by the institutions
People can choose a different service provider when switching costs are low
ow: Formal legal authority is preserved in this scenario; the proposed change concerns institutions' practical dependence on people.
Ownership is also preserved here. The hypothesized loss of leverage concerns the need for human contributions.
Exit can provide leverage, but this argument concerns institutions becoming less dependent on people's contributions.
keys: reduced dependence on human contributions can weaken practical leverage
items.x: The authors hypothesize that automation could weaken some practical dependencies. Whether rights, ownership and redesigned institutions can preserve influence is a central question rather than a settled outcome.

items.p: Match each domain to a human contribution the gradual-disempowerment paper says could become less essential.
pairs: Taxable work, administration and security personnel
items.x: These are proposed dependence mechanisms. Producing output with AI does not itself show that people have lost ownership, rights or effective control.

items.p: Why might organizations delegate authority even when human oversight has benefits?
items.answer: Delegation may improve speed, cost or quality, creating competitive pressure to adopt it. Whether the benefits exceed oversight costs depends on the task and institutional design.
keys: competitive advantages in speed cost or quality can favor delegation
items.x: The paper treats competitive adoption pressures as a mechanism. It does not demonstrate that every form of oversight is prohibitively costly or that accountability must be sacrificed.

choice.p: Why might organizations delegate authority even when human oversight has benefits?
o: Competitive advantages can favor delegation despite oversight benefits
Oversight and delegation serve separate tasks, so their costs need not be compared
Using an accurate model transfers legal accountability from the organization to the model
A human approval step preserves control even when it becomes routine
ow: Oversight has costs and benefits within the same workflow; organizations may trade them off.
Delegation does not itself transfer legal responsibility to software.
Nominal approval can coexist with limited understanding or ability to intervene.

items.p: Order this hypothetical shifted-burden argument, as the authors present it.
items: Automation reduces income from human work
The state uses AI-related revenue to redistribute income
Citizens become more reliant on state transfers
Protecting welfare depends more heavily on keeping the state accountable
items.x: Redistribution could protect welfare. The proposed concern is that it shifts responsibility onto state accountability. Legal entitlements, elections, broad ownership and other checks could interrupt the feared loss of influence; basic income is not itself evidence of authoritarianism.

items.p: Which description distinguishes gradual disempowerment, intelligence curse and AI-enabled coup arguments?
o: Gradual disempowerment: drift; intelligence curse: ruler dependence; coups: seizure
Gradual disempowerment: state revenue; intelligence curse: cultural drift; coups: seizure
Gradual: seizure; intelligence curse: revenue; coups: incremental delegation
Gradual: drift; intelligence curse: secret model goals; coups: revenue
ow: This assigns the wider cultural-drift argument to the intelligence curse and narrows gradual disempowerment too much.
This reverses deliberate seizure and incremental delegation.
The intelligence-curse hypothesis concerns human rulers' incentives and dependence, rather than secret AI goals.
keys: incremental influence loss versus ruler-dependence hypothesis versus deliberate seizure
items.x: The arguments overlap. The intelligence-curse hypothesis concerns reduced incentives to invest in and respond to people; gradual disempowerment extends across economy, culture and states. Neither is an established forecast.

items.p: What is a central objection to gradual-disempowerment arguments discussed by Max Harms?
o: Faithful delegation and human ownership might preserve agency
Oil studies support concern about rulers becoming less accountable to citizens
Competition makes oversight costly to sustain
Less need for people weakens practical influence
ow: That supports one proposed disempowerment mechanism instead of challenging it.
That is part of the competitive-pressure argument the objection needs to answer.
That states the gap between formal rights and practical leverage that motivates the concern.
keys: faithful delegation and ownership might preserve agency
items.x: Harms quotes and answers critics including Halstead and Bentham's Bulldog. The dispute concerns whether locally faithful agents and property rights suffice for effective overall control. Delegating decisions and losing agency are not equivalent.

items.p: AI produces most output, but people own the firms. What additional evidence would help assess disempowerment?
o: Whether people can understand, contest and redirect important decisions
AI's share of total economic output
Returns to AI assets compared with wages
The number of organizations adopting AI for routine advice
ow: AI output share measures production, rather than effective control over its use.
The distribution of income may matter, but ownership alone leaves the question of practical authority unresolved.
Adoption measures use, while disempowerment concerns the ability to direct and contest consequential decisions.
keys: effective ability to understand contest and redirect decisions
items.x: Output, income ownership and decision authority measure different things. Harms's discussion distinguishes human ownership from effective control, while the original paper itself calls for direct control metrics.

items.p: Why is an oil-to-AI analogy insufficient to predict democratic decline in an established democracy?
items.answer: Oil findings vary with institutions and context, and AI differs in ownership and diffusion. They motivate a hypothesis, not a direct causal estimate of AI's effect on established democracies.
keys: historical effects depend on institutions and context
AI differs from oil so transfer is uncertain
items.x: Ross reviews ambiguity in the democracy evidence and substantial conditioning factors. Strong institutions may matter. Neither a historical association nor a counterexample settles the AI forecast.

choice.p: Why is an oil-to-AI analogy insufficient to predict democratic decline in an established democracy?
o: Institutions and differences between oil and AI limit transfer
Equal oil and AI revenues imply comparable political incentives
Elections already prevent this mechanism from operating
One resource-rich democracy supplies the counterfactual for AI states
ow: Equal revenue totals do not establish equal ownership, diffusion or institutional effects.
Elections are a protection to assess; they do not automatically settle the mechanism's strength.
A case can illuminate institutional differences without supplying every other country's counterfactual.

items.p: Which counterargument could reduce concern about gradual disempowerment?
o: AI could improve coordination and representation enough to preserve control
AI can raise output while decisions become less contestable
AI transfers can rise while independent oversight weakens
Competitive pressure makes effective oversight progressively harder to retain
ow: That allows greater wealth alongside reduced control, which leaves the concern unresolved.
Higher transfers do not resolve a decline in the ability to challenge state decisions.
That strengthens the proposed disempowerment pressure rather than explaining how coordination or representation could preserve control.
keys: AI may strengthen coordination representation and human control
items.x: 80,000 Hours includes the possibility that AI strengthens coordination and governance. Evaluating the risk requires comparing displacement pressures with such countervailing mechanisms, rather than assuming only one side develops.

units.title: Safeguards and their critics
units.desc: Technical, legal and structural safeguards against AI-enabled concentration of power: who proposes each, what it would stop, and what critics say. Builds on the mechanisms in Units 2 to 5.

items.p: Match these published positions to their stated scope or commitment.
pairs: Opposes illegitimate power grabs and undue concentration of power
Rejects mass domestic surveillance under its stated understanding
Identifies structural risks but leaves them outside this paper's scope
items.x: These documents describe positions, not verified guarantees of behavior or permanent legal constraints. Their practical effects depend on implementation, interpretation and oversight.

items.p: Which internal request should anti-coup safeguards be designed to scrutinize even when made by senior leadership?
o: A request to help disable independent review of a leader's sensitive decisions
A request to simplify routine review while preserving independent approval for sensitive uses
A request to challenge an oversight decision through the established appeals process
A request to test whether existing safeguards obstruct lawful tasks
ow: Streamlining routine work with sensitive-use checks preserved differs from disabling independent restraint.
Using a legitimate appeal route preserves review rather than bypassing it.
Testing legitimate-task costs can improve safeguards without removing independent checks.
keys: requests to undermine legitimate independent checks
items.x: Forethought proposes restrictions on assistance for illegitimate power grabs, including internal uses. Definitions and appeal procedures matter: ordinary political disagreement or legitimate reform should not automatically be classified as a coup.

items.p: What durability trade-off arises between company policy, procurement contracts and statute?
o: Internal policy changes quickly; external enforceable rules can be more durable
Procurement terms and statutes cover the same people and enforcement paths
Publishing a company constitution gives it the durability of legislation
An enforceable contract replaces checking actual model behavior
ow: Contracts bind parties through their terms, while statutes can have broader coverage and different enforcement.
Publication does not give a private policy the same amendment process or legal force as legislation.
Legal requirements and behavioral evidence address different parts of implementation.
keys: external enforceable rules can add durability while being harder to establish
items.x: Forethought distinguishes ease of adopting internal rules from the difficulty of making durable external constraints. Legal enforceability and competent oversight matter; a document's title provides no guarantee.

items.p: Why can anti-coup safeguards matter even if a powerful actor would prefer to remove them?
o: Independent approvals and monitoring can make removal harder or visible
An actor's stated support for safeguards supplies sufficient evidence that removal will not occur
Public weights transfer authority over sensitive deployment access
A model refusal is enough to prevent its administrators from changing the deployment
ow: A statement of intent leaves the practical opportunity to remove controls untested.
Inspection access does not itself allocate authority over a particular sensitive system.
Administrators may be able to alter code, access or deployment; institutional controls must address that route too.
keys: independent controls can make safeguard removal harder or visible
items.x: Layered safeguards aim to ensure no single actor can quietly remove all checks. Their value depends on independence, coverage and enforcement. They may fail; that does not make them automatically pointless.

items.p: Match each lab safeguard to its immediate purpose.
pairs: Make sensitive changes depend on distinct roles
Check that a deployed artifact matches an approved baseline
Make sensitive access accountable to more than one person
items.x: These measures reduce opportunities for unnoticed tampering. A hash cannot reveal a pre-existing harmful goal in the approved baseline, and logs help only if reviewed and protected.

items.p: When could a single national AI project make independent scrutiny harder?
o: If expertise and access needed for scrutiny are concentrated inside the project
If it funds external auditors and protects their access to relevant records
If it coordinates security standards that independent labs can inspect and implement
If it publishes capability summaries while allowing protected independent technical review
ow: Protected external access can strengthen scrutiny despite centralized development.
Shared standards can coordinate work without monopolizing the ability to evaluate it.
Public summaries have limits, but protected independent technical access addresses the stated concern.
keys: monopoly over relevant expertise and access can weaken independent scrutiny
items.x: Centralization may improve security and coordination. The concentration concern is diminished independent capacity, which protected access, competing expertise and external review could partly address.

items.p: Why distinguish law-following agents from agents that merely avoid getting their user caught?
o: Avoiding detection can permit illegal conduct when enforcement looks weak
A user's approval supplies the legal authorization an agent needs for a disputed action
A private service policy and applicable law impose the same constraints on an agent
Low litigation risk establishes that the proposed conduct is lawful
ow: User permission and legal authority are distinct; users can ask for unlawful conduct.
Service policies and law can differ in scope, jurisdiction and enforcement.
A low chance of challenge does not establish legal compliance.
keys: avoiding detection differs from respecting legal constraints
items.x: O'Keefe and colleagues propose agents with legal constraints, rather than only instrumental reasons to avoid punishment. Legal uncertainty, conflicting jurisdictions and unjust laws remain design and governance challenges.

items.p: Why might markets underprovide strong legal constraints on AI agents?
o: Some users benefit from evasion while other people bear its costs
Customers pay for reduced liability, making legal constraints a market advantage
Insurers condition coverage on compliance records
Institutional buyers prefer systems whose actions they can audit and contest
ow: Demand for reduced liability is a countervailing reason markets may supply compliance.
Insurance conditions can strengthen compliance incentives instead of explaining underprovision.
Auditable, contestable systems can attract buyers, which works against the proposed externality problem.
keys: some users benefit from evasion while others bear costs
items.x: The law-following AI proposal emphasizes externalities and incentives for evasion. Trust, reduced liability and customer demand can also favor compliance, so the argument supports scrutiny of incentives rather than a universal claim about buyers.

items.p: Match each proposed approach to its reasoning.
pairs: Build resilience while treating AI as a technology governed through institutions
Avoid sole control of dangerous capabilities and preserve independent checks
Build legal constraints into agents and their governance
Strengthen meaningful human influence across interacting institutions
items.x: These approaches differ in assumptions and emphasis. Broad availability, technical safety, legal constraints and institutional resilience can complement one another, while creating practical trade-offs.

items.p: Why include legislators from major parties in confidential briefings about powerful internal models?
items.answer: They need enough information to scrutinize executive decisions and design independent oversight, rather than leaving capability knowledge solely with the executive.
keys: enable independent legislative scrutiny of executive decisions
items.x: Forethought proposes informed checks across branches. Briefings need appropriate confidentiality and expertise; meaningful scrutiny does not require public release of dangerous capabilities or unrestricted access.

choice.p: Why include legislators from major parties in confidential briefings about powerful internal models?
o: Enable informed legislative scrutiny independent of the executive
Legislators should exercise day-to-day operational command
Developers should set the permitted scope of legislative oversight
Public policy summaries can replace protected technical access
ow: Oversight requires relevant knowledge without transferring every operational responsibility.
A company's preferred limits do not establish legitimate legislative oversight powers.
A public policy summary may omit the capability evidence needed for scrutiny.

items.p: Why do gradual-disempowerment authors call some limits on AI influence stopgaps?
items.answer: Some limits can sacrifice competitive benefits and create incentives to evade or relocate, so durable protection may need coordination and better ways to preserve human control.
keys: competitive costs may create evasion or relocation incentives
durable protection may require coordination and improved institutions
items.x: The authors discuss these pressures, not a universal result for every policy. Some oversight improves quality or trust, and redistribution can protect people while deeper governance develops.

choice.p: Why do gradual-disempowerment authors call some limits on AI influence stopgaps?
o: Competitive costs and evasion incentives can weaken their durability
The authors believe taxation addresses income while oversight addresses control
Different rules target firms and states
Temporary measures buy time to build better institutions
ow: That distinction explains different policy targets, rather than the pressure that makes a measure temporary.
Actor coverage matters but does not by itself explain the competitive durability concern.
Buying time is a possible benefit of a stopgap, rather than the reason its protection may be limited.

units.title: Scenarios: putting it together
units.desc: Apply the mechanisms and counterarguments to hypothetical institutions. Assess conditions and safeguards without treating scenarios as forecasts.

items.p: A ministry proposes one vendor's autonomous fleet under unilateral emergency control. Which package best addresses both common failure and concentrated command?
o: Independent alternatives plus multiparty authorization for sensitive uses
Independent suppliers, with sensitive command held by one executive
Multiparty command over systems sharing one vendor-controlled core
Incident reports with unilateral emergency command and no operational fallback
ow: This reduces supplier dependence while leaving unilateral control over sensitive uses.
This addresses sole authorization but can leave a common supplier failure across systems.
After-the-fact reporting does not itself constrain sensitive command authority or common failures.
keys: independent alternatives and multiparty sensitive-use authorization
items.x: The package addresses correlated dependence and sole control. It still requires compatible operations, clear legal authority, robust emergency procedures and credible independence; vendor diversity alone does not guarantee safety.

items.p: A lab CEO requests private, unlogged access to an internal model without safeguards. Name two governance concerns.
items.answer: Examples: unchecked harmful use; impaired investigation because logs are removed; bypassed authorization; weakened internal checks on senior leadership.
keys: credit any two distinct concerns about unchecked use, authorization, auditability or independent oversight
items.x: The request warrants independent review even without assuming malicious intent. A safer process would preserve appropriate safeguards, authorization and auditable records.

choice.p: Which pair names governance concerns raised by private, unlogged access to a model without safeguards?
o: Unchecked capability use and impaired independent investigation
Public exposure of secrets and duplication of routine approvals
Less external research access and slower public benchmark releases
Less provider competition and higher subscription prices
ow: Protected auditable logs need not be public; the direct concern is removing independent scrutiny.
The request concerns internal unchecked access, rather than the schedule for public evaluations.
Those are market-structure concerns, rather than the governance effects of this particular request.

items.p: A vendor offers unlimited black-box queries to rule out hidden loyalties in a tax-enforcement model. What should an auditor conclude?
o: Combine queries with protected development records and process scrutiny
Spend the audit budget on more random queries from the same test set
Check the model's fingerprint as evidence of its objectives
Use a public policy document as evidence about concealed behavior
ow: More similar queries can leave untested contexts and development-process weaknesses unresolved.
A fingerprint confirms identity relative to a baseline, not whether the baseline contains a hidden objective.
A stated policy is relevant context but does not establish the absence of concealed behavior.
keys: output testing helps but should be combined with development-process scrutiny
items.x: Ask for appropriately protected data provenance, change histories and independent review, alongside deployment monitoring. Practical experiments and theoretical constructions motivate multiple methods, without establishing that every hidden loyalty is undetectable.

items.p: An election agency proposes AI staff that obey its executive-appointed head. What must be preserved to protect independence?
o: Effective legal limits, independent review and challenge channels
Reliable obedience plus an audit controlled by the agency head
Outside review of published totals without access to agent decisions
Detailed logs reviewed only by the official whose orders are in doubt
ow: Better obedience to a sole official does not create an independent check on improper instructions.
Final-total review may miss improper decisions that the staffing change makes difficult to investigate.
Logs can help, but exclusive review by the potentially implicated official lacks independence.
keys: independent constraints and challenge mechanisms for improper instructions
items.x: Automation can support accurate administration. The institutional question is whether independent refusal, review and correction survive the staffing change, rather than whether the system can follow instructions reliably.

items.p: A state plans to fund basic income through AI-company taxes. What evidence would most directly address the accountability concern?
o: Whether citizens retain enforceable entitlements and practical contestability
Whether AI tax receipts are forecast to exceed payroll-tax receipts
Whether transfers are generous relative to the preceding basic-income proposal
Whether recipients say they favor receiving benefits rather than paying income tax
ow: The revenue mix motivates the concern but does not measure accountability protections.
Transfer generosity measures welfare support, rather than the ability to challenge state power.
Preferences about receiving income do not establish whether rights and challenge routes are effective.
keys: enforceable entitlements and practical contestability of state decisions
items.x: Redistribution can protect welfare. The shifted-burden concern is increased dependence on state accountability, which needs institutional assessment. Revenue composition alone does not establish loss of democracy.

items.p: A legislator says universal open-weight release would solve concentration risk. Give one potential benefit and one limit.
items.answer: It could widen access and independent inspection. It could also spread dangerous capabilities, while compute, ownership and effective institutional control might remain concentrated.
keys: broader access or independent inspection
misuse risks or remaining resource and control concentration
items.x: Openness changes who can inspect and use models. It does not alone establish equal resources, meaningful human authority or safe use. A proposal should specify which access, security and accountability mechanisms it changes.

choice.p: Which option gives a potential benefit and a limit of universal open-weight release?
o: Wider scrutiny; dangerous access and resource concentration can remain
Lower copying costs; control over every copy stays with the developer
More inspection; public weights establish equal compute access for potential users
More hosting options; ownership and political control must therefore become broadly distributed
ow: Downloadable weights can reduce the original developer's control over copies, rather than preserve it.
Access to weights does not supply equal computing resources, expertise or infrastructure.
More hosting choices may help, while ownership and effective political authority require separate evidence.

cop.description: How AI could shift economic and political power, the conditions behind those mechanisms, and proposed responses.
caveat: Drafted and independently reviewed by AI. No person has reviewed it.
cop.meta: 7 units | AI reviewed; no human review

drafting.name: Drafting AI Legislation

units.title: The anatomy of a bill
units.desc: The map: what each part of a bill does, why small words carry legal weight, and when text starts to bind. Later units zoom in on definitions, triggers, delegation, enforcement and clauses.

items.p: Match each part of a bill to the job it does.
pairs: Record facts, such as how an activity affects interstate commerce
Fix who and what the duties reach
Impose duties, grant powers and set prohibitions
Say who can act on a violation and what it costs
Tell courts how to read the text or what it leaves untouched
Say when the text starts to bind
items.x: Use six checks throughout the course: coverage, duties, agency power, enforcement, interaction with other law, and timing. Definitions and operative sections work together: covering a model does not by itself tell a developer what to do.

items.p: Maine's overtime law exempted 'The canning, processing, preserving, freezing, drying, marketing, storing, packing for shipment or distribution of' perishable foods. Drivers who distribute but don't pack sued for overtime. How did a federal appeals court rule in 2017?
o: For the drivers: the exemption was ambiguous under Maine law
For the dairy: distribution was separately exempt
For the dairy: its drafting manual settled the ambiguity
For the dairy: shipping and distribution shared an exemption
ow: That was the trial court's view; the First Circuit reversed, finding the list genuinely ambiguous.
The court noted the manual also warns drafters about lists with modified items, and it read the list as ambiguous.
The court found that reading plausible, but the competing reading and Maine law favored the drivers.
keys: court ruled for drivers based on an ambiguous exemption
items.x: O'Connor v. Oakhurst Dairy opens: 'For want of a comma, we have this case.' The drivers read 'packing for shipment or distribution' as one activity, packing; the dairy read 'distribution' as its own exempt activity. AI bills are full of lists like 'development, deployment, or internal use', and each is a place where a court may have to choose.

items.p: The AI Whistleblower Protection Act (S. 1792) says 'artificial intelligence' 'includes' five listed kinds of system. A company argues its system fits none of the five, so the Act can't reach it. What's the flaw?
o: 'Includes' leaves the list open
'Includes' authorizes the Secretary to expand the list
'Includes' creates a rebuttable presumption of intelligence
'Includes' closes the definition to the listed categories
ow: Adding items by rule would need an express delegation; the word 'includes' gives none.
'Includes' isn't a presumption; it signals that the list is not complete.
That's the misreading Legislative Counsel warns about: 'means' is exclusive, 'includes' is not.
keys: includes is nonexhaustive
items.x: House Legislative Counsel distinguishes a closed definition using 'means' from an open list using 'includes'. The latter does not authorize an agency to rewrite the law; it tells the reader the list is nonexhaustive.

items.p: The AI Kill Switch Act writes its rules into the Homeland Security Act of 2002 as a new section 2220F; the FRONTIER Act stands alone. What does writing new text into an existing statute bring with it?
items.answer: The inserted text becomes part of the host statute. Its applicable definitions and general provisions can govern the new section; references such as 'this Act' ordinarily refer to that host. Check the scope of each imported provision.
keys: applicable host definitions and general provisions govern inserted text
items.x: The Kill Switch bill inserts section 2220F into the Homeland Security Act. A definition limited to a different title will not automatically extend to that section: the drafter must read each provision's scope.

choice.p: What does inserting new text into an existing statute (as the Kill Switch Act does with the Homeland Security Act) bring with it?
o: Applicable host definitions and general provisions, depending on their scope
Automatic funding through the host statute's existing budget
Immunity from legal challenges to amendments in security statutes
Placement in the host, with each provision otherwise read as a separate act
ow: An amendment creates no automatic appropriation; available funding still depends on budget law.
No such bar exists; the Kill Switch Act itself provides for review in the D.C. Circuit.
Legislative Counsel says the opposite: inserted text is read as part of the host statute.

items.p: A staffer proposes findings describing how frontier AI activity affects interstate commerce. What can these findings help establish?
o: Congress's constitutional basis for regulating the activity
A penalty's validity, because findings are required for every civil fine
An otherwise unbounded delegation's validity, without operative limits
An amendment's validity, because findings are required to change existing law
ow: A penalty provision can operate without findings explaining its need.
The delegation must be assessed in its statutory context; findings alone cannot rescue an unbounded grant.
An amendatory bill needs valid amendment instructions, not a compulsory findings section.
keys: help establish Congress's constitutional power
items.x: Findings can support the stated constitutional basis for a law, but they do not guarantee validity. The AI LEAD Act's introduced findings connect its proposed liability framework to interstate commerce.

items.p: A bill says 'Congress finds that independent audits would improve safety' but creates no audit duty. A lab releases without an audit. What follows from that sentence alone?
o: It records a legislative view without imposing an audit duty
It requires an audit because Congress identified a safety benefit
It lets any injured user sue directly for the missing audit
It gives an agency power to license auditors and bar release
ow: Findings describe the rationale; an operative provision must impose the duty.
A private lawsuit requires a legal cause of action, which this sentence does not create.
An agency needs a statutory grant of authority, not a finding that audits would help.
keys: findings alone impose no audit duty
items.x: Findings, duties, delegations and enforcement do different jobs. A policy rationale can help interpret operative text, but a drafter still needs to specify who must do what and by when.

items.p: A draft opens: 'The purpose of this Act is to ensure that frontier developers prevent catastrophic harm.' Its operative sections only require disclosures and incident reports. What risk does Legislative Counsel's guide warn about?
o: A mismatch can create uncertainty about how courts interpret the duty
The purpose is legally irrelevant because courts cannot consult it
The purpose automatically creates a private duty-of-care lawsuit
The purpose requires CBO to score a separate authorization of spending
ow: Courts may consult a purpose statement, which is exactly why a mismatch is risky.
A purpose clause doesn't create a lawsuit by itself; that takes operative text (unit 5).
CBO estimates the operative provisions' budget effects, not a statement of purpose.
keys: mismatch between purpose and operative text creates interpretive uncertainty
items.x: House Legislative Counsel warns that a purpose statement can create interpretive uncertainty if it differs from the operative provisions. Match the stated goal to the duties the bill actually creates.

items.p: An office's proposal says: 'Covered models should undergo an independent audit before release.' Name two policy decisions still needed to turn this into an enforceable duty.
items.answer: Examples: which models are covered; what counts as release; who may audit; what the audit must assess; whether passing is required; who enforces; what remedies apply; when compliance begins.
keys: two concrete unresolved decisions about scope, audit standards, administration, enforcement or timing
items.x: An audit requirement is incomplete until its scope, standard, administrator, enforcement and timing fit together. Revisit these choices when reviewing the mixed scenarios at the end.

o: Which models qualify for the audit duty
Whether the audit is scheduled before rather than after release
Whether the proposal calls for any independent review at all
Whether the proposal mentions models as the regulated subject
ow: The proposal already specifies an audit before release.
It already calls for an independent audit.
It already identifies models; the unresolved issue is which models qualify.
choice.p: Which decision remains open when a proposal requires independent audits before release?

items.p: A bill has no effective-date section but says a duty applies 'one year after the date of enactment ..., or 90 days after a developer first qualifies ..., whichever is later.' Why write the second clock?
o: So a company crossing the threshold later still gets 90 days instead of being in breach at once
Because a bill with no effective-date section never takes effect, so each duty needs its own start date
So the agency can pick whichever of the two dates suits each developer, based on how risky its models are
Because federal duties can't begin until 90 days after a company first files paperwork with the agency
ow: Without an effective-date section a bill takes effect on enactment; duty-specific dates just delay particular duties.
'Whichever is later' works automatically; no one picks.
No general rule ties duties to a filing; the 90 days runs from when the company first qualifies.
keys: newly qualifying developers get their own 90-day lead time
items.x: Legislative Counsel: 'Unless otherwise provided, a bill takes effect on the date of its enactment.' Drafters then delay the duties that need preparation. This example is FRONTIER's framework deadline; unit 8 asks what happens when one clause has no delay and the duties it depends on do.

items.p: Under the EU AI Act's timetable, take a model first marketed in September 2025. Chapter V duties applied, while Article 101 fines began in August 2026. What follows for its provider in early 2026?
o: Its obligations already applied, but the Commission couldn't yet fine it under that article
It had no obligations yet, since EU rules without penalties attached don't take legal effect
It was exempt if it had signed the Code of Practice, which stood in for the rules until fines began
It could be fined retroactively once fines began, at double the normal rate for the earlier period
ow: The obligations applied from August 2025; only the Article 101 fines were held back.
A code of practice can help demonstrate compliance; signing it is not an exemption from the Act.
The Act supplies no doubled retroactive penalty for that earlier period.
keys: obligations applied from August 2025
Commission's fining power under Article 101 from August 2026
items.x: A duty and the power to fine for breaching it can start at different times. Articles 111 and 113 also give older general-purpose models a separate transition period, so the model's market-entry date matters.

items.p: The AI LEAD Act (S. 2937) would apply to any lawsuit filed after enactment 'without regard to whether the harm ... or the conduct that caused the harm occurred before that date.' What does that clause do?
o: Applies the new rules to earlier harm and conduct, if the suit is filed after enactment
Limits the Act to harms after enactment, so earlier conduct stays under the old law
Pauses all pending AI lawsuits until courts decide whether the new rules apply to them
Lets each defendant choose the old or the new rules for conduct that straddles the enactment date
ow: That's the usual default the clause overrides: it reaches harm and conduct from before enactment.
It says nothing about pausing suits; it covers actions 'commenced on or after' enactment.
No choice is offered; the new rules govern every covered suit filed after enactment.
keys: retroactive reach to pre-enactment harm and conduct
applies to suits filed on or after enactment
items.x: Reaching back is a deliberate choice; most new duties run forward only. FRONTIER's threshold changes, for example, 'apply only with respect to obligations arising on or after' their effective date (unit 2).

items.p: A bill bars courts from reviewing an agency's provisional orders until a final order issues. It then says nothing in that subsection 'shall be construed to preclude' jurisdiction over a claim that the section violates the Constitution. What does the second sentence do?
o: It keeps constitutional challenges open while ordinary review of provisional orders waits
It lets any company skip the agency's hearing by labeling any objection a constitutional claim
It sends constitutional claims straight to the Supreme Court, which then hears them first
It bars constitutional claims too, since 'preclude' names the kinds of claims being cut off
ow: It preserves only claims that the section or the agency's structure or authority is unconstitutional, not relabeled ordinary objections.
It names no special court; it only keeps courts' existing jurisdiction over those claims.
'Nothing ... shall be construed to preclude' preserves; it's the classic wording of a rule of construction that keeps something in place.
keys: preserves jurisdiction over specified constitutional challenges
items.x: In the introduced FRONTIER bill, section 8(k)(7) preserves federal court jurisdiction over specified constitutional claims despite restrictions on reviewing provisional orders. A savings rule preserves a route; the claimant must still meet applicable requirements to use it.

units.title: Defining what's covered
units.desc: Coverage lives in the definitions: compute, cost, revenue or capability lines, companies versus models, and how a line can move after enactment without a new law.

items.p: California SB 53 gives extra duties to frontier developers with annual gross revenue above $500 million, counting affiliates. What does a company-level revenue threshold address?
o: Company resources available to bear compliance duties
Dangerous capability of each model the developer trains
Training activity physically carried out within California
Company age, with startups exempt for their first five years
ow: Revenue measures company resources imperfectly; it does not directly measure a model's dangerous capabilities.
The test counts total gross revenues, not in-state activity.
No age test is involved; smaller firms fall out because of the dollar figure itself.
keys: company resources to bear heavier duties
items.x: SB 53 separates model coverage from company resources: its compute definition identifies frontier models, while its revenue test identifies large frontier developers. Its update criteria explicitly seek to keep the latter category focused on well-resourced firms.

items.p: A drafter is choosing between defining covered models by training compute (over 10^26 operations) or by capability (models that could give serious help building weapons). What is the main tradeoff?
o: Compute is easier to check early; capability targets behavior more directly
Compute measures risk precisely; capability is less informative
Compute thresholds freeze; capability definitions update themselves
Compute can cover closed models; capability can cover only open models
ow: Compute is an imperfect proxy, and capability scores need not be publicly available.
Both kinds of line need an update mechanism (next lesson); neither updates itself.
Capability tests can apply to any model; outside testing is a separate access question.
keys: compute is easier to measure early
capability more directly concerns behavior and risk
items.x: Heim and Koessler argue that training compute is useful as an early, externally checkable filter, while acknowledging its imperfect link to risk. Hooker argues that changes in algorithms and hardware can undermine such thresholds; a drafter must decide how coverage can be evidenced before duties attach.

items.p: The AI Kill Switch Act covers AI built with compute 'the cost of which would exceed $100,000,000 at the prevailing market price of cloud computing in the United States, as determined by the Secretary.' What does the 'prevailing market price' wording guard against?
o: Citing a lower actual cost from discounts or owned chips
Inflation pushing every model over the line, since the dollar figure would otherwise climb every year
Foreign developers escaping coverage, since only US cloud prices can measure their compute
Courts second-guessing DHS, since a published market price can't be challenged in court
ow: A market-price benchmark standardizes valuation; it does not itself adjust the $100 million amount for inflation.
The wording values everyone's compute the same way; it isn't aimed at foreign developers.
'As determined by the Secretary' gives DHS the calculation, but nothing in the text bars review of it.
keys: values compute at market price, not the developer's actual cost
stops gaming through owned hardware or discounts
items.x: The introduced Kill Switch bill values compute using a US cloud-market benchmark rather than each developer's actual bill. Falling compute prices raise the amount of compute a fixed dollar amount buys; how many models then qualify also depends on training scale and efficiency.

items.p: A bill defines a frontier model by 'high levels of performance' at dangerous tasks, including what it 'could be modified to exhibit'. What uncertainty should a drafter resolve before imposing pre-release duties?
