items.answer: How to determine coverage before release: specify the relevant tasks, testing conditions and extent of modification. Otherwise developers and enforcers can disagree about whether the duty attaches.
keys: coverage must be determinable before the duty attaches
clarify tasks, testing conditions or allowed modifications
items.x: S. 5576's introduced definition uses this capability language. SB 53's review criteria emphasize advance notice and outside verifiability; those are useful design goals for a capability test as well as a compute test.

choice.p: A bill defines a frontier model by 'high levels of performance' at dangerous tasks, including what it 'could be modified to exhibit'. What uncertainty should a drafter resolve before imposing pre-release duties?
o: Which tests and modifications establish coverage before duties attach
It covers only models above 10^26 operations, missing smaller capable ones
It exempts open-weight models, which can't be modified after release
It makes every AI model frontier, since any model can be fine-tuned
ow: The quoted definition uses capability language, with no compute cutoff in that test.
Open-weight models are easy to modify, so 'could be modified' points the other way.
'High levels of performance at tasks that pose a serious risk' still limits it; the problem is uncertainty, not universality.

items.p: SB 53's 'large frontier developer' test counts revenue 'together with its affiliates'. What could happen without those words?
o: A group could keep each company under the line by splitting into separate subsidiaries
A foreign parent company would be counted twice, once directly and once through its US branch
Only revenue earned in California would count, pushing national companies below the line
Every investor holding a stake in a developer would become a frontier developer itself
ow: The affiliate language requires aggregation; how to avoid double counting still depends on how revenue is calculated.
The test has no California limit with or without the affiliate words.
Affiliates are tied by control; a passive investor isn't swept in by these words.
keys: aggregation stops splitting into subsidiaries to stay under the line
items.x: Aggregation limits avoidance through corporate structure. SB 53 covers direct control, indirect control and common control; the introduced FRONTIER bill uses different wording, creating a useful question about what an affiliate definition reaches.

items.p: Order the EU AI Act's classification steps when a provider knows a general-purpose model will exceed 10^25 training FLOP and contests systemic-risk status.
items: The provider knows the model meets or will meet the compute condition
Within two weeks, it notifies the Commission and submits its exceptional rebuttal
The Commission decides whether to accept the substantiated rebuttal
If classified as systemic-risk, the model is included in the published list
items.x: Articles 51 and 52 create a presumption with a rebuttal route, rather than an irrebuttable compute cutoff. Notification can be due before training finishes, once the provider knows the condition will be met.

items.p: Match each law or introduced bill to its mechanism for changing coverage.
pairs: An agency recommends updates; the Legislature must amend the law
The Under Secretary may raise the lines by regulation, but not lower them
DHS must update the definitions by rule every year
A new definition takes effect only once a joint resolution approving it is enacted
items.x: Check who moves the line, whether it can move up or down, and which procedure is required. FRONTIER permits increases; this leaves a different response to more efficient dangerous models than a power expressly allowing decreases.

items.p: S. 2938 lets the Energy Secretary propose a new definition of 'advanced artificial intelligence system', but it takes effect only once 'a joint resolution approving the rule is enacted into law.' What does that mean in practice?
o: A new law approving the definition must be enacted first
The definition starts after 60 days without an objection
The House approves the change without Senate action
The definition starts now and awaits renewal a year later
ow: This bill requires affirmative enactment; silence leaves the old definition in place.
A joint resolution must pass both chambers and go to the President, like a bill.
Nothing takes effect until the approval is enacted.
keys: joint resolution must be enacted
both chambers and presentment, with usual constitutional enactment routes
items.x: The introduced S. 2938 requires a new definition to win enactment of a joint resolution. That requires both chambers and presentment to the President, with the usual constitutional alternatives to signature; congressional silence does not approve the definition.

items.p: A bill says a regulation changing its coverage thresholds 'shall take effect not earlier than 180 days after publication in final form and shall apply only with respect to obligations arising on or after its effective date.' Why write both halves?
items.answer: The 180 days gives developers notice and time to prepare for new duties, and the prospective rule means a change can't turn past conduct into a violation. Together they let the agency move the line without surprising anyone.
keys: lead time to prepare
no retroactive application to past conduct
items.x: The introduced FRONTIER text separates preparation time from prospective application. APA section 553 generally provides 30 days between publication and effect for substantive rules, subject to exceptions; Congress can specify a longer period.

choice.p: Why delay threshold changes 180 days and apply them only to obligations arising after they take effect?
o: To give notice and time to prepare, and to keep changes from reaching back
To give Congress a special 180-day window to veto each change
Because the APA forbids any rule from taking effect within six months
To give developers time to sue before the change can be enforced
ow: The clause creates no congressional veto; Congress always has the Congressional Review Act.
The APA's general minimum is 30 days, with exceptions; this clause chose a longer delay.
Challenges are possible anyway; the delay is about preparation.

units.title: Triggers and standards
units.desc: How bills say when a duty or power kicks in: bright-line rules versus judgment standards, the numbers and qualifiers inside 'catastrophic', and what open words like 'imminent' leave to others.

items.p: A draft bars deployment that creates an 'unreasonable risk of critical harm'. It gives no numeric risk cutoff. Who would give that standard concrete meaning in a contested enforcement case?
o: Enforcers and courts applying it to the facts
The developer alone through its published safety framework
The findings through a binding cutoff not given in the text
CBO through its calculation of the program's expected losses
ow: A developer's framework may supply evidence, but it does not control the legal standard.
The hypothetical supplies no numeric cutoff in findings or elsewhere.
CBO estimates budget effects; it does not adjudicate a deployment standard.
keys: reasonableness is a standard applied by enforcers and courts
items.x: Standards such as reasonableness need interpretation in context. They can accommodate varied cases, while a precise deadline settles more of the answer in advance; neither approach eliminates all uncertainty.

items.p: One draft says incidents must be reported 'within 72 hours'; another says 'promptly'. In the rules-versus-standards terms legal scholars use, what's the tradeoff?
o: The deadline fixes more in advance; 'promptly' requires contextual judgment
The number gives more discretion than the word promptly
Promptly is unenforceable without a statutory number
Courts interpret both as the same 72-hour deadline
ow: It's the reverse: a number leaves little discretion, a standard leaves a lot.
Courts enforce standards like 'promptly' and 'reasonable' all the time, deciding their meaning case by case.
There's no default number; a court would decide what 'promptly' meant on the facts.
keys: deadline fixes more content in advance
promptly requires contextual judgment
items.x: Kaplow distinguishes rules whose content is settled in advance from standards whose content is worked out later. Precision can improve predictability but requires design choices, such as when the 72-hour clock starts; a short number alone does not settle that question.

items.p: SB 53 bans materially false or misleading statements about catastrophic risk, but the ban 'does not apply to a statement that was made in good faith and was reasonable under the circumstances.' A lab honestly overstates its testing after a careless review. Is it protected?
keys: two conditions: good faith AND reasonable under the circumstances
honest but careless may not qualify
items.x: SB 53 joins good faith and reasonableness with 'and', so both conditions must be met. This is an exception to its false-statement prohibition, not a general immunity from other duties.
items.answer: Not necessarily. Good faith and reasonableness are separate conditions; an honest statement based on a careless review may fail the reasonableness condition.

o: Not necessarily: it must be both honest and reasonable, and a careless review may fail the second
Yes: any honest statement is protected, because the exception turns only on what the lab intended
No: the exception covers only statements the lab corrects within 30 days
Yes, as long as its outside auditor approved the statement before it was published
ow: The text joins two tests with 'and'; honesty alone isn't enough.
SB 53 has no correction window; that idea resembles the Kill Switch Act's cure period (unit 5).
SB 53 has no auditor sign-off rule; the test is good faith plus reasonableness.

items.p: SB 53's catastrophic-risk definition excludes harm 'caused by a frontier model in combination with other software if the frontier model did not materially contribute to the harm.' What does this exclusion do?
o: Excludes combined-software harm when the model made no material contribution
Exempts AI agents altogether, since agents always run inside other software to do anything
Shifts the reporting duty to the other software's vendor whenever several tools were involved
Excludes any harm involving open-source code, which the law treats as 'other software'
ow: Agents count when the model materially contributes; the test is the model's role, not the setup.
It assigns no duty to anyone else; it narrows what counts as the developer's catastrophic risk.
'Other software' isn't limited to open source, and the test is whether the model materially contributed.
keys: excludes combined-software harm without model material contribution
items.x: The material-contribution test requires a meaningful causal role for the model, even when other software is involved. Mere presence in a software stack does not settle the question, and the statute gives no numeric percentage for materiality.

items.p: SB 53's catastrophic-risk definition concerns the risk of more than 50 deaths or serious injuries, or over $1 billion in property loss, from a single incident and specified AI conduct. What does 'single incident' prevent?
items.answer: Adding expected or actual harm across unrelated incidents to satisfy this severity threshold. Several separate incidents each threatening 40 deaths do not cross the people threshold just because their totals exceed 50.
keys: prevents aggregation across unrelated incidents
items.x: This defines a risk category, so harm need not already have happened. The separate critical-safety-incident definition determines which events must be reported; do not collapse a risk threshold into a completed-harm requirement.

choice.p: What does 'arising from a single incident' keep out of SB 53's definition of catastrophic risk?
o: Large totals of harm built up from many separate, smaller events
Incidents involving more than one AI model at the same time
Harm caused by a model's users rather than by the model itself
Incidents that happen outside California's borders
ow: Nothing requires a single model; the limit is on adding up separate incidents.
Misuse can count: weapons help to users is one listed pathway.
The definition has no territorial limit.

items.p: Match each law or introduced bill to one distinct event covered by its incident definition.
pairs: Weight theft or loss of control counts only if it causes death or bodily injury
Any unauthorized access to or theft of weights counts, with no harm needed
Includes unintended conduct killing 10 people or causing $100 million in damage, outside red-teaming
Any event that materially increases the risk of endangering life, health or property
items.x: Compare individual branches of each definition before judging its breadth. SB 53 requires injury for its weight-theft and loss-of-control branches, but its deceptive-monitoring branch can qualify without completed injury.

items.p: S. 5576 defines a safety incident by an event that 'materially increases the risk' of endangering life, health, property or the environment. What tradeoff does this create?
o: It catches near misses before anyone is hurt, at the cost of a vaguer line labs must judge themselves
It narrows reporting to true disasters, at the cost of missing incidents where people are only injured
It makes reporting fully objective, at the cost of needing a numeric threshold the agency must set
It removes duties for internal testing, at the cost of more paperwork for deployed systems
ow: It's broader, not narrower: no harm at all is needed.
'Materially increases the risk' is a judgment, not an objective test, and the bill sets no number.
The definition says nothing about testing; it reaches any event that raises the risk.
keys: covers near misses before harm
less certain: 'materially increases the risk' needs judgment
items.x: The introduced bill can reach events before injury, while materiality and the underlying risk require interpretation. SB 53 also includes a specific category without completed harm: deception that subverts developer controls and demonstrates materially increased catastrophic risk.

items.p: A bill defines 'imminent catastrophic risk' as 'a present or impending catastrophic risk'. What timing issue should a drafter clarify?
items.answer: How close in time the anticipated harm must be. Replacing imminent with impending supplies no concrete time horizon; the surrounding risk definition and procedures provide other limits.
keys: how close in time the harm must be
a near-synonym does not supply a concrete time horizon
items.x: The introduced FRONTIER definition uses this wording. Severity, likelihood, timing and the evidence required to act are separate design questions; a high severity threshold does not itself answer how imminent harm must be.

choice.p: A bill defines 'imminent catastrophic risk' as 'a present or impending catastrophic risk'. What timing issue should a drafter clarify?
o: How soon the anticipated harm must be
Whether the risk must involve frontier models, since 'catastrophic' is undefined
Whether courts may review orders, since 'impending' strips their jurisdiction
Nothing: 'impending' is a defined legal term meaning within 72 hours
ow: In FRONTIER 'catastrophic risk' is defined in detail and tied to frontier models.
Review comes from separate provisions, not from the word 'impending'.
No such defined meaning exists; 72 hours is an incident-reporting deadline elsewhere.

items.p: A bill lists numeric incident thresholds and, as an alternative, an AI model disregarding instructions in a 'high-stakes context'. What should a drafter check about the broad alternative?
o: Whether it reaches ordinary failures well below the numeric thresholds
Whether the numeric branches automatically narrow it
Whether combining numbers and words voids the definition
Whether every branch already requires completed harm
ow: These are alternative branches; the numerical branch does not automatically narrow every other branch.
Mixed definitions are common and valid; the issue is how much discretion one prong adds.
Only one prong mentions deaths or damage; the others need no harm at all.
keys: check whether broad alternative reaches failures below numeric thresholds
items.x: The introduced Kill Switch bill combines distinct alternatives. A broadly worded alternative may extend coverage far beyond the numeric branches; how far it reaches depends on the whole definition and the applicable procedures.

units.title: Delegation after Loper Bright
units.desc: Congress can't write every detail, so bills hand some to agencies. With Chevron gone, the words of a delegation decide how much room an agency gets, and vague grants of big powers invite challenge.

items.p: In 2025, the Supreme Court reviewed Congress's delegation for the FCC's universal-service program and its use of a private administrator. What did the Court hold?
o: Upheld the scheme: Congress had supplied an intelligible principle
Affirmed, adopting a stricter test that requires a numeric cap on any fee an agency sets
Affirmed on narrower grounds: the fee was a tax, and Congress can't delegate its taxing power
Dismissed the case, holding that fee disputes belong in the Court of Federal Claims
ow: The Court rejected a special rule requiring 'a numeric cap, a fixed rate, or the equivalent'.
The Court refused a stricter test for revenue-raising laws, relying on earlier cases that rejected it.
The Court decided the merits.
keys: upheld delegation under intelligible-principle test
items.x: FCC v. Consumers' Research upheld the scheme under the intelligible-principle test. Congress had identified the policy, beneficiaries and relevant considerations; the result does not guarantee that any broad AI delegation would survive.

items.p: Loper Bright (2024) names three ways a statute can give an agency discretion. Match each to an example from 2026 AI bills.
pairs: Expressly delegating what a term means
DHS 'shall update by rule the definitions' of covered entity and covered technology
The Under Secretary issues minimum requirements for frontier AI frameworks
The Under Secretary updates framework rules as 'necessary or appropriate'
items.x: Loper Bright recognizes that a statute may expressly confer discretion. Courts independently determine the delegation's boundaries and review whether the agency stayed within them; an ambiguity alone does not automatically confer policymaking power.

items.p: A staffer wants the Commerce Department to be able to redefine 'frontier model' as technology changes, and wants that power to hold up in court now that Chevron is gone. Which drafting choice does that best?
o: Say the term has the meaning given in the Secretary's regulations, and list criteria for them
Leave 'frontier model' undefined, so Commerce can fill the gap as the expert agency
Define the term in the findings section, so courts treat it as background rather than law
Add a rule of construction that the Act 'shall be broadly construed' to reach new technology
ow: Ambiguity alone no longer triggers Chevron deference; a court independently identifies whether Congress delegated discretion.
Findings don't delegate anything, and a definition there could clash with the operative text.
A broad-construction rule guides courts; it doesn't give Commerce power to redefine the term.
keys: express delegation of power to define the term
with criteria or factors to guide it
items.x: An express grant and guiding criteria make the intended discretion easier to identify. Loper Bright preserves statutory delegations, while rejecting automatic deference merely because statutory language is ambiguous.

items.p: Under the intelligible-principle test, which draft delegation is most exposed to challenge?
o: 'The Secretary may issue such rules regarding artificial intelligence as the Secretary deems appropriate'
'The Under Secretary may raise the compute threshold so that it covers models presenting catastrophic risk, considering hardware efficiency and cost'
'DHS shall update the covered-entity definition yearly, considering small-business burden and national security capabilities'
'The Secretary shall set incident-report formats, which shall include the date and the reason the incident qualifies'
ow: This tracks FRONTIER: a stated goal and listed factors bound the power.
This tracks the Kill Switch Act: a narrow task with stated factors.
A narrow technical task with set contents needs little guidance.
keys: no stated policy or boundaries
a grant over all of 'artificial intelligence' with no goal
items.x: A court reads the whole statute, so the vulnerability depends on surrounding limits too. Of these isolated clauses, the first supplies the least guidance about the policy and boundaries of the proposed authority.

items.p: A drafter wants Commerce to decide whether to license frontier AI labs, a choice with vast economic and political stakes. Why should the bill grant that power in plain terms rather than through a general clause like 'carry out the purposes of this Act'?
items.answer: Courts applying the major questions doctrine may demand clear congressional authorization for an agency power of vast economic and political significance. State the licensing power and its scope expressly to reduce an avoidable dispute about whether Congress granted it.
keys: major questions doctrine may require clear congressional authorization
state the significant power and its scope expressly
items.x: West Virginia v. EPA required clear authorization for the power claimed there. An explicit licensing grant addresses that interpretive problem; separate constitutional limits on delegation and other requirements still matter.

choice.p: Why should a bill grant a licensing power over frontier labs in plain terms, not through a general 'carry out this Act' clause?
o: Courts may demand clear authorization for so significant a power
General clauses lapse after five years unless Congress renews them
Licensing needs Senate approval of each license under the Constitution
Agencies may act only under clauses that name a specific dollar amount
ow: Statutes don't lapse by age; only those with sunset clauses do.
No constitutional rule requires Senate approval of licenses.
Many delegations name no dollar amount; the issue is how clearly the power is granted.

items.p: A new statute incorporates APA section 553 without extra restrictions. An agency wants binding incident-reporting rules without notice and comment. Assuming no other exemption applies, what must it do?
o: Find good cause that comment is impracticable, unnecessary or contrary to the public interest, and say so in the rule
Nothing extra, because section 553 lets agencies skip comment on any rule a new statute specifically requires them to write
Get Congress to pass a separate waiver, because only Congress can excuse an agency from notice and comment
Show that the rule is temporary, because rules lasting under a year are exempt from section 553
ow: A statutory mandate to write rules doesn't by itself excuse notice and comment.
Congress can waive it in a statute, but section 553 also has its own good-cause exception.
Section 553 has no exemption for short-lived rules.
keys: good cause finding
impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest
finding and reasons stated in the rule
items.x: Section 553(b) permits a documented good-cause exception to notice and comment. Making a substantive rule effective immediately also requires satisfying the distinct effective-date rules in section 553(d).

items.p: An agency misses an express statutory rulemaking deadline. A party has standing. What APA remedy may it seek?
items.answer: It may seek an order under APA section 706(1) compelling the discrete, legally required rulemaking action.
keys: APA 706(1) order compelling the discrete legally required rulemaking action
items.x: Norton v. Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance limits this remedy to discrete action legally required. A missed statutory deadline may support a claim; it does not entitle anyone to judicial management of the whole program.

choice.p: An agency misses an express statutory rulemaking deadline. A party has standing. What APA remedy may it seek?
o: An order compelling the discrete, legally required action
Ask the court to write the rules in the agency's place
Treat the statute as void, since its deadline has passed
Petition Congress, since courts can't review missed deadlines
ow: Courts can order the agency to act; they don't write its rules.
A missed deadline doesn't void the statute; the duty remains.
APA section 706(1) lets courts compel delayed action.

items.p: A bill expressly lets an agency set incident-report formats. The agency uses that clause to prohibit model releases. What question should a reviewing court ask first?
items.answer: Whether Congress delegated the power to prohibit releases. Authority over report formats does not itself supply that separate substantive power.
keys: identify the statutory scope of the delegation
report-format power does not by itself authorize release bans

o: Whether Congress delegated power to prohibit releases
Whether the agency is more technically expert than the reviewing judge
Whether the format rules were published at least 30 days earlier
Whether the report form asks about catastrophic risk
ow: Expertise can inform decisions within authority; it cannot create a missing statutory power.
Publication timing cannot expand the substantive grant.
A topic appearing on a form does not grant a power to ban releases.

items.x: Loper Bright directs courts to identify the boundaries of delegated authority. This is separate from whether the agency followed notice-and-comment procedure or reached a sensible safety judgment.

units.title: Obligations and enforcement
units.desc: A duty is only as strong as its enforcement: who can sue, how penalties are sized, the safety valves that soften duties, and how bills protect whistleblowers and sensitive reports.

lessons.title: Who can enforce and for what

items.p: Match each law or bill to who can enforce it.
pairs: The California Attorney General brings civil penalty actions
Individuals or classes, alongside federal and state public enforcement
DHS assesses civil penalties after notice and an opportunity for hearing
The Commission may fine general-purpose model providers
items.x: Choose both the enforcer and the remedy. Agency assessment of a civil penalty, a public lawsuit and a private damages claim are distinct enforcement paths; creating one does not automatically create the others.

items.p: The introduced AI LEAD Act would let injured individuals or classes bring specified federal claims. What does a private right of action add compared with public enforcement alone?
items.answer: Eligible private claimants can enforce the specified legal right in court without waiting for a public official to sue. The statute must still specify or support the available claims and remedies.
keys: eligible private claimants can sue without waiting for public enforcement
items.x: The introduced AI LEAD Act specifies eligible claimants and remedies including damages and attorney fees. A private right of action alone does not guarantee a class action, a fee award or success on the merits.

choice.p: The introduced AI LEAD Act would let injured individuals or classes bring specified federal claims. What does a private right of action add compared with public enforcement alone?
o: Eligible private parties can sue without public enforcement
Attorneys general gain the power to seek criminal penalties
Developers must get a license before deploying covered products
Federal agencies gain the power to issue binding rules
ow: Criminal penalties come from separate provisions; a private right of action is a civil suit by private parties.
Licensing is a separate tool; a private right is about who can sue.
Rulemaking power is a delegation (unit 4), not an enforcement right.

items.p: An introduced federal bill would let opted-in state attorneys general sue, with federal notice, intervention and priority rules. What problem are those coordination clauses designed to reduce?
o: Duplicative or conflicting proceedings among public enforcers
State enforcement before a federal violation finding
Removal of cases from state court into federal court
Federal settlements made without state governments' consent
ow: States can sue once they opt in; no prior finding is required.
The suits arise under federal law; the clauses coordinate who sues, not which court.
It's the reverse: the federal action takes priority.
keys: reduce duplicative or conflicting public enforcement
items.x: FRONTIER pairs additional public enforcers with coordination procedures. These can reduce duplicative or conflicting proceedings without guaranteeing that officials will agree on every enforcement choice.

items.p: Article 101 of the EU AI Act caps certain fines at the higher of 3% of annual worldwide turnover or EUR 15 million. What does the turnover component change compared with a fixed monetary cap?
o: The cap scales with worldwide revenue
The maximum shrinks for the largest providers
The maximum becomes a mandatory fine in every case
The calculation counts revenue from EU sales alone
ow: For any firm with turnover above EUR 500 million, 3% exceeds EUR 15 million, so the cap rises.
The EU Court of Justice 'may cancel, reduce or increase the fine'.
The base is 'annual total worldwide turnover'.
keys: maximum can rise with worldwide revenue
items.x: The maximum scales with worldwide turnover, while the fixed amount governs where it is higher. A cap is not an automatic fine: Article 101 addresses intentional or negligent violations and requires consideration of relevant circumstances.

items.p: The AI Kill Switch Act says 'a de minimis violation ... or a technical defect' corrected within 30 days of discovery 'is not considered a violation.' What job does this clause do?
o: It spares firms penalties for small or technical lapses they fix quickly
It gives DHS 30 days to decide whether to bring a case before the violation expires
It excuses any company that reports its own violation, however serious the violation is
It delays the shutdown-capability duty until 30 days after the law is enacted
ow: It's about the company's fix, not a deadline for DHS.
Only de minimis violations or technical defects qualify, and only if corrected within 30 days.
The duty's timing comes from the rulemaking deadlines; this clause is a cure period.
keys: cure period for minor or technical violations
corrected within 30 days of discovery
items.x: The introduced Kill Switch bill contains a limited cure rule for small or technical defects. Contrast a content-equivalence rule: SB 53 lets a system card satisfy specified transparency-report requirements when it contains all the required information.

items.p: A draft says compliance 'creates no immunity, safe harbor, or presumption against liability under otherwise applicable state law'. What drafting issue does it address?
o: Whether meeting federal duties shields a developer from state liability
Whether the agency has enough staff to enforce the federal duties
Whether a company can challenge federal rules in a chosen court
Whether the federal duties apply before the agency issues rules
ow: Staffing and funding require separate implementation provisions.
Judicial review and venue require separate procedural provisions.
Effective dates and rulemaking dependencies determine when duties begin.
keys: compliance does not itself confer immunity from preserved state liability
items.x: Federal compliance and state liability are separate questions. A clause preserving liability clarifies one part of the relationship, but its interaction with any preemption provisions must also be checked.

items.p: An introduced whistleblower bill defines a 'covered individual' to include employees, former employees, contractors and former contractors. What does adding contractors change?
o: Worker status alone no longer excludes those contractors from coverage
Contractors receive protection even when no protected disclosure occurred
Contractors automatically win any retaliation claim against a client
Every customer using the company's AI gains employment protections
ow: Other elements, including protected conduct and retaliation, still apply.
Coverage is eligibility to invoke the law, not automatic success on the merits.
Customers are not contractors merely because they use a product.
keys: express coverage extends beyond employees to specified contractors
items.x: S. 1792 uses this inclusive worker definition. Coverage, protected conduct and remedies are separate parts of the drafting chain, just as model coverage alone did not establish an audit duty in unit 1.

items.p: Order the proposed S. 1792 route for a worker who uses the federal-court option after agency delay and requests a jury.
items: The worker alleges retaliation for protected conduct
The worker files a complaint with the Secretary of Labor
No final decision issues within 180 days, without delay caused by the worker's bad faith
The worker brings an action in the appropriate federal district court
If the case reaches trial on the eligible claim, the requested jury hears it
items.x: This is a conditional path in the introduced bill, not a promise every complaint reaches a jury. The bad-faith-delay condition matters: the worker cannot create the qualifying delay through their own bad faith.

items.p: SB 53 and FRONTIER let developers redact published reports to protect trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety or national security. What keeps that power from swallowing the duty to disclose?
o: Redactions must be justified and the material kept; FRONTIER also gives the regulator the full text
A court must approve each redaction before the developer is allowed to publish the report
Redactions are capped at a tenth of each report, with the exact cap set by regulation
Redacted passages are published automatically one year after the report comes out
ow: No court approval is required; the safeguards are justification, retention and regulator access.
Neither text caps redactions by length.
Neither text sets an automatic release date.
keys: describe and justify each redaction
retain the redacted information (five years)
FRONTIER: unredacted copy to the Under Secretary
items.x: SB 53 permits necessary redactions for specified protections, with justification to the extent permitted by those concerns and five-year retention of unredacted information. FRONTIER separately requires delivery of unredacted reports to its regulator; publication exceptions and regulator access should be drafted together.

units.title: Federalism and clause craft
units.desc: The clauses at the back of a bill: preemption (express, field and conflict), savings clauses, exclusive courts, severability and sunsets. Small words here decide what survives in court.

items.p: A federal auto-safety law barred state standards that differed from federal ones, but said compliance didn't exempt anyone 'from any liability under common law.' A driver sued Honda over a car with no airbag, which federal rules allowed. What did the Supreme Court hold in 2000?
o: Preempted anyway, because it conflicted with the federal goal of allowing a mix of restraints
The suit could go ahead, because the savings clause protects every common-law claim against carmakers
The suit was expressly preempted, because a jury verdict counts as a state safety standard
The suit could go ahead, because federal safety rules set only a floor that states may raise
ow: The savings clause defeated express preemption only; it didn't block implied conflict preemption.
The Court rejected express preemption, partly because of the savings clause.
The Court read the airbag rules as a deliberate choice to allow options, which a duty to install airbags would undo.
keys: suit preempted because of conflict with federal restraint-mix objective
items.x: Geier v. American Honda illustrates a limit of a general savings clause: the Court held this particular tort theory conflicted with the federal regulatory objective. Drafters preserving state claims should address the whole preemption scheme, including potential conflict preemption.

items.p: Match each kind of preemption to how it arises.
pairs: The statute's text says which state laws are displaced
Federal rules occupy a whole area, leaving no room for states
A party can't comply with both federal and state law
State law frustrates Congress's goals, such as a federal ceiling
items.x: Express preemption is the drafter's own choice; the other three are implied, which means courts infer them, as in Geier. CRS calls Congress's purpose the 'ultimate touchstone', and courts sometimes presume against displacing states' traditional powers.

items.p: A preemption clause reaches state laws 'relating to artificial intelligence'. What drafting concern does this phrase raise?
o: It may displace more state duties than intended
It reaches only state statutes expressly naming AI
House rules require a state-by-state list instead
It automatically creates invalid field preemption
ow: Courts may reach state rules that do not expressly name AI; wording and context matter.
No such rule exists; Congress uses 'relating to' clauses often.
The wording keeps it express preemption; the problem is breadth.
keys: may sweep beyond the intended state duties
items.x: CRS explains that courts interpret relational language in statutory context: it can sweep broadly, but its reach is not limitless. Naming the particular duties to displace and those to preserve gives courts more guidance than an unqualified subject label.

items.p: The AI LEAD Act says it 'supersedes State law only where State law conflicts' with it, and that nothing in it prevents states from enacting protections 'that are stronger'. What kind of preemption is this?
o: A floor: federal rules set the minimum, and states may go further
A ceiling: federal rules set the maximum, and stricter state laws are void
Field preemption: Congress occupies AI liability, leaving states no role
No preemption at all: conflicting state laws stay in force alongside it
ow: A ceiling would bar stronger state rules; this text expressly allows them.
Field preemption leaves no room; this text invites stronger state laws.
Conflicting state law is displaced; only stronger, non-conflicting law survives.
keys: floor preemption
conflicting state law displaced
stronger state protections allowed
items.x: The Landscape and Toolkit courses cover the politics of floors versus federal standards. The drafting point is that two sentences decide it: one on what is displaced, one saving what isn't.

items.p: SB 53 lets California's emergency office designate a federal incident-reporting standard that is 'substantially equivalent to, or stricter than' the state's. A developer that opts in is 'deemed in compliance'. How does this differ from federal preemption?
o: State law stays; meeting the federal standard counts, and failing it is a state violation
It works like preemption, except the state rather than Congress repeals the state's own rule
The state law lapses for every developer as soon as any federal standard is designated
Developers must meet both standards but send their reports only to the federal agency
ow: Nothing is repealed: the developer can revoke its election, and the office must revoke a designation that stops qualifying.
Only developers that declare their intent get the benefit, and only while the designation stands.
The point is to avoid double compliance: meeting the federal standard is enough.
keys: state law remains in force
federal compliance counts as state compliance
failing the federal standard is a state violation
items.x: SB 53 offers an elected path to compliance using a designated federal reporting standard; California's duty and enforcement remain. The designation must meet statutory conditions, so this is a specified substitution mechanism rather than a repeal of state law.

items.p: Political consultants challenged a 2015 exception letting robocalls collect federal debts while political robocalls stayed banned. They asked the Supreme Court to strike the whole 1991 robocall ban. What happened in 2020?
o: Only the debt exception fell, so political robocalls to cell phones stayed banned
The Court struck the whole ban, since the exception showed Congress didn't really need it
The Court upheld both, since collecting federal debts is a compelling government interest
The Court sent the law back to Congress to choose which part to keep
ow: Seven justices applied severability principles and cut only the 2015 exception.
Six justices found the exception violated the First Amendment.
Courts don't send laws back to Congress; they decide what survives.
keys: debt exception severed
robocall restriction survived
items.x: Barr v. American Association of Political Consultants severed the government-debt exception while preserving the robocall restriction. The challengers did not obtain permission to make political robocalls; a successful constitutional claim does not by itself determine which statutory provisions survive.

items.p: A draft gives one named federal court exclusive jurisdiction over statutory challenges to specified agency orders. What does that clause principally decide?
o: Which court hears the covered challenges
Bar court challenges entirely, leaving the agency's own hearing as the last word on an order
Let a company file in any federal court it likes, as long as it meets the filing deadline
Send challenges directly to the Supreme Court, skipping the lower federal courts
ow: Choosing a court preserves a review route for covered claims; it does not itself eliminate review.
Exclusive jurisdiction channels the covered claims to the specified court, subject to the statute's scope and exceptions.
Each names a lower court; the Supreme Court can still review later.
keys: channels covered statutory challenges to a named court
items.x: The introduced FRONTIER and Kill Switch bills select different courts for reviewing orders. A venue or jurisdiction clause answers where review proceeds; separate provisions determine timing, available relief, standards of review and exceptions.

items.p: A bill trades preemption of state frontier AI laws for new federal safety duties. Supporters fear a court might strike the federal duties but leave preemption standing. What clause addresses that, and how?
items.answer: An express nonseverability clause can link the specified safety duties and preemption: if the duties are held invalid, the linked preemption provision loses effect too. Define precisely which invalidity triggers that result.
keys: nonseverability clause
links specified duties and preemption upon invalidation
items.x: Barr explains that Congress can specify nonseverability. Without an express link, survival depends on severability analysis; do not assume a political bargain will automatically rise or fall as a package.

choice.p: Which clause can make specified preemption provisions lose effect if linked federal safety duties are held invalid?
o: A nonseverability clause linking them
A severability clause covering the whole act
A savings clause for state common law claims
A sunset clause on the federal safety duties
ow: A severability clause does the reverse: it keeps the rest alive.
A savings clause protects some state law from preemption; it doesn't tie provisions' fates together.
A sunset ends provisions on a date; it doesn't respond to a court ruling.

items.p: A draft says its testing program terminates after seven years unless Congress renews it. What does that sunset change?
items.answer: The program ends on the stated date without renewal, making continuation require fresh legislative action. Congress can schedule an earlier review to inform that choice, but a sunset cannot guarantee Congress acts.
keys: program ends by default unless Congress renews it
items.x: The introduced AI Risk Evaluation Act has a seven-year program sunset. Check the object of the sunset: terminating a program, ending an authorization of appropriations and repealing every related duty can have different legal effects.

choice.p: What does adding a sunset clause change about a law?
o: The program ends by default unless renewed
It ends automatically if a court strikes any part of it
It lets the President end it early by proclamation
It must be renewed every year in an appropriations bill
ow: That describes nonseverability, not a sunset.
Some laws add early-termination options, but that's separate from a sunset.
A sunset sets its own date, often years away; it isn't tied to annual appropriations.

units.title: Who helps, and what slips through
units.desc: The offices that turn policy into text and price it (Legislative Counsel, CRS, CBO), and the errors that get past them: broken references, missing conforming changes and unchecked AI-drafted text.

items.p: Match each congressional support office to its main job on an AI bill.
pairs: Turns a member's policy into bill text, confidentially
Gives nonpartisan policy and legal analysis to members and staff
Estimates budget effects and the cost of mandates on companies
items.x: Bring counsel the intended policy and boundary cases, ask CRS for legal and policy analysis, and involve CBO early on budget effects. These tasks complement each other; an accurate cost estimate does not establish that the legal text implements the policy.

items.p: An office sends Legislative Counsel: 'Make powerful AI safe.' What addition would most help turn the request into workable bill text?
o: A concrete duty, the actors it reaches, and examples at the coverage boundary
A list of cosponsors, leaving the legal design entirely to counsel
A demand for the shortest possible bill, leaving implementation unspecified
A purpose statement alone, asking counsel to infer every policy choice
ow: Cosponsors matter politically; they do not resolve the substantive design.
Brevity cannot substitute for decisions about scope, administration, enforcement and timing.
A goal leaves multiple legal designs open; the office must specify its policy preferences.
keys: specify scope, duties and policy choices before requesting text
items.x: Legislative Counsel translates policy choices into effective language. Its pre-drafting questions ask about scope, administration, enforcement, timing and interaction with existing law.

items.p: A bill orders an agency to run a new AI oversight office, with no automatic funding and no dollar amount. Why might CBO estimate costs subject to appropriation?
o: New duties require resources even when the bill names no funding amount
Unnamed appropriations are automatically scored as zero cost
Regulatory implementation costs are outside CBO's responsibility
New duties without dollar amounts count as direct spending
ow: CBO says it estimates the cost of new requirements even when a bill authorizes no money.
CBO estimates federal budget effects of legislation; the implementing agency may provide information.
Duties paid for through future appropriations are spending subject to appropriation, not direct spending.
keys: new duties require implementation resources, even without a specified funding amount
items.x: CBO estimates resources needed to carry out new requirements even when authorizing text names no amount. Actual funding can still depend on a later appropriation; estimated cost and money made available are different concepts.

items.p: CBO's estimate of a bill requiring frontier developers to publish safety frameworks and report incidents would include a section on mandates. Why?
o: A 1995 law makes CBO flag enforceable duties on companies and whether their costs pass a threshold
CBO must certify that companies can afford new duties before a bill can be considered on the floor
Duties on private companies count as federal spending, so CBO adds their costs to the deficit
UMRA treats frontier developers as federal contractors, so their new duties count as contract terms
ow: CBO reports costs; it doesn't certify affordability or decide floor action.
Private compliance costs aren't federal spending; CBO reports them separately as mandate costs.
UMRA covers duties on any private-sector entity; contracting has nothing to do with it.
keys: Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
enforceable duties on the private sector
compare costs with an inflation-adjusted threshold
items.x: UMRA requires CBO to assess covered enforceable duties on governments and the private sector, using inflation-adjusted cost thresholds. Private compliance costs are reported separately from federal budget effects; exceptions and the stage of congressional action matter.

lessons.title: Reading text in its legal context

items.p: The Affordable Care Act gave tax credits for insurance bought on 'an Exchange established by the State.' Challengers said that barred credits where the federal government ran the Exchange. How did the Supreme Court rule in 2015?
o: Federal Exchanges qualified: in context the phrase was ambiguous, and the narrow reading would wreck the Act
Credits were limited to state-run Exchanges, since the text was plain and only Congress can fix its own drafting errors
The IRS's reading won under Chevron deference, because the phrase was ambiguous and the IRS had chosen a reasonable meaning
The case was dismissed, since only states, not individuals, could challenge how the tax credits were being paid out
ow: The Court found the phrase ambiguous in context and read it to fit the Act's design.
The Court declined Chevron: a question of 'deep economic and political significance' wasn't one Congress would leave to the IRS.
The Court decided the merits.
keys: credits available for insurance on federal Exchanges
items.x: King v. Burwell held that the ACA's tax credits extended to insurance bought on federally established Exchanges. The Court read the phrase in its statutory context rather than applying Chevron deference; the dissent disagreed, showing why drafters should not rely on courts to repair a contested design.

items.p: The introduced FRONTIER bill refers to 'subsection (l) of section 2', but section 2 numbers its definitions. What drafting error should be fixed before introduction?
items.answer: A broken cross-reference. The apparent target is paragraph (12), the frontier-model definition. Correct the pointer explicitly; whether a court would repair an enacted error depends on context and cannot be assumed.
keys: broken cross-reference to nonexistent subsection
items.x: The introduced bill's letter references track the positions of numbered definitions. Courts sometimes correct obvious drafting errors, as in United States National Bank of Oregon, but a drafter should fix the reference instead of depending on that possibility.

choice.p: FRONTIER's section 3 refers to 'subsection (l) of section 2', but section 2's definitions are numbered (1) to (22). What kind of error is this?
o: A broken cross-reference, apparently aimed at paragraph (12), frontier model
A missing conforming amendment to the table of contents of the U.S. Code
A circular definition, since frontier model is defined by reference to itself
An ambiguous list, since section 2 leaves out serial commas between items
ow: A conforming amendment updates other laws or tables to match; this is an internal pointer to nothing.
Frontier model is defined by compute, not by itself; the problem is the pointer.
Punctuation isn't the issue; the reference names a subsection that doesn't exist.

items.p: Besides adding a new section 2220F, the AI Kill Switch Act amends the Homeland Security Act's table of contents to list it. What kind of change is that, and why do such changes matter?
o: A conforming (here clerical) amendment, keeping related text and tables consistent
A savings clause, without which the older sections of the Homeland Security Act would be repealed
A rule of construction, without which courts would decline to give the new section any effect
A technical correction that takes effect only once DHS adopts it by rule after enactment
ow: Savings clauses protect other law from being displaced; a table-of-contents entry saves nothing.
Courts apply enacted text whether or not a table lists it; the table keeps the statute consistent and findable.
Amendments in an enacted bill are law at once; no agency adoption is needed.
keys: conforming or clerical amendment
keeps related provisions, tables and cross-references consistent
items.x: The introduced Kill Switch bill adds both a statutory section and a matching table-of-contents entry. House Legislative Counsel prepares comparative prints for reported amendments, helping reviewers inspect changes in their existing legal context.

items.p: An AI-assisted draft cites section 802(c), a definition in an existing statute. Before relying on it, what should the staffer verify?
o: That the provision exists, is current, and applies where the draft uses it
That another model repeats the same citation and interpretation
That the number looks consistent with neighboring section numbers
That the draft contains a source link alongside the quoted language
ow: A second model can reproduce the same error; check the underlying legal text.
Plausible numbering does not establish existence, meaning or scope.
A link helps locate a source but does not prove that it supports the draft.
keys: verify existence, current wording and applicable scope against legal text
items.x: Read referenced provisions in context, including definitions and amendments. Then trace every internal pointer again after renumbering; the introduced FRONTIER bill illustrates how a seemingly small reference error can survive into public text.

units.title: Spot the drafting problem
units.desc: Mixed practice: short excerpts and paired clauses that pull together definitions, triggers, delegation, enforcement and federalism. Pick the better clause or name what's wrong.

items.p: A draft says violators 'shall be fined not less than $1,000,000 per day'. What does this amount language establish?
items.answer: A daily minimum of $1 million, with no maximum stated in that clause. It does not by itself identify the enforcer or the penalty procedure.
keys: minimum of $1 million per day
no maximum stated in the clause
items.x: The introduced S. 2938 uses this wording. Compare the introduced Kill Switch bill's explicit civil-penalty caps, notice-and-hearing procedure and listed assessment factors; penalty amount and penalty machinery need separate drafting.

o: At least $1 million per day, no stated cap
A reducible daily cap of $1 million
One total fine of $1 million
A criminal fine plus imprisonment
ow: A maximum would use language such as not more than.
Per day makes duration affect the amount; it is not a single total.
Amount language alone does not establish criminal procedure or imprisonment.

items.p: A draft defines 'covered developer' as 'a person that develops a covered model' and 'covered model' as 'an AI model developed by a covered developer.' What's wrong?
o: The definitions are circular, so neither says what's actually covered
The definitions use 'means' where they should use 'includes'
The definitions belong in the findings, not in the definitions section
Nothing, as long as an agency later writes rules defining both terms
ow: Changing the introductory verb would not supply an independent coverage condition.
Placement isn't the flaw; definitions belong in the definitions section.
A general hope that an agency will fix the text does not establish coverage or a delegated power to define it.
keys: circular definitions
no independent test (compute, revenue or capability) anchors coverage
items.x: Anchor at least one definition in an independently checkable condition. SB 53 anchors frontier-model coverage in training compute; model and developer definitions can then refer to one another without leaving the scope wholly circular.

items.p: A draft covers models trained above 10^26 operations but imposes reports only on developers above $500 million group revenue. A covered model's developer has $100 million group revenue. Under these clauses, what follows?
o: The model is covered, but this developer has no reporting duty
Model coverage automatically makes every developer subject to reports
The model is excluded because its developer falls below the revenue line
The developer must report because the two thresholds are alternatives
ow: Coverage and the operative duty use distinct conditions; the developer does not meet the revenue condition.
A company-level exception to a duty does not rewrite the model definition.
The scenario places one condition on coverage and a second on the duty; it does not join them with or.
keys: model coverage does not itself impose this reporting duty
developer fails the stated revenue condition
items.x: Trace the whole chain: model definition, regulated person, operative duty, exceptions and timing. If the sponsor wants every frontier developer to report, the duty must say so; changing only the model definition will not accomplish that.

items.p: One draft definition says 'deploy includes release, sale, or licensing, but is not limited to these'; another says 'development includes training and fine-tuning'. What ambiguity can this inconsistent wording invite?
o: 'Not limited to' in one place suggests the plain 'includes' lists are closed
'Includes' always makes a closed list unless it's followed by 'but is not limited to'
Definitions can't mention fine-tuning unless a compute threshold is attached to it
Mixing styles makes both definitions void for vagueness under the Constitution
ow: Legislative Counsel says the reverse: 'includes' is already open, which is why the extra words are redundant.
Definitions can list activities freely; thresholds are a separate choice.
Inconsistent style doesn't void a definition; the risk is an unintended reading.
keys: 'includes' is already non-exhaustive
using 'but is not limited to' selectively implies the others are limited
items.x: House Legislative Counsel advises that 'includes' is already nonexhaustive. Selectively adding 'not limited to' may invite an unintended contrast between otherwise open lists; consistent language reduces that avoidable argument.

items.p: A governor wants a federal frontier AI law to displace state catastrophic-risk reporting rules but leave her state's chatbot child-safety law alone. Which clause fits best?
o: Name the reporting duties displaced and expressly preserve child-safety law
Displace any state law 'relating to artificial intelligence', to keep the national rules simple and uniform
Displace nothing in the text, and let courts sort out case by case which state laws actually conflict
Displace all state AI laws, while letting each governor apply to the agency for a yearly waiver
ow: 'Relating to' would likely sweep in the chatbot law (unit 6).
Implied preemption depends on context; silence gives less guidance about the sponsor's intended boundary.
A waiver scheme makes the child-safety law depend on yearly federal approval, the opposite of leaving it alone.
keys: narrow, express preemption of named duties
an explicit savings clause for the law to protect
items.x: Draft a targeted preemption clause and an express preservation clause, then check whether implied conflict preemption could undermine the intended protection. Geier illustrates why the survival of state claims can depend on the whole statutory and regulatory design.

items.p: A draft preempts state reporting laws on enactment, while its federal reporting duty starts after rulemaking. What timing change best avoids a period with neither reporting duty?
items.answer: Make preemption contingent on the federal reporting duty becoming operative, rather than starting it immediately at enactment.
keys: delay preemption until federal reporting duty becomes operative
items.x: Coordinate the trigger with the actual start of federal duties, including any compliance lead time after final rules. An agency deadline alone does not ensure that replacement rules will exist by then.

choice.p: A bill's preemption starts on enactment, but its federal duties start only after rulemaking. Which device closes the gap?
o: Start preemption when the federal reporting duty becomes operative
Add a severability clause covering the preemption section
Add a sunset so that preemption ends after five years
Require the agency to finish its rules within 30 days
ow: Severability matters only if a court strikes something; it doesn't change timing.
A sunset limits how long preemption lasts, not when it starts.
A short deadline doesn't guarantee rules exist; agencies miss deadlines (unit 4).

items.p: Two drafts allow compute-threshold updates. A: 'The Administrator may revise it as appropriate.' B states a risk goal, lists efficiency and cost factors, requires periodic review, and gives advance notice. Why does B give clearer guidance?
o: It states what should guide updates and when changes can bind firms
It avoids notice and comment, since listed factors replace the need for public input
It lets the agency move faster, since courts can't review decisions based on listed factors
It makes the threshold permanent, since a review cycle bars any change between reviews
ow: Listed factors don't replace the APA; FRONTIER, which reads like draft B, also requires section 553 rulemaking.
Courts can review B's decisions; the factors give them something to review against.
A review cycle sets how often the agency must look; it doesn't freeze the threshold.
keys: goal and factors supply an intelligible principle and boundaries
review cycle and notice add predictability
items.x: Draft B combines substantive boundaries with procedural safeguards, echoing features of the introduced FRONTIER bill. Courts still interpret the scope of the delegated power and review whether the agency applied it lawfully; drafting clarity does not immunize a rule from review.

items.p: A bill requires its first report by January 1, 2028. An office plans to reuse the text in a later Congress. What should a drafter check?
o: Fixed dates that may be too soon or already past; dates tied to enactment avoid this
The bill number, which must stay the same across Congresses for its deadlines to keep their meaning
Nothing, since Legislative Counsel automatically updates every date when a bill is reintroduced
The cosponsor list, since a bill's deadlines lapse unless all original cosponsors sign on again
ow: Bills get new numbers each Congress; numbering has nothing to do with deadlines.
Reintroduced text is whatever the office submits; date updates have to be asked for and checked.
Cosponsorship has no effect on a bill's text.
keys: check whether the fixed deadline is stale or leaves inadequate lead time
items.x: The introduced FRONTIER bill mixes a fixed January 2028 reporting date with duties tied to enactment. Fixed dates may be appropriate, but reuse can make them too short or already past; relative deadlines preserve the intended lead time more reliably.

drafting.description: Build an AI bill from definitions and coverage to duties, enforcement, legal review and implementation.
caveat: Revised October 23, 2026. Federal bills are drafting examples from their cited introduced versions, not a claim that those provisions are law. Legal interpretation is simplified; check the current text and its context. AI reviewed; no person has reviewed it.
drafting.meta: 8 units | AI reviewed; no human review

timelines.name: AI Timelines and Forecasting

units.title: The map: milestones and forecasts
units.desc: Define the event, inspect its evidence and assumptions, then use a probability distribution to guide a decision.

items.p: Match each part of an AI timeline forecast to the question it should answer.
pairs: What observable capability or impact counts as arrival?
Which measurements or observations inform the forecast?
Which future growth rates or constraints are being supposed?
How much uncertainty remains over arrival times?
items.x: A date becomes useful when the event and assumptions are clear. Later units examine compute and feedback loops, check measurements, practice probability scoring and apply forecasts to policy.

items.p: In a 2023 AI-researcher survey, even odds for machines outperforming humans at every task were put at 2047. Was the forecast for fully automatable occupations similar?
o: No: it was decades later, around 2116
Yes: it was the same year, because tasks and jobs coincide
No: it was much earlier, around 2035
Yes: the gap was just a few months
ow: An occupation bundles tasks and conditions, and respondents produced very different forecasts.
The occupation forecast was later, rather than earlier.
The aggregate dates differed by roughly seven decades.
keys: the occupation forecast was much later, around 2116
items.x: Grace and colleagues reported 2047 and 2116 for the two questions. This shows sensitivity to wording and milestones; it does not establish that identical events were forecast differently. Check definitions before treating a gap as disagreement about the pace of progress.

items.p: Why is the AI Futures Project's Automated Coder milestone useful for studying an AI research feedback loop?
o: It could speed up the development of better AI
Coding automation would establish every occupation is automatable
It would remove the need to run compute-intensive experiments
It would establish a common definition of AGI accepted by labs
ow: A coding milestone is narrower than automating every occupation.
Experiments and other research inputs can remain bottlenecks.
This is one group's milestone, rather than a shared industry standard.
keys: It could speed up the development of better AI
items.x: The group defines Automated Coder through a leading company preferring AI coding access over its human software engineers. That makes the target economically motivated, though judging when it is met still requires assumptions. Coding is one part of AI R&D.

items.p: Why should a forecast for passing a bundle of AI tests be kept separate from a forecast for automating most jobs?
items.answer: Test performance and job automation are different events. Jobs also require reliability, integration and performance on tasks the tests may omit.
keys: test performance differs from job automation

choice.p: Why should a forecast for passing a bundle of AI tests be kept separate from a forecast for automating most jobs?
o: Passing tests can precede or lag reliable automation of whole jobs
Test scores directly measure the share of jobs already automated
Job automation follows as soon as test scores exceed a human average
Different events become equivalent when they share an AGI label
ow: Benchmarks sample tasks and need not measure end-to-end job performance.
An average score does not establish reliability across all tasks in a job.
A label does not align different resolution criteria.

items.x: This distinction explains part of the survey gap and the disagreements covered later. The joint AI 2027 and AI as Normal Technology statement separates high benchmark scores from robust real-world performance.

items.p: A forecast assigns 50% to AGI by 2050, conditional on AGI arriving by 2100. Which additional probability is needed to obtain its unconditional chance of AGI by 2050?
o: Its probability of AGI arriving by 2100
Its most likely arrival year before 2100
Its average arrival year conditional on AGI by 2100
Its probability of job automation after AGI arrives
ow: A most likely year does not supply the probability of the conditioning event.
A conditional average also omits how likely arrival by 2100 is.
Job automation is a different event, so that probability does not complete this calculation.
keys: probability of AGI arrival by 2100, the conditioning event
items.x: For one consistent forecast, the unconditional chance here is 0.5 times its probability of arrival by 2100. LEAP reports timing percentiles conditional on panel agreement before 2100. Preserve that condition in a briefing, and do not combine aggregate statistics from different participants as if they were one forecast.

items.p: Match each forecasting source to the kind of evidence it supplies.
pairs: Explicit models and scenarios with judgment-based inputs
Datasets and analyses of inputs and measured capabilities
Task evaluations and studies of effects on work
Surveys of researchers about future milestones
A community aggregation of forecasters' predictions
items.x: These sources are not independent votes: a model may use Epoch data and METR measurements, while community forecasters read the same research. Agreement between sources can therefore partly reflect shared evidence.

items.p: AI 2027's authors say 2027 was their most likely year at publication, while their median dates were later. How can both be true?
o: A long tail can put half the probability after the most likely year
The median is the year with the greatest probability of arrival
The most likely year must contain more than half the probability
The median is the arithmetic average of the authors' scenario dates
ow: The median divides cumulative probability in half; the mode identifies a peak.
A modal year can have a small probability when probability is spread across many years.
A median is a percentile of a distribution, rather than an average of scenario dates.
keys: A long tail can put half the probability after the most likely year
items.x: The authors clarified that they were uncertain and had never confidently predicted a specific year. A vivid scenario can depict one plausible path without representing the median of a broad distribution.

items.p: Two forecasters use the same timeline model and get medians several years apart. What would most help explain their disagreement?
o: Compare their uncertain input values and sensitivity tests
Average the dates and report that as the model's official forecast
Prefer the earlier date because it gives more preparation time
Discard both results because a model should return a shared date
ow: An average can hide the assumptions responsible for the gap.
Preparation needs do not establish which forecast is better supported.
A transparent model can show how reasonable input differences change conclusions.
keys: Compare their uncertain input values and sensitivity tests
items.x: The AI Futures Model includes judgment-based parameters as well as measured inputs. Its authors emphasize that users can change these values. Separating sensitivity to assumptions from new empirical evidence makes updates easier to interpret.

items.p: Why can a lab leader's forecast be informative while still needing independent checks?
items.answer: Leaders may see unreleased models and internal evidence, while commercial interests and self-defined milestones can influence their public interpretation.
keys: access to internal evidence
incentives and milestone definitions justify outside checks

choice.p: Why can a lab leader's forecast be informative while still needing independent checks?
o: Internal access adds information; incentives still warrant outside checks
Internal access makes the forecast an independent assessment of the whole industry
Commercial incentives make every public forecast devoid of useful information
A public date becomes reliable once a lab repeats it across several announcements
ow: A lab's own assessment is not independent of that lab.
Biased or interested sources can still possess relevant information.
Repetition does not validate the underlying evidence or event definition.

items.x: OpenAI and Anthropic publish measurements of their own research automation, while discussing measurement limits. Give the evidence appropriate weight and ask what an outside assessment could corroborate.

items.p: The AI Futures Project dates an arrival conditional on development going as fast as technically feasible. What would be wrong with quoting it as an unconditional deployment date?
o: It omits possible policy, organizational or other delays
Technical feasibility means the system is already available to the public
A conditional date describes a worst case with negligible probability
The condition changes the milestone from coding to robot manufacturing
ow: Feasibility forecasts concern what could be built under assumptions, rather than public availability.
Conditional forecasts can have broad distributions; they are not inherently worst cases.
The condition changes circumstances, rather than necessarily changing the capability target.
keys: It omits possible policy, organizational or other delays
items.x: The August 2026 update explicitly states its technical-feasibility condition. Compare forecasts under similar conditions before interpreting different dates as a substantive disagreement.

units.title: Inputs: compute, algorithms and constraints
units.desc: Combine inputs carefully, then ask where physical, data or financial constraints could change their growth.

items.p: Suppose training compute grows 5x in a year and algorithms use one-third as much compute for the same performance. In a simple effective-compute model, what is the combined gain?
o: 15x: multiply compute by the efficiency gain
8x: add the physical and algorithmic gains
5x: efficiency changes cost without changing capability
3x: whichever input grows less sets the combined gain
ow: Multiplicative gains combine by multiplication, rather than addition.
Efficiency can increase achievable performance with a fixed compute budget.
The simple model multiplies the inputs; a separate bottleneck would need to be specified.
keys: 15x: multiply compute by the efficiency gain
items.x: Effective compute expresses physical compute in units of an older method's efficiency. Epoch's historical pretraining study estimated an eight-month halving of compute needed for selected language-model performance levels; that does not establish the rate for all modern post-training.

items.p: A timeline model uses a historical pretraining-efficiency trend as the rate for all future AI software progress. What is the main concern?
o: The estimate may not transfer across methods, scales or tasks
Efficiency improvements reduce spending but cannot improve test performance
Historical algorithmic trends contain no information about future progress
A rate measured over several years must apply equally to later methods
ow: The effective-compute idea captures how efficiency can increase achievable performance.
Historical evidence can inform a forecast without fully determining it.
Transfer to new methods needs evidence and uncertainty.
keys: The estimate may not transfer across methods, scales or tasks
items.x: Anson Ho's February 2026 analysis emphasizes uncertainty in post-training progress and scale-dependent innovations. Estimates spanning different scopes are not interchangeable. Treat the software-growth rate as a major sensitivity test.

items.p: A lab has funding and chip orders, but cannot secure enough power for its new cluster. Which forecast assumption should a reviewer revisit first?
o: When its planned compute will actually become usable
Whether algorithms can improve efficiency on existing chips
Whether its benchmark scores measure the intended milestone
How a prediction market resolves disputes about model releases
ow: Algorithmic efficiency may matter, but the immediate constraint is usable physical capacity.
Benchmark validity is a separate forecast component.
Resolution procedures do not determine when this cluster can run.
keys: When its planned compute will actually become usable
items.x: Epoch's scaling analysis treats power and chip manufacturing as potential constraints. Planned capacity is a lead indicator, with uncertainty about completion and utilization. A technically possible scale-up is different from a completed one.

items.p: Why would a limit on available public human-written text fail to establish a hard stop for AI progress?
items.answer: Progress may also use synthetic data, other modalities and learning from environments, though their quality and usefulness must be demonstrated.
keys: other data sources and learning methods may help
substitutes need validation

choice.p: Why would a limit on available public human-written text fail to establish a hard stop for AI progress?
o: Other data and learning methods may help, with validation
Repeating the same text supplies the same information as equally much new text
More human writing necessarily appears fast enough to match frontier demand
A model stops benefiting from improved training data once it learns grammar
ow: Repetition and new information need not have equal value.
Future text supply need not keep pace with rapidly growing demand.
Data quality and task coverage can continue to matter.

items.x: Epoch's AI in 2030 analysis distinguishes scarcity of human-generated text from data limits overall. Synthetic data can be useful without being an unlimited replacement for fresh, reliable information.

items.p: A forecast assumes frontier investment keeps growing rapidly despite rising capital costs. Which evidence most directly tests its financial sustainability?
o: Revenue, financing capacity and expected investment returns
A benchmark leaderboard showing the highest score from any provider
A count of papers that use the phrase artificial general intelligence
The number of months until a model passes a fixed puzzle benchmark
ow: Capability results matter indirectly, but do not establish a return sufficient to finance spending.
Mentions in papers are not a measure of financing capacity.
A puzzle milestone alone does not establish investment returns.
keys: Revenue, financing capacity and expected investment returns
items.x: Epoch's August 2026 revenue analysis reported rapid growth while warning that growth could slow. Revenue run rate annualizes recent revenue; it is neither annual realized revenue nor profit. Financial constraints can bend a compute trend even when larger runs remain technically feasible.

units.title: The AI research feedback loop
units.desc: Distinguish the possibility of self-sustaining acceleration from measured coding help and overall research progress.

lessons.title: What would make the loop accelerate?

items.p: Anthropic told METR in early 2026 that AI gave substantial researcher productivity gains. What did Anthropic estimate for its overall pace of research progress?
o: An increase of less than 2x
An increase of more than 10x
No increase, because AI cannot contribute research
Exactly the same increase as its code-production rate
ow: The report gives a much smaller overall estimate.
The company reported some overall acceleration, rather than zero contribution.
Code production and overall research progress are different quantities.
keys: Anthropic estimated less than 2x overall acceleration
items.x: METR reports Anthropic's own estimate, rather than an independently measured treatment effect. Experiments, compute and other tasks can constrain how much faster research progresses. More productive researchers need not produce a proportional increase in overall progress.

items.p: Put one proposed AI research feedback cycle in order, starting with an existing AI assistant.
items: Use the existing AI to help develop a better research method
Train or configure an improved model using the method
Use the improved model to assist the next research cycle
