Gifts to a (c)(4) aren't deductible, though they are free of federal gift tax.

items.p: A donor asks her donor-advised fund to pay for two $500 tickets to a charity's gala, where she and her spouse will have dinner. What is the problem?
o: DAF grants that give the donor more than an incidental benefit are taxed, and tickets are one
None, because the gala benefits a 501(c)(3), which is exactly where DAF grants are meant to go
None, as long as she doesn't also deduct the value of the dinner on her own return
The charity owes the tax on the dinner's value, since it is the one that served the dinner
ow: Grants must also give the donor no personal benefit beyond an incidental one.
She took her deduction when she funded the DAF; the issue is the personal benefit, taxed at 125% of its value.
The tax falls on the donor who advised the grant (125% of the benefit) and on fund managers who knowingly agreed (10%); the charity owes none.
keys: DAF grants can't give the donor a more-than-incidental benefit
event tickets are such a benefit
items.x: Section 4967 taxes a donor 125% of a more-than-incidental benefit from a DAF grant, and fund managers who knowingly agree 10% (up to $10,000). In Notice 2017-73 the IRS said it views even a split, with the DAF paying only the deductible part of a ticket, as such a benefit; it also let a DAF pay a charity the donor pledged to if the sponsor doesn't mention the pledge and she claims no deduction. As of October 2026 no rules on these points had been proposed or finalized. The simple fix: buy the tickets personally.

items.p: A 501(c)(3) must show its annual Form 990 return to anyone who asks. What does the public copy reveal about its donors?
o: Gift amounts may appear, but donors' names and addresses are withheld
The names of everyone who gave $5,000 or more during the year
The names of everyone who gave more than $200, as for campaign committees
The names of its largest donors, listed with its officers in Part VII
ow: The charity reports its larger donors (generally $5,000 or more) to the IRS on Schedule B, but names and addresses are removed from public copies.
The $200 threshold applies to federal campaign committees and 527 political groups, not charities.
Part VII lists officers, directors and top-paid staff with their pay, which is public; it doesn't list donors.
keys: donor names and addresses are withheld from the public copy
larger donors (generally $5,000 or more) are reported to the IRS on Schedule B
items.x: Public charities list larger donors (generally $5,000 or more; many use a higher cutoff) on Schedule B for the IRS, but names and addresses stay off public copies. Private foundations and 527 political groups are exceptions: their donors are public. Since 2020, (c)(4)s don't report donor names to the IRS at all, though they must keep the records. In 2021 the Supreme Court struck down California's rule requiring charities to file their Schedule B donor lists with the state (Americans for Prosperity Foundation v. Bonta).

lessons.title: Receipts, disclosures and the 2026 tax changes

items.p: A donor gives a 501(c)(3) $1,000 in March and never gets a receipt. Her bank statement shows the payment. When she files her taxes the next April, can she deduct the gift?
o: No: at $250 or more she needs the charity's written acknowledgment, received by the time she files
Yes: a bank statement or canceled check is enough proof for a cash gift of any size
Yes, as long as the charity lists her gift on the Schedule B it files with the IRS
Yes: the charity owes a penalty for not sending a receipt, but her deduction stands
ow: Bank records suffice only for gifts under $250; at $250 or more the law requires the charity's written acknowledgment.
Schedule B is the charity's own filing; it doesn't replace the donor's acknowledgment.
The charity owes no penalty for a missing acknowledgment; the cost falls on the donor, who loses the deduction.
keys: no deduction without a written acknowledgment for a gift of $250 or more
received by the earlier of the filing date or the return's due date
items.x: The acknowledgment must give the charity's name, the cash amount (or a description of property), and whether the donor got anything in return, with a good-faith estimate of its value. 'Contemporaneous' means she has it by the earlier of the date she files or her return's due date, including extensions. The IRS notes charities typically send these by January 31.

items.p: A 501(c)(3) sells $250 tickets to its gala, where each guest gets a dinner worth $90. What must the charity tell ticket buyers?
o: In writing, that only $160 is deductible, with its estimate of the dinner's value
Nothing, since this disclosure is required only for payments of more than $250
That the full $250 is deductible, since the dinner is part of a charity fundraising event
That nothing is deductible, since each ticket buyer receives a dinner in return
ow: $250 is the threshold for the donor's acknowledgment; the quid pro quo disclosure applies to payments over $75.
Only the amount above the value of what the donor receives is deductible.
The part above the dinner's value is still a deductible gift.
keys: a written statement that only the amount above the benefit's value ($160) is deductible
a good-faith estimate of the dinner's value
items.x: A quid pro quo contribution is part gift, part purchase. For payments over $75, the charity must give a written statement, when it asks for or receives the money, saying the deduction is limited to the excess over the value of goods or services and estimating that value. The penalty is $10 per contribution, up to $5,000 per event or mailing. Token items and some low-cost membership benefits are exempt.

items.p: A 501(c)(4) with $2 million a year in revenue sends a fundraising email. What federal tax rule applies to the email?
o: It must say clearly that gifts aren't tax-deductible as charitable contributions
It must promise each donor of $250 or more a written acknowledgment, as charities do
It must be listed, with its recipients, on the group's Schedule B for the IRS
None: the tax rules on fundraising requests apply only to 501(c)(3) charities
ow: The $250 acknowledgment backs up a charitable deduction, which (c)(4) donors don't get.
Schedule B lists contributors, not solicitations, and since 2020 (c)(4)s don't report donor names on it at all.
Section 6113 covers non-charity exempt groups and political organizations, with a penalty of $1,000 a day, up to $10,000 a year.
keys: a conspicuous statement that contributions are not tax-deductible
items.x: Section 6113 covers (c)(4)s, unions, trade associations and 527 political groups whose gross receipts are normally over $100,000. The statement must be 'conspicuous and easily recognizable.' It's the mirror image of the charity rules: (c)(3)s document what donors may deduct, while other exempt groups must warn that donors may deduct nothing.

items.p: Match each change to charitable deductions in the July 2025 tax law, effective for 2026, to the taxpayers it affects.
pairs: People who take the standard deduction
May deduct up to $1,000 ($2,000 joint) of cash gifts to public charities, though not gifts to DAFs
Only charitable gifts above 0.5% of adjusted gross income count
Each dollar deducted saves at most 35 cents in tax
Only gifts above 1% of taxable income count, still capped at 10%
items.x: These changes come from Public Law 119-21 (the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act'), signed July 4, 2025, and apply to tax years beginning after December 31, 2025. The non-itemizer deduction also excludes gifts to supporting organizations. The law made permanent the limit allowing cash gifts to public charities of up to 60% of income.

units.title: When things go wrong
units.desc: How a group loses exemption and fights back, the limits on politically driven audits and leaks, and the criminal, state and donor-privacy risks beyond the IRS.

items.p: In 1975 the IRS ruled on an antiwar group whose main activity was protests where it urged demonstrators to block traffic and disrupt the work of government, breaking local law. Could the group qualify as a 501(c)(3) or a 501(c)(4)?
o: Neither: planning illegal acts is not a charitable or social-welfare purpose
Only as a (c)(4), since the bar on illegal purposes applies to charities alone
As both, because its goals of peace and disarmament were themselves charitable
As both, unless its members were later convicted of crimes at the protests
ow: The ruling denied both: illegal acts are not 'permissible means of promoting the social welfare' under (c)(4) either.
The ruling turned on the means: sponsoring planned law-breaking as the main activity showed an illegal purpose, whatever the goals.
No conviction was needed: the ruling rested on the group intentionally encouraging violations of local law.
keys: qualifies as neither a (c)(3) nor a (c)(4)
items.x: Rev. Rul. 75-384 said the 'intentional nature' of the encouragement ruled out treating it as an 'isolated or inadvertent violation'; lawful protest is fine. A related limit: in Bob Jones University v. United States (1983) the Supreme Court upheld revoking a university's exemption over racially discriminatory rules, holding a charity must not be 'contrary to established public policy.' In 2024 and 2026 letters, the House Ways and Means chairman cited Rev. Rul. 75-384 in asking the IRS to examine groups he said had supported unlawful protests, including campus encampments.

items.p: Match each way a group can lose its federal tax exemption to what sets it in motion.
pairs: The IRS finds the group no longer qualifies; the group can protest, appeal and go to court
Three straight years without filing a required annual return or e-Postcard
A federal designation of the group as a terrorist organization
items.x: Only audit-based revocation comes with full appeal rights. Automatic revocation has no appeal, though the group can apply for reinstatement, sometimes retroactively. A 501(p) suspension lasts until the designation is lifted and can't be contested in any tax proceeding. In each case the IRS removes the tax benefits only; it has no power to shut the organization down, which can keep operating as a taxable entity.

items.p: Put in order the steps by which an IRS audit can end a group's exemption and the group can challenge that in court.
items: The IRS opens an examination and asks for documents
The IRS sends a letter proposing to revoke exemption
The group files a written protest, which goes to the IRS Independent Office of Appeals
The IRS issues a final letter revoking exemption
The group asks a court for a declaratory judgment under section 7428
items.x: The protest is due within 30 days of the proposed letter, and skipping it can lead a court to find the group didn't exhaust its IRS remedies. The court petition (Tax Court, Court of Federal Claims, or the federal district court in D.C.) is due within 90 days of the final letter. The group keeps its exemption until the final letter. The IRS may also tell state charity officials about a proposed revocation.

items.p: After an audit, the IRS mails a 501(c)(4) a final letter revoking its exemption. The group never filed a protest, and a month later it petitions the Tax Court under section 7428. What is its main legal problem?
o: It never protested to IRS Appeals, so it likely hasn't exhausted its remedies
Section 7428 covers only 501(c)(3) charities, so a (c)(4) has no route to court
It filed too late, since petitions are due within 30 days of the final letter
The Tax Court can't hear exemption cases; only a federal court of appeals can
ow: Section 7428 also covers other 501(c) groups, including (c)(4)s.
Thirty days is the deadline to protest the proposed letter; a court petition is due within 90 days of the final letter.
The Tax Court, the Court of Federal Claims and the federal district court in D.C. can all hear these cases.
keys: failure to exhaust administrative remedies
it didn't protest to IRS Appeals before going to court
items.x: A court can rule under section 7428 only if the group 'has exhausted administrative remedies available to it within the Internal Revenue Service,' and the IRS warns that a group that doesn't protest may be found not to have done so. The same section helps applicants the IRS ignores: remedies count as exhausted 270 days after a group applied, if it took all reasonable steps, so it can then ask a court to decide its status.

items.p: The IRS revokes a charity's 501(c)(3) status after an audit and announces it. Three months before the announcement, a donor who knew nothing of the problems gave $5,000. Can the donor deduct the gift, and on what basis?
o: Yes: unaware donors may rely on the IRS listing until the public announcement
No, because the revocation reaches back to when the charity stopped qualifying
Only the first $1,000, the most any individual may deduct once a charity loses status
Only if the charity later wins its court case and has its exemption restored
ow: A revocation can reach back for the charity itself, but IRS rules protect unaware donors until the public announcement.
The $1,000 cap is a separate rule for gifts made after the announcement while the charity's court challenge is pending.
Donor reliance turns on timing and knowledge: an unaware donor's gift made before the announcement stays deductible whatever a court decides.
keys: yes
unaware donors may rely on the IRS listing until a revocation is publicly announced
items.x: Under Rev. Proc. 2018-32, donors lose this protection if they knew of the revocation, knew it was imminent, or were partly responsible for the conduct behind it. The announcement can come in the Internal Revenue Bulletin or on the IRS website. Separately, section 7428(c) keeps gifts deductible, up to $1,000 per individual, from the announcement until a court rules, if the charity challenges in time; people responsible for the problems don't qualify.

items.p: Which route can take away a nonprofit's tax exemption because of a decision made outside the IRS, with no IRS audit and no challenge allowed in any proceeding about federal tax?
o: A federal terrorism designation, which suspends exemption under section 501(p)
A congressional committee's letter referring the group to the IRS for revocation
A written request from a White House official that the IRS revoke the group's status
A state attorney general's finding that the group misused its charitable assets
ow: A referral can prompt an audit, but revocation still runs through the IRS exam, appeal and court process.
Section 7217 makes it a crime for White House staff to request an audit of a particular taxpayer, and revocation still needs the IRS process.
A state attorney general enforces state law in state court; federal exemption remains an IRS decision.
keys: suspension under section 501(p)
triggered by a federal terrorism designation, with no IRS audit
items.x: Section 501(p), added in 2003, suspends exemption and bars deductions while a group is on a State Department terrorist list, is named in a terrorism sanctions order such as Executive Order 13224, or is named as supporting terrorism in an executive order that expressly cites 501(p). The group must attack the designation itself, and gets back overpaid tax if it proves erroneous. In 2003 the IRS applied it to three US charities, including the Holy Land Foundation. The September 2025 executive order calling Antifa a 'domestic terrorist organization' doesn't cite 501(p).

lessons.title: Pressure on the IRS and its limits

items.p: From 2010 to 2012, IRS staff reviewing exemption applications flagged groups with names like 'Tea Party' and 'Patriots' for extra scrutiny. In 2013 the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA) reported on it. What harm did TIGTA find?
o: Years-long delays and demands for unneeded information, such as donor lists
Most of the flagged groups were denied exemption in the end and had to shut down
Donors to flagged groups were audited using the lists the groups supplied
White House officials had written the screening criteria for the IRS staff
ow: None of the 296 cases TIGTA reviewed had been denied; 108 were approved, and 160 were still open after 206 to 1,138 days.
TIGTA reported needless requests for donor lists, and IRS officials said donor information they received was later destroyed.
IRS officials told TIGTA no one outside the IRS influenced the criteria; in 2015 the Justice Department closed its inquiry without charges.
keys: long processing delays, some over three years
unnecessary information requests, such as donor lists
items.x: TIGTA said the criteria picked groups by 'names or policy positions instead of indications of potential political campaign intervention.' A 2015 bipartisan Senate Finance Committee report, quoted in a 2017 TIGTA review, found most flagged groups were conservative but that the IRS also flagged some left-leaning applicants; TIGTA found criteria such as 'Progressive' and 'Occupy.' In 2017 the IRS apologized in a consent order settling a suit by 41 groups, and it later agreed to pay $3.5 million to settle a separate class action by 428 groups.

items.p: A written presidential directive tells the IRS Commissioner to make sure no tax-exempt groups finance political violence. Why might section 7217, which bars the President and senior officials from requesting audits, not clearly reach it?
items.answer: Section 7217 makes it a crime to request, directly or indirectly, that the IRS start or stop an audit or investigation of a particular taxpayer. A general directive about a category of conduct names no particular taxpayer, so it falls outside the ban's text.
keys: section 7217 covers requests about a particular taxpayer
a general enforcement directive names no particular taxpayer
items.x: Section 7217 (1998) covers the President, Vice President, their staffs and cabinet-level officials other than the Attorney General; IRS staff must report such requests to TIGTA, and violations carry up to 5 years in prison. Follow-up requests that single out named groups would raise a different question, since the ban covers requests made 'directly or indirectly.' The September 2025 presidential memorandum NSPM-7 contained a general directive of this kind. In September 2026 Senators Wyden and Warnock raised section 7217 concerns about reported Treasury reviews of named groups; as of mid-October 2026 those reviews were known publicly only through press reports.

choice.p: Why might section 7217 not reach a presidential directive telling the IRS to ensure no tax-exempt groups finance political violence?
o: It bans requests to audit a particular taxpayer, and this names none
It binds cabinet officers but exempts the President and Vice President
It covers criminal cases only, not the civil audits that lead to revocation
It applies only to oral requests, and this directive was put in writing
ow: The President and Vice President are the first officials the section lists.
It covers any request to 'conduct or terminate an audit or other investigation.'
It covers requests made 'directly or indirectly'; its few exceptions include forwarding a taxpayer's own written request.

items.p: Federal agents investigating a nonprofit for a non-tax crime want copies of the records the group itself gave the IRS during an audit. Under section 6103, what do they generally need?
o: An order from a federal judge, on reasonable cause that a specific crime occurred
Only a request, since an audit file stops being confidential once a crime is suspected
Nothing will work, because tax information stays inside the IRS in non-tax cases
Nothing beyond the group's Form 990, since the rest of the IRS file is off limits
ow: Audit files stay confidential; the law lists specific routes for sharing, each with conditions.
Section 6103(i) sets out several routes for sharing with law enforcement, including court orders and terrorism requests.
A 990 is public anyway under section 6104; other records can be shared through the routes in section 6103(i).
keys: an ex parte order from a federal judge or magistrate
reasonable cause to believe a specific crime was committed and the records are relevant
items.x: Records a taxpayer supplies generally need a judge's ex parte order under section 6103(i)(1). Information the IRS got from others is easier to share: an agency head's written request can be enough, the IRS may volunteer evidence of a federal crime, and terrorism investigations have their own request routes. Unauthorized disclosure is a felony (section 7213) and lets the taxpayer sue for damages (section 7431).

items.p: Match each way government power could be misused against a nonprofit to the legal protection that addresses it.
pairs: A White House aide asks the IRS to audit a named group
Section 7217: a crime, and IRS staff must report the request to the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration
An IRS employee leaks a group's donor list
Sections 7213 and 7431: a felony, plus damages the group can sue for
The IRS sits on an exemption application for a year
Section 7428: the group can go to court once 270 days have passed
A state regulator pressures a group's insurers to drop it
First Amendment: officials can't coerce private parties to punish speech
items.x: The NOM case shows the timing: an IRS clerk released its donor schedule (inadvertently, the government said), it was published in 2012, and the IRS paid NOM $50,000 in 2014. In NRA v. Vullo (2024) a unanimous Supreme Court let the NRA pursue its claim against a New York financial regulator who allegedly pressed insurers to drop it. Earlier episodes: the House Judiciary Committee's 1974 impeachment article charged President Nixon with seeking discriminatory tax audits, and the Senate's Church Committee found the IRS began a 1961 'test audit' of right-wing groups President Kennedy had criticized, later adding one left-wing group.

items.p: In 1956 Alabama demanded the NAACP's membership lists in a suit to bar it from the state. The NAACP refused and was fined $100,000 for contempt. What did the Supreme Court decide in 1958?
o: Forcing it to reveal its members would violate their freedom of association
The lists had to be produced, but sealed from public view
Alabama could demand them over the NAACP's failure to register in the state
Only members, not the NAACP, could raise the members' privacy rights
ow: The Court shielded the names from the state itself, given the risk of reprisals.
The Court found the members' names had no 'substantial bearing' on the registration dispute.
The Court let the NAACP assert its members' rights, since making members sue themselves would destroy the privacy at stake.
keys: compelled disclosure of members violated their freedom of association
items.x: The NAACP showed that identified members had faced 'economic reprisal, loss of employment, threat of physical coercion.' In Americans for Prosperity Foundation v. Bonta (2021) the Court applied the same idea to donors, striking down California's blanket demand for charities' donor lists: under 'exacting scrutiny,' disclosure rules must be narrowly tailored to the government's interest. The rule protects groups across the political spectrum.

items.p: A 501(c)(4) promises donors privacy, citing NAACP v. Alabama and AFP v. Bonta. Name two ways its donors could still be identified.
items.answer: Examples: a subpoena or document demand in a specific investigation (by prosecutors, a legislative committee or a state attorney general) that meets the constitutional test; an FEC report naming donors who gave over $200 to further the group's independent expenditures; a leak or mistaken release of records that contain donor names.
keys: a targeted subpoena or demand in a specific investigation
FEC reports naming donors who gave to fund independent expenditures
a leak or mistaken release of records
items.x: Bonta struck down an up-front demand covering every charity and pointed to narrower tools, such as a subpoena or audit letter in a particular investigation. Those demands still face 'exacting scrutiny': a substantial relation to a sufficiently important government interest, with narrow tailoring, which a targeted demand is better placed to meet. Leaks happen too: Bonta's challengers found nearly 2,000 confidential donor schedules posted on California's website.

choice.p: Which of these can still expose a (c)(4)'s donors despite NAACP v. Alabama and AFP v. Bonta?
o: An FEC report naming donors who gave over $200 to fund its independent ads
Its public Form 990, which names every donor who gave $5,000 or more
A public records request to the IRS for the donor list it keeps on file
The Form 8976 notice it filed at the start, which lists its founding donors
ow: Public copies of a 990 omit donor names, and since 2020 (c)(4)s no longer list donor names on the Schedule B they file.
Section 6103 keeps tax records confidential, and since 2020 (c)(4)s don't list donor names on their returns.
Form 8976 asks for basic facts such as the group's name, address, formation date and purpose; it asks nothing about donors.

items.p: A US human-rights group wants to train members of a group the State Department lists as a foreign terrorist organization to use international law to settle disputes peacefully. Under Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project (2010), is that legal?
o: No: it is banned 'training' or 'expert advice,' even with a peaceful aim
Yes: teaching peaceful methods is speech that the First Amendment fully protects
Yes, as long as no money, weapons or equipment ever reaches the designated group
No, and the human-rights group also can't publish op-eds backing the group's cause
ow: The Court upheld the ban as applied to this training, 6 to 3, reasoning that such help lends legitimacy and can be diverted to violence.
'Material support' covers services, training and expert advice as well as money; only medicine and religious materials are excluded.
The Court said the law doesn't reach independent advocacy, only support coordinated with or directed by the group.
keys: not legal: it is material support (training or expert advice)
banned even though the aim is peaceful
items.x: 18 U.S.C. 2339B bars knowingly giving material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization. No federal law creates a matching list of domestic groups (CRS; still true as of October 2026), though Florida and Indiana passed state designation laws in 2026. Support for domestic actors is a federal crime under section 2339A only if given knowing or intending it to be used for listed terrorism crimes. The foreign list changes: in 2025 the State Department added drug cartels and four European groups it called violent antifa groups. Check partners against the current list.

items.p: A European foundation gives a US nonprofit a grant for the nonprofit's own campaign on US climate policy. When would the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) require the nonprofit to register?
o: If it does US political work at the foundation's request, direction or control
Once foreign grants make up more than a quarter of the nonprofit's annual budget
Never, because FARA covers only people acting as agents of foreign governments
Only if it lobbies Congress directly, since campaigns aimed at the public are exempt
ow: Foreign money alone doesn't require registration; the test turns on whether the group acts at a foreign principal's request or direction.
A 'foreign principal' includes foreign organizations, companies and individuals as well as governments.
'Political activities' include trying to influence any section of the US public on US policy.
keys: acting at the order, request, direction or control of the foreign principal
while engaging in US political activities
items.x: In a 2024 advisory opinion the Justice Department said a US nonprofit funded by a foreign nonprofit needn't register because its work served its own goals and wasn't 'significantly influenced' by the funder. Exemptions can also apply, such as for groups registered under the Lobbying Disclosure Act when no foreign government or party is the main beneficiary. The International Center for Not-for-Profit Law advises against 'on behalf of' wording in grant documents. The September 2025 presidential memorandum NSPM-7 directed terrorism task forces to investigate nonprofits with close foreign ties engaged in FARA violations or money laundering that fund or support domestic terrorism.

items.p: Compared with the IRS, what power does a state attorney general typically have over a charity incorporated in the state?
o: Suing in state court to recover misused assets, remove directors or dissolve it
Revoking the charity's federal tax exemption after a state investigation finds misuse
Prosecuting its leaders for federal crimes such as material support for terrorism
Deciding whether the charity's application for federal tax exemption is approved
ow: Only the IRS revokes federal exemption, though it may tell state officials about proposed revocations.
The Justice Department prosecutes federal crimes; state attorneys general enforce state law.
The IRS decides exemption applications; states run their own charity registration.
keys: sue in state court to recover assets, remove directors or dissolve the charity
the IRS can end tax benefits but can't shut a group down
items.x: In New York the Trump Foundation agreed in 2018 to dissolve under court supervision, and in 2019 a court ordered Donald Trump to pay $2 million for misusing its funds. In the attorney general's suit against the NRA, a judge in 2022 refused dissolution, calling it 'the last option, not the first,' and a 2024 jury found executives liable. In 2025 the Texas Supreme Court let Texas's attorney general pursue a suit to revoke the charter of Annunciation House, a migrant shelter, without ruling on the merits.

units.title: Scenarios
units.desc: Founder and board situations that mix rules from the whole course: elections, lobbying, donors, affiliated groups, filings and investigations.

items.p: Your 501(c)(3)'s executive director wants to endorse a Senate candidate on her personal social media, where her bio lists her job title. Name two conditions that keep the post from counting as the charity's endorsement.
items.answer: She speaks only for herself; she uses no charity resources or official channels (the charity's accounts, newsletter, events, staff or money); and her title appears only for identification.
keys: she speaks in a personal capacity only
no charity accounts, publications, events or money are used
her title is used for identification only
items.x: IRS guidance (Rev. Rul. 2007-41) says leaders may speak 'for themselves, as individuals' but 'cannot make partisan comments in official organization publications or at official functions.' A leader's endorsement at a candidate's press conference was not the organization's; a personal column in the official newsletter was, even though the leader paid for the space. The same rule applies whatever the candidate's party. A sister (c)(4) or PAC can endorse instead.

choice.p: What keeps a 501(c)(3) executive director's endorsement on her personal social media from counting as the charity's?
o: She speaks only for herself and uses no charity accounts, money or events
Nothing, because any endorsement by a charity's top executive is the charity's own
She posts it after work hours, even if she uses the charity's own account
She runs it instead as a signed column in the charity's newsletter, paid for personally
ow: IRS guidance lets leaders endorse speaking for themselves, as individuals, with titles shown for identification.
The charity's own accounts are official channels, so partisan posts there are the charity's speech at any hour.
IRS guidance treats a personal column in an official publication as the charity's endorsement, even if the leader pays.

items.p: A challenger for a US Senate seat asks to speak at your 501(c)(3)'s annual gala. Her opponent hasn't asked. What does the IRS look at in deciding whether hosting her is campaign intervention?
o: Equal opportunity for her rivals at a comparable event, no endorsement, no fundraising
Whether she avoids naming her opponent, which alone makes a solo appearance acceptable
Whether she pays for her own seat, so the charity spends nothing on her appearance
Whether her opponent is offered a speaking slot at a smaller weekday meeting instead
ow: For a candidate invited as a candidate, the IRS asks whether rivals got an equal opportunity, whatever she says on stage.
The ban covers support even when it costs the charity nothing, so who pays for her seat doesn't settle it.
IRS guidance says a banquet for one candidate and a sparsely attended meeting for the other likely violates the ban.
keys: equal opportunity for other candidates for the same office, at a comparable event
no sign of support or opposition, and no campaign fundraising
items.x: Rev. Rul. 2007-41 lists these factors for candidates invited in their capacity as candidates. A candidate can also appear in a non-candidate capacity, such as an officeholder speaking on policy or an expert in her field, if the event doesn't mention the race and stays nonpartisan. A forum inviting every candidate, with neutral questions and moderator, is the safer format.

items.p: A donor offers your 501(c)(3) $50,000 'to fund lobbying for the clean-water bill.' What is the tax problem with accepting the gift on those terms?
items.answer: The donor can't deduct it: the IRS treats a gift earmarked for lobbying as nondeductible, even when it goes to a 501(c)(3).
keys: the donor's gift isn't deductible
because it is earmarked for lobbying
items.x: The position comes from Rev. Rul. 80-275 and a Treasury regulation barring deductions 'for lobbying purposes'; the nonprofit law site Nonprofit Issues notes the IRS will likely deny the deduction if it sees the earmark on audit. Fixes: the donor gives genuinely unrestricted support, leaving the charity to decide how much to spend on lobbying within its limits, or gives to an affiliated 501(c)(4), knowing that gift isn't deductible either. Either way, the charity's lobbying still counts against its own limit.

choice.p: A donor offers a 501(c)(3) $50,000 'to fund lobbying for the clean-water bill.' What is the tax problem?
o: The donor can't deduct a gift earmarked for lobbying
None, since gifts to any 501(c)(3) are deductible however a donor restricts them
The charity must list the donor by name on the public copy of its Form 990
The gift is deductible only if the charity has already made the 501(h) election
ow: The IRS has long held that gifts earmarked for lobbying aren't deductible (Rev. Rul. 80-275).
Public copies of a 990 omit donor names; donors appear only on the Schedule B the IRS keeps confidential.
The 501(h) election sets the charity's lobbying limit; it doesn't make earmarked gifts deductible.

items.p: Founders plan to have their 501(c)(4) run TV ads urging voters to defeat a Senate candidate, funded by three donors who each give $1 million for that purpose and want privacy. What should the founders tell the donors?
o: Because they gave to fund the ads, the (c)(4) must report their names to the FEC
A (c)(4) keeps donor names off its public filings, so their privacy is assured
They can deduct the gifts, since the (c)(4) is itself a tax-exempt organization
The ads are allowed only if the (c)(4) first registers with the FEC as a super PAC
ow: Public 990s omit donor names, but groups that make independent expenditures must report donors who gave over $200 to further them.
Gifts to (c)(4)s generally aren't deductible as charitable contributions.
A (c)(4) may make and report independent expenditures itself, as long as election work isn't its primary activity.
keys: donors who gave over $200 to fund the ads are reported to the FEC
items.x: Federal law requires anyone making independent expenditures over $250 to identify donors who gave over $200 'for the purpose of furthering' one; a 2018 court ruling struck down a narrower FEC rule, so donors whose gifts weren't for political purposes are generally not reported. The fix: tell donors up front that gifts made to fund the ads will be reported. A (c)(4) may do some election work but not as its primary activity, and its political spending can be taxed under section 527(f).

items.p: Your 501(c)(4) wants to use its sister 501(c)(3)'s email list for a fundraising drive. How should the (c)(3) let it?
o: Rent it at fair market value under a written agreement
Lend it free, since the groups share a mission and most of a board
Refuse, since a (c)(3) can't share assets with a group that lobbies
Lend it free if the (c)(4) promises not to use it for lobbying
ow: Free use means deductible (c)(3) assets subsidize the (c)(4), which can put the (c)(3)'s exemption at risk.
Practitioner guides list renting lists at fair market value to other organizations as a permitted (c)(3) activity.
Any free use is a subsidy, whatever the (c)(4) does with the list.
keys: rent at fair market value
under a written agreement
items.x: Alliance for Justice lists renting mailing lists 'at fair market value' as allowed for (c)(3)s, and law-firm guidance calls for a written contract for any (c)(3) resource a (c)(4) uses. Extra care is needed if the list will serve candidate work: the IRS treats renting a list to one candidate's campaign while turning others away as campaign intervention (Rev. Rul. 2007-41).

items.p: Your new treasurer finds that your small charity, which could have filed the short 990-N e-Postcard, filed nothing for three years. It now appears on the IRS automatic revocation list. What is the best fix?
o: Apply for reinstatement within 15 months under the streamlined retroactive process
Protest to IRS Appeals within 30 days, as a group would after a revocation from an audit
File the three missing e-Postcards, which restores the exemption automatically
Petition the Tax Court for a declaratory judgment restoring status under section 7428
ow: The IRS says the law gives no appeal from a proper automatic revocation; the route back is reinstatement.
Late filings don't undo the revocation; the group must apply again and pay the user fee.
Section 7428 reviews IRS determinations once a group has exhausted its IRS remedies; for automatic revocation the remedy is reinstatement.
keys: apply for reinstatement (for example on Form 1023-EZ) within 15 months
the streamlined process makes it retroactive to the revocation date
items.x: Revocation takes effect on the due date of the third missed return. A small group eligible for the 990-EZ or 990-N that hasn't been auto-revoked before can be reinstated back to that date if it applies within 15 months of the revocation letter or listing. Donors may deduct gifts made before the group's name was posted, if they didn't know. A reinstated group stays on the list, with its reinstatement date shown.

items.p: Your 501(c)(4) receives an IRS letter opening an examination of its political spending. The executive director wants to delete old internal emails before the agent's first visit. What should the board do first?
o: Bring in experienced counsel and suspend routine deletion of anything relevant
Let the deletion go ahead, since the group's retention policy already allows it
Set the letter aside, since an examination, like a compliance check, is voluntary
Have staff answer the agent directly, without lawyers, to show good faith
ow: Destroying records in contemplation of a federal investigation can be a crime under 18 U.S.C. 1519, and a written policy doesn't excuse it.
Only a compliance check, which the IRS labels as one, is voluntary; an examination can be enforced by summons.
Groups may have representatives, and an IRS interview must pause if the group asks to consult one.
keys: bring in experienced counsel
preserve records by suspending routine deletion (a litigation hold)
items.x: The IRS's own Form 990 instructions warn that the Sarbanes-Oxley ban on destroying records 'with the intent to obstruct a federal investigation' applies to exempt organizations. The International Center for Not-for-Profit Law also advises naming one point of contact for the IRS and the press. An examination can end with no change, with taxes, or with revocation, and the group keeps its exemption while it protests and appeals.

items.p: After reading about politically charged reviews of nonprofits, your board asks what to put in place now so the group is easier to defend if it is investigated. Name two practices.
items.answer: Examples: complete, accurate 990s and clean books; written document retention and whistleblower policies, with a way to suspend deletion; separate accounts, time records and cost-sharing agreements among the (c)(3), (c)(4) and PAC; counsel experienced in IRS and criminal matters identified in advance; D&O insurance that covers investigation costs; one designated contact for regulators and press.
keys: clean books and accurate filings
a written retention policy that can be suspended
documented separation among affiliated groups
counsel and investigation-covering insurance lined up in advance
items.x: These steps track guidance from the International Center for Not-for-Profit Law and the Nonprofit Resiliency Network, whose D&O guide warns that coverage of an investigation depends on how a policy defines a 'claim,' and that fines are usually excluded. Form 990 asks whether a group has written whistleblower and retention policies. Nonprofit lawyer Ellis Carter notes that the groups best placed are those whose compliance file 'was already in order before anyone was looking for a reason to open it.'

choice.p: Which of these makes a nonprofit easier to defend if it faces a politically charged investigation?
o: A written records policy that can be paused once an investigation looks likely
Keeping no written policies, so investigators have no policy to say the group broke
Running the (c)(3), (c)(4) and PAC from one bank account to keep the books simple
Telling donors their names can never be disclosed to any government body
ow: Written policies followed in practice help show good faith, and Form 990 asks whether a group has whistleblower and retention policies.
Mixing funds makes it hard to show that (c)(3) money didn't pay for political work.
Targeted subpoenas, FEC reports and leaks can all expose donors, so the promise can't be kept.

nonprofit.description: How 501(c)(3)s, 501(c)(4)s, PACs and super PACs differ, and the rules on elections, lobbying, money, disclosure and enforcement that anyone founding, running or funding one should know.
caveat: Prepared October 23, 2026 from statutes, IRS and FEC guidance, court opinions and practitioner guides. US federal law, simplified; states add their own rules on charities, lobbying and elections.
Not legal advice: talk to a nonprofit or election lawyer before acting. Drafted and fact-checked by AI agents working independently; no person has reviewed it.

basics.name: AI Policy Basics

units.title: Shared foundations
units.desc: Concepts used across the AI courses.

items.p: Policy documents talk constantly about a model's 'weights.' What are they?
o: Numbers set during training that determine what the model outputs
A compressed copy of the documents the model was trained on
The written rules a developer gives the model about what it may say
The ranking of answers human labelers preferred during training
ow: Weights encode patterns learned from the data. Models do memorize some passages word for word, yet nothing in the weights works like a stored, searchable copy of the documents.
Those are instructions or policies; they sit outside the weights.
Labelers' rankings are training data for RLHF; the weights are what training produces.
keys: numerical values learned in training
they determine the model's outputs
not a copy of the training data
items.x: Weights are the learned numerical parameters of a model. With the necessary software and hardware, someone with the weights can run the model.

items.p: Why do security researchers treat a frontier model's weights as the key asset to protect?
items.answer: The weights embody costly training. A thief can run or modify the model without retraining it from scratch, outside the developer’s access controls and monitoring, and can work to remove learned safeguards.
keys: Weights embody expensive training
A thief can run or modify the model without repeating training
Outside developer access controls and monitoring; safeguards can be modified
items.x: RAND (2024): 'once the attacker has access to the weights of a model, abusing the model without restrictions or monitoring is eminently feasible.' It contrasts reported training costs of $78 million (GPT-4) and nearly $200 million (Gemini Ultra) with under half a cent per thousand tokens to run.

choice.p: Why do security researchers treat a frontier model's weights as the key asset to protect?
o: They capture costly training and let a thief run or modify the model independently.
They hold the developer's customer conversations and payment records
They contain the training data, which can be rebuilt from them if lost
Losing them forces the developer offline, so theft mainly causes outages
ow: Weights encode learned patterns, not customer records.
Weights encode patterns learned from the data; they aren't a copy of it, and the threat is what a thief can do.
The issue is what a thief can do with them, not the developer's own uptime.

items.p: Why do analysts say that releasing a model's weights publicly can't be undone?
items.answer: Once the weights are downloaded, copies spread (for example by torrent), and the developer can't recall them, monitor how they're used, or stop people from changing them.
keys: copies spread and can't be recalled
the developer can't monitor or control how they're used
items.x: Once weights have been distributed, the original developer cannot reliably recall every copy. Recipients can run or modify their copies independently.

choice.p: Why is publicly releasing a model's weights described as irreversible?
o: Copies spread beyond the developer's control, so it can't recall them or police their use
Released weights can't be updated, so the model's knowledge stays frozen at release
Published weights are cryptographically locked, so no one can modify them after release
Federal law treats a published model as public domain, ending the developer's rights in it
ow: Knowledge cutoffs apply to every model; the problem is that released copies spread and can't be recalled.
The reverse: anyone with the weights can modify them cheaply, including to strip safeguards.
No such law exists; the problem is practical, not legal.

items.p: AI policy often uses a model’s training compute as a threshold. What does training compute measure?
o: The total number of arithmetic operations used to train the model
How many operations per second the developer's computers can run
The number of parameters, or weights, in the finished model
The number of words of text the model was trained on
ow: That's a rate (FLOP per second). The threshold is a total, like miles driven rather than miles per hour.
Parameter count is a different measure; Biden's 2023 order used it in a separate definition.
Training data is measured in tokens; compute depends on both data and model size.
keys: total floating-point (arithmetic) operations
used in training
a total amount, not a speed
items.x: Training compute is the total number of arithmetic operations used in training, usually stated in FLOP (floating-point operations). Biden's 2023 order counted 'integer or floating-point operations' and had both kinds of trigger: 10^26 operations for a model and 10^20 operations per second for a computing cluster. Newer laws, including SB 53, also count fine-tuning and later training.

items.p: Match each law or proposal to the compute line it uses.
pairs: Presumes a model has 'systemic risk' above 10^25 FLOP
Covers models above 10^26 operations, with extra duties for developers over $500M in revenue
Reports above 10^26 operations, or 10^23 for biology-focused models
items.x: Compute lines are legal coverage thresholds, rather than precise measures of danger. California and New York use a 10^26 training-operations threshold, with New York’s law starting in 2027; the EU systemic-risk presumption uses 10^25.

items.p: As of October 2026, is there a US federal requirement to report large AI training runs to the government? What existed before?
items.answer: No. Biden's Executive Order 14110 (2023) used the Defense Production Act to require such reports, and Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security proposed quarterly reporting rules in September 2024, but the order was revoked in January 2025.
keys: No current federal requirement
EO 14110 required reports (2023)
Revoked January 2025
items.x: State laws such as SB 53 use 10^26 operations only to define who is covered. A June 2026 executive order set up only a voluntary framework for pre-release government testing. By contrast, the EU AI Act (Article 52) requires providers to notify the European Commission within two weeks once a model crosses its 10^25 systemic-risk threshold.

choice.p: As of October 2026, which best describes US federal reporting of large AI training runs?
o: None now: Biden's 2023 order required reports but was revoked in January 2025
Developers must notify Commerce within two weeks of crossing 10^26 operations
The FRONTIER Act now requires quarterly training-run reports to the Commerce Department
A June 2026 executive order requires reports for every training run above 10^25 operations
ow: Two-week notice after crossing a threshold is the EU AI Act's rule, at 10^25.
The FRONTIER Act is a bill in House committee, not law.
The June 2026 order created a voluntary pre-release testing framework, not training-run reporting.

items.p: What is a frontier AI safety framework?
keys: published risk evaluation process
safeguards and development or deployment decisions
items.x: Frameworks often connect capability or risk thresholds to safeguards. The strength of the commitments varies. Anthropic’s February 2026 RSP v3.0 changed its approach, so an unconditional pause pledge should not be assumed for every framework.
items.answer: A developer’s published process for evaluating serious risks and describing safeguards and development or deployment decisions. Commitments differ by lab and framework version.

o: A published process connecting risk evaluation with safeguards and development decisions.
A binding government license giving a developer permission for each new training run.
A public leaderboard ranking models solely by their scores on capability benchmarks.
An insurance contract guaranteeing compensation for all harms caused by a model.
ow: A lab framework is distinct from government licensing.
Risk management includes decisions and safeguards, beyond benchmark rankings.
Frameworks describe a process and commitments, rather than guaranteeing compensation.

items.p: What is a system card?
o: The developer's own report on a model's capabilities, safety tests and safeguards
An independent audit of a model, written by a government safety institute
A legal filing every developer must make with the Commerce Department before release
A short user guide that explains a model's features and pricing to customers
ow: A system card is developer documentation; an independent audit is a different kind of assessment.
No federal filing like this exists.
System cards describe capabilities, risk evaluations and safeguards, rather than focusing on features and pricing.
keys: Developer-published documentation
Capabilities, safety evaluations and safeguards
items.x: System cards are documentation published by developers about model capabilities, safety evaluations and safeguards. Their content and level of detail vary.

items.p: AI risk discussions separate 'misuse' from 'loss of control'. What is the main difference?
o: Misuse: a person uses AI to cause harm on purpose. Loss of control: AI systems act outside anyone's control
Misuse: mistakes and bugs in AI systems cause harm. Loss of control: criminals take over AI systems to attack
Misuse: harm from models whose weights are published. Loss of control: harm from models kept inside labs
Misuse: harm to individual users. Loss of control: harm only to the developer's own computer systems
ow: This mixes them up: misuse is deliberate harm by people, bugs count as malfunctions, and criminals taking over a system is still misuse.
Either risk can involve open or closed models; the difference is whether a person or the AI is driving the harm.
Misuse can be catastrophic at scale, and loss of control is defined by AI escaping anyone's control, whatever it harms.
keys: Misuse: a person deliberately uses AI to cause harm
Loss of control: AI systems operate outside anyone's control
items.x: The International AI Safety Report, chaired by Yoshua Bengio, groups risks into malicious use (such as cyberattacks and biological or chemical weapons), malfunctions (including loss of control) and systemic risks. The split matters for policy: misuse tools aim at bad actors and dangerous capabilities, while loss-of-control tools aim at the AI systems themselves.

items.p: As of October 2026, how does US government pre-deployment testing of frontier AI models work?
items.answer: Testing is voluntary. NIST’s testing center, now CAISSI, has voluntary agreements with five labs. EO14409 of June 2026 directs agencies to design a voluntary framework for government access to covered models for up to 30 days before developers release them to other trusted partners.
keys: Voluntary government testing through NIST’s center, now CAISSI
Agreements with five labs
June 2026 order seeks up to 30 days of government access before trusted-partner release
items.x: The US center was called CAISI before its October 2026 rename to CAISSI. The June 2026 order directs a voluntary framework, rather than itself creating mandatory pre-release approval.

o: Voluntary testing through NIST’s CAISSI; the June 2026 order seeks up to 30 days of access before trusted-partner release.
Mandatory: under a May 2026 executive order, developers must give CAISSI 90 days of access to each model before release
Mandatory: the AI Risk Evaluation Act requires Energy Department testing of each model before deployment
None exists: CAISSI was abolished in 2025 and all frontier model testing moved over to the EU AI Office
ow: A draft order with 90 days of access was shelved in May 2026; the June order is voluntary and allows up to 30 days.
The Hawley-Blumenthal bill would do this, but it has not passed.
CAISSI exists and runs voluntary testing; the EU AI Office has no role in US release decisions.

items.p: For covered large developers, match these California SB 53 duties to what each concerns.
pairs: Publish and follow the developer’s approach to catastrophic risk
Publish specified information about a covered frontier model
Protect covered employee disclosures against retaliation
items.x: This is an outline. Coverage, exceptions, deadlines and enforcement details belong in AI Policy Landscape.

democracy.name: US Democratic Backsliding

units.title: The map: how democracies erode
units.desc: How elected leaders can weaken checks and competition, the guardrails scholars emphasize, and how to distinguish erosion from ordinary political conflict.

items.p: Observers called Hungary’s 2022 parliamentary election well administered. Did they also judge its overall competition fair?
o: No: well-run polling coexisted with unequal campaign conditions
Yes: accurate polling established overall fairness
They declined to assess conditions before election day
They found the opposition had been barred from running
ow: OSCE assessed media and state-resource advantages as well as polling.
The observers examined the campaign and broader electoral environment.
Contestants could largely campaign freely, despite unequal conditions.
keys: well administered
uneven competition
items.x: OSCE found professional administration alongside overlapping state and governing-party activity and media bias. This course follows three routes to erosion: weakening checks, restricting rivals and changing competition rules. Elections can survive while these safeguards deteriorate.

items.p: A government uses successive laws to weaken legislative oversight and judicial independence. In Bermeo’s framework, what mechanism is this?
o: Executive aggrandizement by an elected government
An executive coup that closes the legislature outright
A military coup replacing civilian government
Routine alternation between elected governments
ow: An executive coup abruptly suspends democratic institutions; this scenario weakens them incrementally.
The elected executive, rather than the military, is concentrating power.
Alternation transfers power between competitors; this action reduces checks on the incumbent.
keys: incremental weakening of checks
elected executive
items.x: Nancy Bermeo calls incremental weakening of checks by elected executives executive aggrandizement. Her research finds overt coups and blatant election-day fraud have declined relative to subtler forms of erosion. Legal procedures can help give these changes legitimacy.

items.p: In Levitsky and Way’s concept of competitive authoritarianism, why can an opposition election victory still be possible?
o: Competition survives despite systematic incumbent advantages
The government permits only candidates it has chosen itself
Election results are routinely fixed before voting begins
The government gives rivals equal access to media and law
ow: Meaningful opposition remains possible in competitive authoritarian regimes.
Predetermined results would remove the meaningful uncertainty central to this concept.
A reasonably level playing field would meet a key democratic criterion.
keys: real competition
systematically unfair playing field
items.x: Levitsky and Way describe regimes where opposition parties can challenge incumbents while state abuses make competition seriously unfair. Holding a competitive election, by itself, therefore cannot establish that the wider system is democratic.

items.p: Match each move to the mechanism in Levitsky and Ziblatt’s account of democratic erosion.
pairs: Loyalists take control of oversight agencies
Tax investigations pressure media owners into silence
Electoral rules entrench the governing party
items.x: Their framework separates control over institutions, pressure on challengers and changes to the rules. Later units examine legal tools that can enable or constrain each mechanism.

items.p: What does mutual toleration require toward a political rival who follows democratic rules?
items.answer: Recognize the rival’s legitimate right to compete and govern if elected.
keys: legitimate right to compete
right to govern if elected
items.x: Levitsky and Ziblatt call mutual toleration a democratic guardrail. It becomes harder to accept losing an election when opponents are treated as enemies who have no right to hold office.

o: Accept the rival’s legitimate right to compete and govern
Agree with the rival’s most important policy proposals
Avoid investigating credible evidence of the rival’s crimes
Promise to share executive offices after every election
ow: Mutual toleration permits strong policy disagreement.
Accepting legitimate opposition does not suspend equal enforcement of law.
The norm concerns rivals’ legitimacy, without requiring coalition government.

items.p: A leader could use a lawful procedural power to disable rivals. Which norm in Levitsky and Ziblatt’s framework would discourage exploiting that opening?
o: Institutional forbearance
Judicial review of unlawful action
Mutual toleration as policy agreement
Electoral accountability after defeat
ow: Judicial review concerns legality; this example asks about restraint when a power is lawful.
Mutual toleration recognizes legitimate rivals; it does not require agreement with their policies.
An electoral defeat is an external sanction rather than voluntary restraint.
keys: restraint in exercising legal power
items.x: Forbearance is restraint in using legal powers in ways that would undermine democratic competition. Its value depends on the purpose and effect of restraint; the framework does not ask officials to abandon legitimate oversight.

items.p: A staffer applies Levitsky and Ziblatt’s warning-sign test. Which statement most directly raises concern about accepting democratic rules?
o: “If I lose this election, I will refuse to recognize its result.”
“Our opponents’ tax proposal would damage the economy.”
“We will ask a court to review disputed ballots.”
“We plan to campaign against the sitting government.”
ow: Harsh criticism of policies can occur within democratic competition.
Seeking lawful judicial review is compatible with accepting democratic rules.
Campaigning to replace the government is part of democratic competition.
keys: conditional acceptance of election results
items.x: Their warning signs cover rejection of democratic rules, denial of opponents’ legitimacy, tolerance of violence and willingness to restrict opponents’ civil liberties. This statement makes acceptance of an election conditional on personal victory. The test is a warning framework, rather than a legal verdict.

items.p: Why does a reform’s passage through lawful procedures fail to settle whether it contributes to democratic backsliding?
items.answer: The reform can still weaken checks or fair political competition.
keys: lawful procedures can weaken democratic checks
items.x: Bermeo emphasizes that modern erosion can proceed through elections, legislative majorities and laws. A staff assessment should examine who gains power and what happens to oversight and rivals’ ability to compete.

o: Its effects may weaken oversight or fair political competition
Approval by an elected majority settles its democratic legitimacy
Legal procedure matters more than effects on future competition
Popularity of the policy determines its effect on democracy
ow: Elected majorities can weaken the institutions that allow future opposition to compete.
Lawful procedure can coexist with erosion of checks and competitive conditions.
A popular policy can still have institutional effects that weaken competition.

units.title: Measuring backsliding
units.desc: What the major assessments measure, what their 2026 releases say about the US, and how to interpret disagreement and uncertainty.

lessons.title: Read the measure before the label

items.p: In reports available as of October 2026, V-Dem calls the US an electoral democracy, Freedom House calls it Free and EIU calls it a flawed democracy. What explains the different labels?
o: Different definitions of democracy and category thresholds
Their labels are interchangeable descriptions of country rankings
Their annual reports necessarily cover different national elections
One measures voting rights while the others measure economic policy
ow: A category is not a rank, and these publishers use different categories.
The cited annual reports all assess 2025; their differences are not simply different elections.
All three assess political institutions; Freedom House and EIU do not substitute economic policy for democratic rights.
keys: different measures and thresholds
items.x: The 2026 annual reports assess 2025: V-Dem’s liberal-democracy score is about 0.57 on its 0 to 1 scale; Freedom House gives 81/100; EIU gives 7.65/10. Their labels answer overlapping questions using different thresholds. None is a legal finding.

items.p: Match each democracy assessment to its main approach.
pairs: Expert-coded indicators combined into multiple democracy indexes
Political-rights and civil-liberties scores combined into freedom status
Five categories including participation and political culture
Surveys of US experts and the public on democratic performance
items.x: V-Dem separates electoral, liberal and other dimensions; EIU includes participation and political culture. Bright Line Watch keeps expert and public samples distinct. These choices affect what each assessment can detect.

items.p: Why can V-Dem’s US liberal-democracy score deteriorate between elections even when no new national vote has occurred?
o: Executive constraints and civil liberties can change between elections
It substitutes presidential approval polls for election data
It treats every executive policy change as an election failure
It assumes the next election’s result from current opinion polls
ow: V-Dem’s liberal index includes institutional constraints and rights rather than a presidential popularity score.
The index distinguishes attributes such as executive constraints from electoral indicators.
It assesses observed conditions, rather than forecasts the next election winner.
keys: constraints and rights change between elections
items.x: V-Dem’s v16 statement attributes large US changes from 2024 to 2025 to executive constraints, rule of law, individual liberties and expression. Some election-specific indicators update around elections, so the electoral and liberal indexes need not move together.

items.p: A briefing cites a “2026 democracy report.” What timing check should you make before treating its score as a picture of October 2026?
items.answer: Check the period the underlying observations cover.
keys: check underlying observation period
items.x: V-Dem’s 2026 report contains data through 2025. Bright Line Watch’s July 2026 surveys provide a later snapshot with a different method. A current briefing should name both the publication date and the period measured.

o: Check the period covered by the underlying observations
Treat the publication year as the final month of observation
Assume every annual index updates continuously through today
Use its rank as a real-time forecast of the next election
ow: Publication and observation dates can differ; these annual reports chiefly assess 2025.
Annual indexes and survey waves have specific reporting periods.
A comparative rank measures assessed conditions rather than future election results.

items.p: A July 2026 Bright Line Watch survey rises while an annual democracy index reports a decline during 2025. Must one of those findings be wrong?
o: No: periods and methods differ
Yes: a later survey cancels earlier annual findings
Yes: the measures must move together if valid
No: the survey measures only satisfaction with the economy
ow: A later snapshot can show a different movement without making the earlier period inaccurate.
Different observation periods and methods need not produce identical movements.
Bright Line Watch asks about democratic performance, rather than only economic satisfaction.
keys: Different periods and methods can produce compatible findings
items.x: Bright Line Watch’s July 2026 expert mean rose to 60/100, with the public around 52, while annual indexes described 2025. Compare observation periods and methods before interpreting disagreement. A later partial recovery need not erase an earlier decline.

items.p: Little and Meng question some global backsliding estimates; Knutsen and colleagues defend broader measures. What is the main empirical disagreement?
o: Changing coder standards versus missed institutional erosion
Country selection versus weighting small and large populations
Economic growth versus the timing of elections across countries
Turnout changes versus different campaign-finance systems
ow: Their central dispute concerns possible coding bias and the institutional damage observable indicators may miss.
Economic performance and election timing are not the central disagreement described by these papers.
The dispute concerns measurement bias and institutional erosion, rather than those two specific electoral features.
keys: subjective coder bias
narrow indicators may miss erosion
items.x: Little and Meng find less global decline in observable indicators such as incumbent turnover and raise changing coder standards. Knutsen and colleagues argue narrow measures miss rights and constraints, and find little evidence of the proposed bias. This global debate does not settle the US’s 2026 condition.

items.p: Match each observation to the distinction it illustrates when reading democracy scores.
pairs: A score falls while remaining in the same category
A small score change crosses a category cutoff
A ranking falls while the country score stays fixed
Relative position can change when other countries change
items.x: Scores describe assessed levels, categories group ranges and rankings compare countries. A memo should explain the underlying institutional change before treating a label or rank as the conclusion.

items.p: A staffer sees a sharp democracy-score decline. How can they check what the decline means before drawing a policy conclusion?
items.answer: Inspect which institutional indicators changed and compare them with independently documented events.
keys: Inspect the changed institutional indicators and compare them with independently documented events
items.x: The coding debate makes triangulation useful: identify the rights, checks or election conditions driving a score and examine the supporting evidence. Several measures pointing in the same direction can strengthen a conclusion while uncertainty remains.

o: Inspect changed indicators against independent factual evidence
Use the headline rank as the complete institutional diagnosis
Discard the score because expert judgment enters its construction
Assume agreement between indexes proves every component is accurate
ow: A rank alone cannot identify the mechanism responsible for a change.
Judgment creates measurement concerns, but does not by itself invalidate a measure.
Indexes can share concepts, evidence or blind spots, so agreement is not proof.

units.title: Lessons from abroad
units.desc: Mechanisms and resistance in six countries, followed by the US constitutional and electoral features that affect comparisons.

items.p: Poland’s 2023 election gave the governing party media and state-resource advantages, according to observers. What happened when a rival coalition secured a parliamentary majority?
o: It formed a new coalition government headed by Tusk
Law and Justice retained office despite losing its majority
The election was voided because competition was unequal
It called another election after coalition talks failed
ow: Law and Justice lost office after eight years; Tusk’s government took office in December 2023.
Unequal conditions did not prevent this election from producing a change in government.
Tusk’s coalition formed a government after winning parliamentary support, rather than requiring another election.
keys: opposition coalition formed government
items.x: Tusk’s coalition took office in December 2023 after an election observers judged competitive but unequal. The case illustrates the meaningful contestation from Unit 1: institutional erosion can coexist with an opposition route to office. Turnover alone does not show that damaged institutions have been repaired.

items.p: Why did Fidesz’s post-2010 parliamentary supermajority matter specifically to changing Hungary’s constitutional framework?
o: It supplied votes for constitutional restructuring
It supplied authority to bypass Parliament through decrees
It moved constitutional review to European courts
It made the prime minister directly elected by voters
ow: The supermajority mattered because constitutional changes could be enacted through Parliament.
The reforms changed domestic institutions; parliamentary strength did not transfer constitutional review to European courts.
Parliamentary voting strength did not create a direct presidential-style election for prime minister.
keys: constitutional change
concentration of power
items.x: CRS describes how Fidesz’s dominant position enabled a new constitution and institutional reforms that critics viewed as concentrating power. Supporters defended reform as addressing corruption and mismanagement. This is a historical example of the legal pathway from Unit 1, rather than a claim about who governs Hungary in October 2026.

items.p: A staffer cites high turnout in Turkey’s 2023 elections as proof of fair competition. What additional evidence is most directly relevant?
o: Media access and restrictions on opposition activity
Turnout compared with the country’s previous election
The winning candidate’s margin over the runner-up
The number of ballots processed by each polling station
ow: Turnout comparisons measure participation, which does not settle whether campaign conditions were fair.
A victory margin alone does not establish equal access to voters or freedom to organize.
Polling administration matters, but it cannot settle whether the wider competition was fair.
keys: High turnout alone does not show fair competition
Check media access and restrictions on opposition activity
items.x: The OSCE found high participation and genuine alternatives alongside restrictions on expression, assembly and association. An assessment should examine the campaign environment as well as whether voting occurred.

items.p: After Venezuela’s 2024 presidential election, why did the Carter Center say it could not verify the announced result?
o: Authorities failed to publish results from each polling station
A nationwide recount had not been completed before the announcement
Opposition parties had not accepted the announced national totals
Observers had not visited every polling station in the country
ow: The stated verification problem was the missing station-level results, rather than a required nationwide recount.
An opposition concession is not what makes election results independently verifiable.
Observers need evidence supporting the result; personally visiting every station is not the requirement described here.
keys: missing disaggregated polling-station results
items.x: The Carter Center said the election failed international integrity standards and could not be considered democratic. Missing polling-station results blocked scrutiny of the announced outcome. Unit 1’s uneven competition and the verifiability of the count are separate issues that can compound one another.

items.p: Israel’s government backed a 2023 amendment eliminating reasonableness review of ministerial decisions. What did the High Court do in January 2024?
o: Struck down the amendment to preserve judicial review
Upheld the amendment while reserving review of ordinary laws
Dismissed the challenge for lack of judicial authority
Required Parliament to hold a referendum on its proposal
ow: The High Court invalidated this amendment rather than upholding it.
The Court reached the amendment’s validity and struck it down.
The decision invalidated the amendment without requiring that referendum.
keys: amendment struck down
judicial check
items.x: The amendment was voided 8 to 7; a separate 12 to 3 majority affirmed authority to review basic laws in exceptional cases. The case shows a court resisting a restriction on its own review powers, while leaving wider questions about the system’s condition open.

items.p: Brazil’s courts resisted attacks on electoral institutions, while critics challenged their speech restrictions. What question should a staffer ask when assessing those responses?
o: Did restrictions meet proportionality and due-process requirements?
Did the President support the restrictions as necessary for stability?
Did the restrictions target demonstrably false claims about elections?
Did the government describe the situation as an emergency?
ow: Executive approval does not establish whether judicial restrictions satisfy rights and procedural safeguards.
A concern about false claims does not settle whether the response was proportionate or afforded due process.
An emergency claim does not by itself answer whether a particular restriction respects rights.
keys: lawfulness
proportionality and due process
items.x: Brazil’s electoral court announced Lula’s 2022 defeat of incumbent Bolsonaro. O’Donohue describes courts’ need for allies; the US State Department’s 2024 Brazil report criticizes disproportionate speech restrictions and due-process failures. Both institutional resistance and limits on the response belong in the assessment.

items.p: Match each dated international case to the mechanism or resistance examined in this unit.
pairs: Constitutional restructuring enabled by a dominant governing party
Opposition route to office survived unequal conditions
Court invalidated a restriction on review of ministers
items.x: These are different institutional pathways, rather than a fixed sequence every country follows. Comparing the mechanism helps identify what evidence a US assessment would need.

items.p: Why does a simple majority in Congress give a US governing party less power to rewrite the Constitution than the power used in Hungary’s post-2010 transformation?
items.answer: Article V requires supermajorities for amendment proposal and ratification across the states.
keys: Article V supermajorities
state ratification
items.x: The congressional route needs two thirds of each chamber to propose and three fourths of states to ratify. US elections are also administered across states and localities. These barriers disperse authority; ordinary statutes, appointments and local pressure can still matter, so structural differences do not establish immunity to erosion.

o: Article V requires supermajorities and ratification across states
Congress can amend the Constitution with two-thirds votes alone
A proposal becomes law after two-thirds of states ratify it
A national referendum can approve a proposal from Congress
ow: Congressional proposal is followed by a separate state ratification stage.
Ratification requires three-fourths of states rather than two-thirds.
Article V specifies ratification through state legislatures or conventions, rather than a national referendum.

units.title: The Supreme Court's role
units.desc: How review, remedies and compliance make courts a check on power.

items.p: In Marbury v. Madison, a claimant asked the Supreme Court to order delivery of his judicial commission. How did the Court resolve the case?
o: It refused the writ because its jurisdiction could not be expanded that way
It ordered delivery because a right to office necessarily supplied jurisdiction
It let Congress decide whether the commission was legally owed to him
It upheld the jurisdiction statute while denying any right to the commission
ow: A legal right does not itself establish the Court's jurisdiction.
The Court decided the legal and jurisdictional questions itself.
It found a right to the commission but rejected the jurisdiction statute.
keys: It refused the writ because its jurisdiction could not be expanded that way
items.x: Marbury established judicial review while denying the requested order. A court needs authority to hear the case before it can supply a remedy.

items.p: A federal statute conflicts with the Constitution in a case properly before a court. What does judicial review allow the court to do?
o: Disregard the statute where it conflicts with the Constitution
Suspend the case until Congress amends the statute
Apply the statute if it passed with a supermajority
Require presidential approval before refusing to apply it
ow: Judicial review allows courts to decide the conflict in a case without waiting for a legislative amendment.
An ordinary statutory supermajority does not override the Constitution.
A court’s judgment on constitutionality does not require presidential approval.
keys: Disregard the statute where it conflicts with the Constitution
