items.x: The Court describes judicial review as authority to invalidate legislative or executive actions that conflict with the Constitution. This is one of the institutional checks in the course map.

items.p: Why did Hamilton argue that judicial decisions depend on the executive branch?
items.answer: Courts rely on executive help to enforce their judgments
keys: Courts rely on executive help to enforce their judgments

o: Courts rely on executive help to enforce their judgments
Courts need presidential approval to publish opinions
Presidents may revise judgments through pardons
Judges lose office if the President rejects their reasoning
ow: Judicial opinions do not require presidential approval.
A pardon does not give the President general authority to revise judgments.
Article III protects judges' tenure during good behavior.

items.x: In Federalist 78, Hamilton emphasized that judges control neither the military nor public spending. A legal ruling and the government's implementation of it are separate things to examine.

items.p: A staffer proposes expanding the Supreme Court. Which legal route changes the number of seats?
o: A federal statute enacted through Congress
An executive order adding seats
An amendment because Article III fixes nine seats
A vote of sitting justices
ow: The President cannot create Supreme Court seats by executive order.
Article III establishes one Supreme Court without specifying nine seats.
Congress sets the number; the justices do not.
keys: A federal statute enacted through Congress
items.x: The Court's size is set by statute. Filling seats is a separate process: presidential nomination and Senate confirmation. This distinguishes changing the institution's structure from appointing its members.

items.p: A headline says the Supreme Court granted a stay of an injunction while an appeal proceeds. What does that immediately change?
o: It pauses the injunction during the specified period
It decides the constitutional merits
It dismisses the lawsuit and prevents further lower-court hearings
It vacates the injunction as legally erroneous
ow: Interim relief need not finally decide the constitutional claim.
A stay does not itself dismiss the underlying litigation.
A temporary pause differs from vacating the injunction as erroneous.
keys: It pauses the injunction during the specified period
items.x: An emergency application asks for interim relief. In Trump v. Cook the Court instead denied a stay, leaving protection against removal in place while litigation continued.

items.p: After Trump v. CASA, why can winning an injunction against an executive order leave other people exposed to the same policy?
items.answer: Relief is limited to fully protecting plaintiffs
keys: Relief is limited to fully protecting plaintiffs

o: Relief must provide complete protection to plaintiffs
A legal win extends relief to everyone affected by the policy
The ruling protects people only within the judge’s district
An injunction can cover nonparties only through separate suits
ow: CASA ties relief to what plaintiffs need, rather than automatic universal coverage.
The relevant boundary is complete relief, rather than simply a district’s geographic boundary.
Class actions remain available, and complete relief may require effects beyond named plaintiffs.

items.x: CASA (2025), 6 to 3, held universal injunctions likely exceed courts' statutory equitable authority. It limited relief to what is necessary for complete relief to plaintiffs; it did not decide the birthright citizenship merits.

items.p: Congress proposes an exception to the Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction. Which constitutional provision is directly relevant?
o: Article III gives Congress an exceptions power
Article III fixes appellate jurisdiction beyond congressional change
Article II transfers appellate jurisdiction to presidential control
Article I permits exceptions only with Supreme Court approval
ow: Article III expressly allows congressional exceptions and regulations.
The relevant exception authority belongs to Congress under Article III.
Article III contains no requirement that justices approve congressional exceptions.
keys: Article III gives Congress an exceptions power
items.x: Article III makes appellate jurisdiction subject to exceptions and regulations Congress establishes. That text does not resolve every constitutional limit on jurisdiction-stripping proposals.

items.p: Match each question about a court challenge to the issue it concerns.
pairs: Can this court hear the dispute?
Who and what does the order protect?
Did officials carry out the order?
items.x: These questions are distinct. Marbury turned on jurisdiction, CASA on remedy scope, and Hamilton's enforcement argument explains why implementation also matters.

units.title: Presidential power before the Court
units.desc: Immunity, statutory interpretation and removal power change different parts of executive accountability.

items.p: In Trump v. United States (2024), prosecutors argued a former President could face criminal charges for conduct in office. What rule did the Court adopt?
o: Immunity depends on the kind of act
Every act during a presidency receives absolute criminal immunity
Immunity expires immediately when a President leaves office
Criminal immunity exists only after Senate acquittal on impeachment
ow: Unofficial acts receive no presidential immunity.
The ruling specifically protects some former presidential acts.
The Court rejected making prior impeachment conviction necessary for prosecution.
keys: Immunity depends on the kind of act
items.x: The 6 to 3 decision distinguishes core constitutional powers, other official acts and unofficial acts. That classification became a threshold issue before prosecution could proceed.

items.p: Match each kind of presidential act to its criminal-immunity tier under Trump v. United States.
items.x: Presumptive immunity means prosecutors must overcome a protective starting point. The official/unofficial boundary matters to the accountability question.

items.p: What was the central disagreement between the majority and Sotomayor's dissent in the presidential criminal-immunity case?
items.answer: Protecting executive independence versus preserving criminal accountability
keys: Protecting executive independence versus preserving criminal accountability

o: Protecting executive independence versus preserving criminal accountability
Whether the Constitution permits any impeachment of former presidents
Whether states may determine which candidates appear on federal ballots
Whether agency experts should interpret ambiguous regulatory statutes
ow: The criminal-immunity dispute concerned prosecution of presidential acts.
Ballot disqualification was at issue in Trump v. Anderson.
Agency interpretation was the issue in Loper Bright.

items.x: The majority feared prosecutions would inhibit presidential decisions. Sotomayor's dissent argued the new protection undermined accountability for criminal official conduct. These are attributed rationales.

items.p: A former President seeks dismissal of charges over conduct a court has classified as purely private. What follows from the 2024 immunity rule?
o: Presidential immunity does not bar those charges
Every act committed while in office becomes an official act
The prosecution needs a Senate conviction before it may proceed
The President's motive alone decides whether immunity applies
ow: Being President when an act occurred does not automatically make it official.
The Court rejected an impeachment-first requirement.
Courts classify conduct without relying on allegations about the President's motives.
keys: Presidential immunity does not bar those charges
items.x: Unofficial conduct receives no presidential immunity. A separate defense or other legal barrier may still matter in a particular prosecution.

items.p: After Loper Bright, how does a court review an agency's interpretation of an ambiguous statute?
items.answer: It independently decides the statute's meaning
keys: It independently decides the statute's meaning

o: It independently decides the statute's meaning
It accepts a reasonable agency reading
It requires a new congressional vote
It treats agency expertise as irrelevant
ow: That describes the Chevron deference Loper Bright overruled.
The decision creates no general requirement for a new congressional vote.
Agency reasoning can persuade courts even without binding deference.

items.x: Loper Bright ended Chevron deference. Courts still recognize statutory delegations of discretion and can consider persuasive agency expertise; ambiguity alone does not transfer the legal judgment.

items.p: Match each removal-power case to the rule it supplied at that point in the doctrine.
pairs: Upheld statutory limits on removing FTC commissioners
Rejected protection for the CFPB's single director
Rejected the FTC's for-cause removal protection
items.x: Slaughter overruled Humphrey's Executor, 6 to 3. The majority linked removal to presidential accountability; Sotomayor's dissent defended Congress's agency-design choices.

items.p: After Slaughter, an FTC commissioner argues that disagreement with presidential priorities is insufficient cause for dismissal. What has changed?
o: The FTC's statutory tenure protection is unconstitutional
The President must prove criminal misconduct
Multi-member commissions have stronger protection than before
The Senate must vote separately on FTC removals
ow: Slaughter rejected the statutory for-cause restriction on FTC removals.
The Court rejected reliance on Humphrey's Executor to protect the FTC.
The decision did not impose a Senate-removal vote.
keys: The FTC's statutory tenure protection is unconstitutional
items.x: In June 2026 the Court ruled for the administration. This increases presidential control over FTC leadership; it does not itself resolve every question about other institutions.

items.p: A staffer says Slaughter also let Trump immediately remove Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook. How did the Court treat Cook's case in June 2026?
o: It kept the injunction protecting Cook in place
It automatically applied the FTC result and approved her removal
It held that all allegations of cause were unreviewable in court
It made the Senate responsible for deciding her mortgage allegations
ow: The Court denied the administration's stay application, 5 to 4.
The Court rejected the claim that the President's cause determination was unreviewable.
Courts could review the legal grounds after proper process; no Senate trial was ordered.
keys: It kept the injunction protecting Cook in place
items.x: Cook distinguished the Federal Reserve's history and protections. It required notice and an opportunity to respond, while leaving factual questions about the asserted cause for later proceedings.

units.title: Cases Trump lost
units.desc: Read the holding, procedural stage and response before deciding what a presidential loss establishes.

lessons.title: Access to courts and due process

items.p: In Trump v. Vance, a state grand jury sought President Trump's private financial records from his accountant. What did the Supreme Court decide?
o: Presidential status did not categorically bar the subpoena
A state subpoena first required impeachment conviction
State investigators had to wait until every presidential term had ended
Private records became executive-privileged when their owner took office
ow: The Court imposed no impeachment-first rule for the subpoena.
The Court rejected categorical immunity for a sitting President.
Personal financial records do not acquire blanket executive privilege on taking office.
keys: Presidential status did not categorically bar the subpoena
items.x: Vance (2020), 7 to 2, rejected categorical immunity and a special heightened-need standard. It allowed ordinary objections to the subpoena and did not decide whether a sitting President could be criminally tried.

items.p: Texas asked the Supreme Court to challenge other states' 2020 election results, and Trump sought to join. Why did the Court refuse Texas's case?
o: Texas lacked standing to challenge how those states ran elections
The Court disproved every allegation at trial
Trump had conceded, making the dispute moot
The Court assigned the dispute exclusively to state courts
ow: The Court denied leave for lack of standing; it did not conduct a trial on every allegation.
The stated ground was Texas’s lack of standing.
The order concerns Texas’s standing rather than a categorical exclusive-state-court rule.
keys: Texas lacked standing to challenge how those states ran elections
items.x: Texas v. Pennsylvania failed for lack of a legally cognizable state interest. Alito and Thomas would have allowed filing but would have granted no other relief; avoid treating this as a simple merits vote.

items.p: Why did the Court block rapid Alien Enemies Act removals in A.A.R.P. v. Trump?
items.answer: Detainees needed meaningful notice and time to seek judicial review
keys: Detainees needed meaningful notice and time to seek judicial review

o: Detainees needed meaningful notice and time to seek judicial review
The proclamation had expired before the removals could occur
Only immigration-court review could authorize the removals
The Court held every use of the Act unlawful
ow: The ruling focused on meaningful notice and access to review, rather than expiration of the proclamation.
The Court required time to seek judicial review; it did not impose that categorical immigration-court prerequisite.
The Court reserved the broader legality of the administration’s use of the Act.

items.x: The May 2025 ruling, 7 to 2, held that the rushed notice did not supply meaningful time to challenge removal. It protected access to a hearing without deciding the full legality of the administration's use of the Act.

items.p: In Noem v. Abrego Garcia, what obligation did the Supreme Court preserve after his removal to El Salvador violated a withholding order?
o: The government had to facilitate his release
The President had to pardon him before any release could occur
The courts could require El Salvador itself to transfer him
The removal became lawful once he left US territory
ow: The preserved obligation was facilitation; no pardon was required.
The Court directed US officials and required attention to foreign-affairs limits.
The government acknowledged the removal violated the withholding order.
keys: The government had to facilitate his release
items.x: The April 2025 order had no recorded dissent. It preserved facilitation while requiring clarification of the lower court's direction to effectuate return, with deference to executive foreign-affairs authority.

items.p: A policy analyst cites Abrego Garcia as proof that a Supreme Court order always produces immediate, complete relief. What does the subsequent record show?
o: Return and further litigation over relief
An immediate return followed by dismissal of every proceeding
A ruling that the original removal was lawful after all
A pardon that permanently barred immigration proceedings
ow: The record describes continuing disputes over the relief after return.
The Supreme Court recognized the acknowledged illegality of removal to El Salvador.
Return did not provide blanket immunity from immigration proceedings.
keys: Return and further litigation over relief
items.x: A July 2025 district-court opinion records his June return to face criminal charges and further litigation over supervision and possible third-country removal. This illustrates the gap between obtaining a ruling and implementing relief.

items.p: In Learning Resources v. Trump (2026), which presidential claim did the Supreme Court reject?
o: That IEEPA authorized the challenged tariffs
That Congress could delegate tariff authority
That a President could declare emergencies
That tariffs could continue after the emergency declaration expired
ow: The ruling concerned what IEEPA actually authorized, rather than a general ban on delegated tariff powers.
The Court rejected this claimed tariff authority rather than the ability to declare emergencies.
The question decided was statutory authorization, rather than extension after an emergency expired.
keys: That IEEPA authorized the challenged tariffs
items.x: The 6 to 3 judgment held IEEPA did not authorize tariffs. As the AI Emergency Powers course explains, the source and scope of statutory authority matter even after an emergency declaration.

items.p: In Trump v. Thompson (2022), Trump sought to stop release of presidential records to the January 6 committee. What did the Supreme Court do?
o: Denied the requested stay and injunction
Upheld a former President’s absolute privilege over the records
Required Congress to prosecute a crime before requesting records
Resolved the dispute by recognizing congressional control over all executive communications
ow: The Court denied relief and left broader former-President privilege questions unresolved.
The denial did not impose a criminal-prosecution prerequisite for congressional access.
The order did not grant Congress unlimited control over executive communications.
keys: Denied the stay and injunction
items.x: The Court denied relief, with only Thomas recording that he would grant it. The appeals court had rejected Trump's claims even under the tests for an incumbent, so the Court left broader former-president privilege questions unresolved.

items.p: Match each ruling to the question it actually resolved.
pairs: How broadly an injunction could protect nonparties
Citizenship for US-born children of unlawfully or temporarily present parents
Categorical immunity from a state criminal subpoena
items.x: CASA was a remedy-scope win for the administration. Barbara later rejected its birthright citizenship position, with a 6 to 3 judgment and five justices joining the majority opinion. A win on procedure does not guarantee a win on substance.

units.title: Impeachment, removal and disqualification
units.desc: How accusation, removal, inability and ballot disqualification use different institutions and thresholds.

items.p: In Trump’s second impeachment trial, 57 senators voted guilty and 43 voted not guilty. What was the result?
o: Acquittal, because conviction required 67 votes
Conviction, because a majority found him guilty
Disqualification, because he had already left office
A retrial, because neither side reached two thirds
ow: Conviction requires two thirds of senators present.
Leaving office does not turn a failed conviction into disqualification.
Failure to reach the conviction threshold produces acquittal.
keys: acquittal
67 needed
items.x: All 100 senators voted in 2021, so 67 guilty votes were needed. Seven Republicans voted to convict; the total was ten short. A cross-party majority can still fail the constitutional threshold.

items.p: Put the usual steps for removing a sitting President through impeachment in order.
items: The House approves articles by a simple majority
The Senate tries the impeachment charges
Two thirds of senators present vote to convict, removing the President
items.x: Impeachment is the House’s accusation. Removal follows Senate conviction, so winning the House vote alone does not transfer presidential power.

items.p: Why can a serious abuse of presidential power be impeachable even if no criminal statute covers it?
items.answer: Impeachment can address serious violations of the public trust; it is not limited to indictable crimes.
keys: serious abuse of public trust
no statutory crime required
items.x: CRS describes congressional practice as reaching serious noncriminal misconduct. The boundaries of “high Crimes and Misdemeanors” remain disputed, and Congress applies the standard in each case.

o: Serious breaches of public trust can qualify
Any policy disagreement qualifies once the House votes
Only offenses punishable by imprisonment qualify
A court must first recognize a new criminal offense
ow: The historical standard concerns serious misconduct, rather than routine policy disputes.
Congressional practice includes noncriminal abuses of office.
Impeachment does not require creating or proving a criminal charge.

items.p: Match each presidential impeachment to its Senate outcome.
pairs: Acquitted after conflict over Reconstruction and removals
Acquitted on perjury and obstruction charges
Acquitted on abuse of power and obstruction of Congress
items.x: These four impeachments produced no presidential removal. An impeachment can expose alleged misconduct and force a vote while still falling short of the Senate threshold.

items.p: The Senate convicts an official. Under Senate precedent, what additional vote can bar that official from future federal office?
o: A separate simple-majority disqualification vote
A second two-thirds conviction vote
A majority vote in both chambers sent to the President
A Supreme Court judgment approving the Senate verdict
ow: Senate practice distinguishes the two-thirds conviction threshold from the later disqualification vote.
Disqualification after conviction is a Senate judgment.
The Constitution gives the Senate the trial power without Supreme Court approval.
keys: conviction first
separate majority vote
items.x: Disqualification can follow conviction; a bare Senate majority cannot use this route to bypass a failed conviction. Article I separately preserves ordinary criminal prosecution.

items.p: Trump left office before his 2021 Senate trial. How did the Senate address the argument that it could no longer try him?
o: It voted that the trial could proceed
Automatic acquittal on departure
It required the Supreme Court to authorize jurisdiction
It converted impeachment into a criminal prosecution
ow: The Senate rejected that jurisdictional objection before acquitting on the charge.
The Senate decided its own authority to proceed.
Impeachment remains separate from criminal prosecution.
keys: Senate allowed trial
items.x: The Senate voted 56 to 44 that a former President could face trial for acts committed while President. Opponents argued removal was unavailable after departure; supporters emphasized the remaining possibility of disqualification.

items.p: A staffer suggests using Section 4 of the 25th Amendment because Congress opposes the President’s policies. What is the central problem?
o: It addresses inability and requires the Vice President
It addresses misconduct and starts with a House majority
It addresses a disputed election and starts in state court
It addresses criminal liability and starts with an indictment
ow: That describes impeachment’s general subject and initial institution.
Section 4 concerns presidential inability to discharge duties.
A criminal charge does not initiate the inability process.
keys: inability
Vice President required
items.x: Section 4 requires the Vice President plus a majority of department heads, or the Vice President plus a majority of an alternative body Congress creates. The VP becomes Acting President; sustaining a contested inability finding requires two thirds of both Houses.

items.p: In Trump v. Anderson, what did all nine justices agree Colorado could not do?
o: Exclude Trump under Section 3 from its presidential ballot
Apply state constitutional rules to congressional elections
Impeach a President for misconduct connected to an election
Disqualify a federal candidate after Senate conviction
ow: Anderson concerned Section 3 eligibility; Moore addresses state election-law constraints.
The Court did not decide Congress’s impeachment powers.
The case concerned unilateral state enforcement, rather than Senate punishment.
keys: state cannot exclude presidential candidate under Section 3
items.x: Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment concerns certain oath-takers who engage in insurrection or rebellion. In 2024 the Court reversed Colorado. Five justices required congressional legislation for federal enforcement; separate opinions objected to that broader reasoning.

units.title: Third terms and the 22nd Amendment
units.desc: Separate the clear election limit, the disputed succession theory and the amendment route.

items.p: Franklin Roosevelt won election to a third and then a fourth presidential term. What constitutional change followed?
o: The 22nd Amendment imposed limits on presidential elections
The 12th Amendment created an eight-year lifetime limit
The 25th Amendment prohibited succession by former presidents
Article II created a renewable single six-year term
ow: The 12th Amendment concerns presidential and vice-presidential election procedure.
The 25th Amendment addresses succession, vacancies and disability.
The four-year term remained; the 22nd added election limits.
keys: The 22nd Amendment imposed limits on presidential elections
items.x: Roosevelt broke the two-term precedent established by Washington. The 22nd Amendment, ratified in 1951, made a presidential election limit binding constitutional law.

items.p: What does the 22nd Amendment expressly prohibit for someone already elected President twice?
items.answer: Being elected President a third time
keys: Being elected President a third time

o: Being elected President a third time
Holding any federal office again
Serving more than eight total years under any circumstances
Serving as a presidential adviser after leaving office
ow: The amendment addresses election to the presidency, not a general ban on federal office.
The successor rule can permit more than eight years of service.
Advisory roles are not presidential elections.

items.x: The text limits election to the presidency. Succession raises a separate interpretive dispute, addressed later in this unit.

items.p: A Vice President succeeds with three years left in the predecessor's term and serves all three. How many times may that person then be elected President?
o: One subsequent presidential election
Two, since inherited service never counts
Three if the terms are nonconsecutive
None, because succession counts as two elections
ow: Serving more than two years of another person's term activates the one-election limit.
The amendment has no nonconsecutive-term exception.
Succession does not prohibit every subsequent election.
keys: One subsequent presidential election
items.x: The amendment permits only one subsequent election after more than two years of another President's elected term. This is why counting elections alone is insufficient for a successor.

items.p: A President wins two elections separated by a term out of office. Does the break permit a third presidential election under the current 22nd Amendment?
o: No; the limit covers consecutive and nonconsecutive elections alike
Yes; the two-election limit resets after a term out of office
Yes; only service under the same party label counts together
No; a former President may never seek even a second nonconsecutive term
ow: The text contains no reset for nonconsecutive terms.
Party labels do not alter the amendment's limit.
A second election is permissible; a third is barred.
keys: No; the limit covers consecutive and nonconsecutive elections alike
items.x: The text says more than twice, without limiting that rule to consecutive elections. Ordinary legislation cannot create a gap-year exception to that constitutional rule.

items.p: Why is the proposal that a twice-elected President become Vice President and then succeed to office legally contested?
o: Whether the election limit also bars vice-presidential eligibility
Whether a new party nomination resets the election count
Whether Senate confirmation can waive constitutional eligibility
Whether the 25th Amendment imposes an eight-year lifetime limit
ow: Changing party nominations does not reset the Twenty-Second Amendment election count.
The dispute is about the interaction of constitutional provisions, rather than a Senate power to waive them.
The Twenty-Fifth Amendment concerns succession and inability, rather than an eight-year lifetime limit.
keys: Whether the Twenty-Second Amendment election limit makes a person constitutionally ineligible under the Twelfth Amendment
items.x: CRS describes the crux: the 22nd limits election, while the 12th bars someone constitutionally ineligible for the presidency from the vice presidency. Peabody and Gant argue election and service differ; other commentators read the provisions as a bar.

items.p: Using Article V's congressional proposal route, what support is needed to change the presidential election limit?
items.answer: Two-thirds of each house, then three-fourths of states
keys: Two-thirds of each house, then three-fourths of states

o: Two-thirds of each house, then three-fourths of states
A majority in each house and presidential signature
Two-thirds of senators and judicial approval
Three-fourths of electors and a referendum
ow: An ordinary bill cannot amend the Constitution.
That combines a treaty-like threshold with an approval step Article V does not require.
Article V assigns neither the Electoral College nor a national referendum this role.

items.x: The state ratification threshold is 38 of 50 states. Article V also permits a convention proposal route initiated by two-thirds of state legislatures; state ratification remains required.

items.p: Put the congressional route for amending the presidential election limit in order.
items: Two-thirds of each house proposes amendment text
The proposed amendment goes to states for ratification
Three-fourths of states ratify, making it part of the Constitution
items.x: Article V separates proposal from ratification. A proposal introduced by one member has completed neither threshold.

items.p: Representative Andy Ogles introduced H.J.Res.29 in 2025. What would its proposed text change if adopted and ratified?
o: Permit three elections, while barring another election after two consecutive elections
Allow any President unlimited elections after a one-term break
Let the President suspend the 22nd Amendment by executive order
Keep the current limit while making vice-presidential succession automatic
ow: The proposal retains a three-election ceiling.
It proposes constitutional change rather than an executive waiver.
Its operative text changes the presidential election limit.
keys: Permit three elections, while barring another election after two consecutive elections
items.x: The proposal would permit three elections while barring any additional election after two consecutive elections. Its introduction did not change the Constitution; the Article V thresholds still apply.

units.title: Elections and certification
units.desc: Who sets election rules, how electoral votes are counted, and which safeguards address certification and districting disputes.

items.p: North Carolina legislators argued that the federal Elections Clause insulated their congressional maps from state constitutional review. What did Moore v. Harper decide?
o: State constitutional limits still apply
State courts lose election authority
Congress must approve state rulings
Presidents resolve conflicts between legislatures and courts
ow: The Court rejected immunity from ordinary state constitutional review.
Moore established no congressional approval requirement.
The President gained no election-law arbitration power.
keys: state constitutional review remains
items.x: The 2023 decision was 6 to 3. States regulate congressional elections, subject to Congress’s power to make or alter rules. State courts remain subject to federal review if they exceed ordinary judicial review.

items.p: A candidate asks the Vice President to reject a state’s electoral votes during the congressional count. What does the Electoral Count Reform Act say?
o: The Vice President cannot make that decision
Rejection after consulting governors
Rejection if one chamber agrees
The Vice President may delay the count to investigate fraud
ow: Consultation does not create unilateral power to reject electoral votes.
Objections go through the statutory process in both chambers.
The presiding role is ministerial and carries no independent dispute-resolution power.
keys: ministerial
no unilateral rejection
items.x: The 2022 law expressly makes the Vice President’s role ministerial, meaning procedural. It denies unilateral authority to determine, accept, reject or resolve disputes over electoral votes.

items.p: Under the Electoral Count Reform Act, how much support is needed to bring an electoral-vote objection before Congress?
items.answer: A written objection signed by at least one fifth of each chamber’s duly chosen and sworn members.
keys: one fifth House
one fifth Senate
written
items.x: Qualifying only opens consideration. Sustaining an objection requires separate agreement by both Houses, and objections are limited to statutory grounds.

o: Written support from one fifth of each chamber
Written support from one representative and one senator
A majority of either chamber plus the Vice President
Two thirds of senators present, with no House signatures
ow: The 2022 law raised the old one-member-per-chamber threshold.
Both chambers must meet the signature threshold, and the VP cannot substitute for it.
That resembles the impeachment conviction threshold, rather than an electoral-count objection.

items.p: A presidential campaign challenges a governor’s certificate naming the state’s electors. Which safeguard did the Electoral Count Reform Act create?
o: Expedited court review that can correct the certificate
A congressional committee that recounts every disputed ballot
A Vice Presidential hearing that selects between competing slates
A new election automatically triggered by a candidate’s challenge
ow: The law provides a judicial route, rather than a congressional ballot recount.
The Vice President has no such power over competing slates.
Filing a challenge does not automatically require another election.
keys: expedited judicial review
court-ordered certificate supersedes
items.x: 3 U.S.C. 5 provides expedited review by three district judges with direct Supreme Court appeal in specified candidate suits. A certificate required by judicial relief granted before electors meet supersedes earlier certificates. Certification deadlines therefore make prompt legal action consequential.

items.p: A redistricting team must distinguish three election-law decisions. Match each case to the rule it changed.
pairs: Federal courts cannot decide partisan-gerrymandering claims
The old formula triggering Section 5 preclearance was invalidated
A Louisiana map failed scrutiny under a narrower Section 2 framework
items.x: These doctrines govern different claims. Rucho leaves state-law remedies available; Shelby County addressed advance approval of voting changes; Callais addressed racial districting. A mid-decade redraw still requires examining the particular legal claim.

items.p: Why did the majority and Kagan’s dissent disagree over Section 2 in Louisiana v. Callais in April 2026?
o: Majority tightened proof rules; the dissent saw an intent test
Whether race may ever be considered when remedying a proven violation
Whether partisan fairness replaces racial vote-dilution analysis
Whether Section 5 preclearance should have applied to the map
ow: The dispute concerns the narrowed test for proving a Section 2 violation, rather than a categorical ban on race-conscious remedies.
Callais addresses racial vote dilution and constitutional scrutiny, rather than a partisan-fairness standard.
The dispute concerns Section 2 liability and racial districting, rather than Section 5 advance approval.
keys: Majority narrowed proof of racial vote dilution where nonracial explanations exist
Kagan said the test effectively required intent despite the effects-based statute
items.x: The 6 to 3 majority said Section 2 did not require Louisiana’s additional majority-Black district, so race could not justify the map. Kagan argued the new test effectively required discriminatory intent despite Congress’s effects-based statute.

items.p: Trump’s March 2025 election order directed documentary proof of citizenship on the federal registration form. Why did a district court pause that directive in April 2025?
o: The President lacked authority to impose it unilaterally
The Constitution gives election regulation solely to federal judges
Federal law allows noncitizens to vote for President
States lack any role in registering federal-election voters
ow: Election authority is distributed between states and Congress, with courts reviewing legal disputes.
Citizenship is required for voting in federal elections.
States administer registration within constitutional and statutory constraints.
keys: President lacked unilateral authority
items.x: CRS explains that the injunction turned on executive authority under existing law. Congress can legislate election rules, and states administer elections; presidential preferences need a legal basis. This dated ruling concerns the specified directive, rather than every part of the order.

items.p: An official proposes armed federal agents inside polling places as routine election security. What does 18 U.S.C. 592 require the legal team to flag?
o: A criminal ban with a narrow armed-enemy exception
Permission during a declared emergency
Permission if agents avoid handling ballots
A rule covering soldiers while exempting civilian federal officials
ow: The statute does not contain a general emergency exception.
The prohibition concerns having troops or armed men at the election place.
Its text covers people in the civil as well as military service of the United States.
keys: troops or armed men at polls banned
armed-enemy exception
items.x: The statutory exception is force necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States. Federal election enforcement authority does not erase this separate restriction on armed presence at polls.

units.title: Executive power tools
units.desc: Military missions, personnel, prosecutions, clemency, spending and oversight each have their own legal limits.

items.p: In December 2025, the administration asked the Supreme Court to lift a block on deploying federalized Guard troops in Illinois. What did the Court do?
o: Denied the stay, leaving the deployment blocked
Granted the stay because federalization authorizes policing
Dismissed the case because Guard orders cannot be reviewed
Required the governor to request an Insurrection Act deployment
ow: The Court found the government had not shown the claimed statutory authority.
The Court decided the stay request and reserved some reviewability questions.
The order imposed no such requirement on the governor.
keys: stay denied
emergency-stage ruling
items.x: The vote was 6 to 3. The Court provisionally read “regular forces” in 10 U.S.C. 12406(3) as the military, affecting when the Guard could be called. This was an emergency-stage ruling; Kavanaugh agreed on narrower reasoning.

items.p: Match each military-power rule to the question it primarily answers.
pairs: Is military execution of civilian law expressly authorized?
Do specified domestic conditions permit military enforcement?
Do statutory conditions permit calling the Guard into federal service?
items.x: Calling the Guard into federal service and deciding what it may do are separate legal questions. Insurrection Act authority depends on its conditions; using it also requires a proclamation ordering dispersal.

items.p: What is the core employment change in OPM’s February 2026 Schedule Policy/Career rule?
o: Fewer removal procedures for designated career policy positions
Senate confirmation for every employee who influences policy
A statutory loyalty oath for every career federal employee
Automatic replacement of the whole civil service after elections
ow: The rule concerns employment protections, rather than Senate confirmation.
OPM says positions remain career jobs without political loyalty requirements.
The classification targets designated policy-influencing positions.
keys: designated career positions
fewer adverse-action procedures
items.x: The restored Schedule F approach was renamed Schedule Policy/Career in 2025. OPM argues fewer removal procedures increase accountability; Senators Shaheen, Kaine and Van Hollen warn that weaker protections invite political pressure. Positions remain career jobs under the rule.

items.p: Why do Justice Department rules restrict White House contacts about particular prosecutions?
items.answer: To reduce partisan or personal influence on individual law-enforcement decisions.
keys: reduce inappropriate influence
individual prosecution decisions
items.x: The published Justice Manual guidelines describe independence and integrity as the purpose. Appointment law supplies a separate check: in November 2025 a court dismissed Comey and James indictments over the prosecutor’s unlawful appointment, without deciding the charges’ substance.

o: To reduce partisan influence on individual cases
To place federal prosecutors outside the executive branch
To require Congress to approve charges
To prevent the Attorney General from supervising prosecutors
ow: DOJ remains within the executive branch.
Congress does not generally approve individual indictments.
Contact rules preserve supervision while limiting inappropriate influence.

items.p: Trump’s January 2025 proclamation pardoned covered January 6 convictions and commuted named sentences. What limit applies to presidential pardons?
o: They cover federal offenses and cannot undo impeachment
They cover state offenses whenever related federal charges exist
They require approval by a majority of the Senate
They automatically prevent victims from bringing civil claims
ow: A presidential pardon does not reach state criminal offenses.
The Constitution grants the pardon power without Senate approval.
A pardon addresses criminal consequences and does not generally extinguish private civil claims.
keys: federal offenses
impeachment exception
items.x: Article II authorizes clemency for offenses against the United States, with an impeachment exception. The January 20 proclamation also directed dismissal of pending covered cases. Legal authority to grant clemency and judgments about its wisdom are separate questions.

items.p: A President wants to cancel appropriated spending for policy reasons. Under the Impoundment Control Act’s rescission process, whose agreement is needed?
items.answer: Congress must enact the cancellation; a presidential proposal alone does not make it permanent.
keys: Congress enacts cancellation
items.x: Under the rescission process, funds may generally be withheld for 45 days of continuous congressional session. GAO reads the Act to require release without enacted cancellation and in time for prudent obligation before funds expire. A proposal does not itself cancel an appropriation.

o: Congress must enact the rescission
The President can cancel after sending Congress notice
The budget office can permanently cancel by memorandum
The Supreme Court must approve every requested rescission
ow: Notice begins the statutory process and does not itself enact cancellation.
An executive memorandum cannot replace the required legislation.
The ordinary rescission process requires congressional action.

items.p: A President orders an inspector general’s immediate removal. Which statutory protection should a staffer check first?
o: Advance notice to Congress with case-specific reasons
A two-thirds Senate vote authorizing the dismissal
A finding of criminal guilt by a federal court
Written approval from the official whose agency was investigated
ow: The statute uses congressional notice rather than an impeachment-style vote.
A criminal conviction is not a general prerequisite for removal.
Agency approval does not replace the President’s statutory notice obligations.
keys: 30-day congressional notice
case-specific reasons
items.x: 5 U.S.C. 403 requires written notice to both Houses at least 30 days before removal, with a substantive rationale and detailed, case-specific reasons. Inspectors general investigate agency waste and misconduct, so removal procedures affect oversight capacity.

items.p: A staffer says federalizing the Guard settles whether troops may conduct civilian arrests. What additional question matters?
o: Whether law expressly authorizes the policing task
Whether the governor’s party supports the President
Whether a declaration calls the operation temporary
Whether Congress has voted to criticize the deployment
ow: Political alignment does not establish a statutory policing exception.
A temporary label does not by itself authorize military law enforcement.
Congressional criticism is distinct from the law governing the mission.
keys: mission needs legal authority
command status separate from policing
items.x: The Posse Comitatus Act generally bars using covered armed forces to execute civilian laws without express constitutional or statutory authorization. The authority to place troops under federal command does not settle every permitted activity.

units.title: Scenarios: applying the checks
units.desc: Use earlier rules in realistic disputes: calculate thresholds, distinguish legal questions, and identify who can act.

items.p: A Senate staffer counts 59 votes to convict a President. Exactly 90 senators are present for the impeachment vote. What should the staffer tell the office?
o: Conviction fails: 60 votes are required
It takes 67 votes regardless of attendance
59 votes satisfies the majority threshold
The Vice President can cast the 60th vote
ow: Two-thirds applies to senators present: 60 of 90, rather than a fixed 67.
A simple majority does not meet the conviction threshold.
The Vice President cannot replace a missing vote to meet the two-thirds threshold.
items.x: Two-thirds of 90 is 60. The denominator is senators present, so the familiar 67-vote figure assumes all 100 attend.
keys: Two-thirds of 90 is 60
59 is one vote short

items.p: At the electoral count, an objection on a statutory ground has 20 Senate signatures and 87 House signatures. All 100 senators and 435 representatives are sworn. What has that support achieved?
o: It meets the threshold for considering the objection
The state’s electors are now invalid
Only Senate approval is now needed to reject the votes
The Vice President decides the objection
ow: Signatures trigger consideration; both chambers must sustain an objection before votes are rejected.
Separate concurring decisions by both chambers are required.
The Vice President has no unilateral power to resolve the dispute.
items.x: One-fifth is 20 of 100 and 87 of 435. The signature threshold opens consideration; it does not decide the objection.
keys: Meets one-fifth signature threshold
Both chambers must separately sustain objection

items.p: A policy aide says presidential criminal immunity supplies legal authority for a disputed executive order. What distinction should counsel make?
items.answer: Immunity limits criminal prosecution of a former President; the order still needs legal authority from the Constitution or a statute.
keys: Criminal immunity concerns prosecution
Order needs constitutional or statutory authority

o: Immunity concerns prosecution; the order needs legal authority
Immunity supplies authority for official orders
Immunity makes an order’s legality unreviewable in civil cases
Immunity bars private-act charges after a Senate acquittal
ow: Immunity from prosecution does not itself supply authority to issue an order.
Criminal immunity and review of an order’s legal authority are separate questions.
The Court recognized no presidential immunity for unofficial acts.

items.x: Trump v. United States separates official and unofficial conduct for criminal immunity. The opinion also repeats that presidential authority must come from a statute or the Constitution.

items.p: An amendment removing presidential election term limits passes Congress by the required two-thirds in each chamber. Thirty-six states ratify it. With 50 states, is it part of the Constitution?
o: No: ratification needs 38 states
Yes: two-thirds of states is enough after Congress acts
Yes: the President can supply the final approval
No: every state must approve this kind of amendment
ow: Article V requires three-fourths of states, which is 38 of 50.
The President has no constitutional role in approving an Article V amendment.
Article V requires three-fourths here; unanimity applies to depriving a state of equal Senate suffrage without its consent.
items.x: Three-fourths of 50 is 37.5, so at least 38 states must ratify. An ordinary statute cannot remove the Twenty-Second Amendment's election limit.
keys: Three-fourths of states
38 needed; 36 insufficient

lessons.title: From a ruling to a remedy

items.p: A nonprofit wins an injunction against a federal policy. Before telling every affected person they are protected, what should its lawyer check after Trump v. CASA?
items.answer: Check the injunction's actual scope, including who receives complete relief and whether a certified class is covered.
keys: Actual scope of injunction
Complete relief and class coverage

o: The order’s beneficiaries and any certified class
A merits ruling makes coverage universal
Living in the judicial district guarantees coverage
Facing the same policy automatically gives coverage
ow: A ruling on legality does not automatically provide universal relief.
The injunction’s scope turns on complete relief and applicable procedures, rather than district residence alone.
Being affected by the policy does not automatically establish coverage under the injunction.

items.x: CASA limited relief exceeding what plaintiffs need for complete relief, while distinguishing class actions. Winning a legal argument and obtaining relief for every affected person are separate issues.

items.p: An opposition coalition wins an election and takes office. A briefing says this proves earlier concerns about unequal media access were unfounded. What is the best assessment?
o: Turnover can coexist with unequal competition
Turnover shows the campaign conditions must have been equal
A coalition government cannot establish a democratic mandate
Earlier institutional problems require annulling the result
ow: An opposition victory does not by itself establish equal campaign conditions.
Coalitions can legitimately govern where they command the required parliamentary support.
An assessment of unequal conditions does not itself establish a requirement to annul an election.
items.x: Poland’s 2023 election was competitive but affected by misuse of public resources and public-media bias, according to international observers. Tusk’s coalition nevertheless took office. Turnover and the fairness of competition answer different questions.
keys: Opposition victory can coexist with unequal conditions
Examine campaign environment separately from turnover

items.p: Researchers Lauren Miller and Will Wilder warn about certification refusals. Which risk persists even if the underlying vote count is accurate?
o: They can delay official completion and force urgent litigation
They make the local board the final judge of fraud allegations
They trigger a recount under a uniform national rule
They send disputed local returns straight to Congress
ow: The researchers describe certification as a mandatory duty, with legal challenges handled through separate procedures.
Recount rules vary by state; refusal does not create a uniform federal recount process.
State and local certification disputes arise before the congressional electoral count.
keys: Certification refusal can delay completion despite an accurate tally
Urgent legal remedies may be needed
items.x: Miller and Wilder describe certification as a mandatory duty that officials have nevertheless tried to obstruct. Their risk scenario concerns delay and disruption, rather than a lawful power to discard votes. State remedies can compel certification or permit other officials to complete it.

items.p: A presidential candidate challenges a governor's elector certificate in federal court under 3 USC 5. Why might speed matter to whether a court order can affect the count?
o: Judicial correction must fit the statutory election calendar
Filing a suit suspends the certification deadline
A pending challenge prevents electors from meeting
Supreme Court review must finish before any certificate can issue
ow: Section 5 provides expedited review rather than an automatic suspension of the calendar.
Filing alone does not prevent the electors from meeting.
The statute contemplates an initial certificate and potential judicial correction, rather than mandatory prior Supreme Court review.
items.x: Section 5 provides expedited three-judge review and direct Supreme Court appeal for specified candidate claims. It gives timely judicially revised certificates priority, making the calendar part of the remedy.
keys: Fixed electoral deadlines
Expedited judicial review

items.p: In this hypothetical, a governor issues a certificate, a candidate wins a timely court order revising it, and electors then vote. Put these certification-to-count events in order.
items: Governor issues the initial elector certificate
Court orders a timely revised certificate
Electors meet and cast their votes
Congress counts the transmitted electoral votes
items.x: This sequence assumes a timely successful suit and compliance with the order. Section 5 gives a timely judicially revised certificate priority; section 15 governs the later count in Congress.

democracy.description: How democracies erode, how to assess the evidence, and which US legal rules shape executive power and elections.
caveat: Prepared October 23, 2026 from public sources. Legal rules are simplified; dated rulings and scenarios are distinguished from predictions. Research and question quality were reviewed by separate AI agents. No person has reviewed this course. Check current law before relying on it.

lingo.name: Staff Talk

units.title: The Polite No
units.desc: Most meetings end warmly. Learn to tell warmth from commitment.

items.q: “We’re monitoring the issue closely.”
o: They’re quietly drafting their own bill on it
No position, and no plans for one soon
They support it but can’t say so publicly
They’re opposed and plan to work against it
items.x: “Monitoring” is the standard holding phrase. It commits the office to nothing. If they were drafting something, they would usually say so, because offices want advocates to know they’re leading.
items.ask: “Is the boss likely to take a position this Congress, or is this one you’re watching for now?”

items.q: “I’ll definitely take this back to the boss.”
o: The member will read your materials personally and get back to you
A routine way to close; it tells you little either way
A soft yes
A soft no
items.x: Staff say this at the end of nearly every meeting. The real signal comes later: a follow-up email with specific questions means it went somewhere. Silence means it probably didn’t.
items.ask: “What would be most useful for me to send before you brief her?”

items.q: “The senator is supportive of the goals of the bill.”
o: She’ll cosponsor if asked; the office just needs a formal request
She likes the idea but isn’t ready to sign on to this text
She’s already a cosponsor
She opposes it
items.x: Praising the “goals” separates the idea from the bill. It lets the office say nice things without signing on. For now, it usually means no cosponsorship.
items.ask: “What would need to change in the text for her to sign on?”

items.q: “That’s a heavy lift this Congress.”
o: It’s hard, but the office will push for it anyway
It probably won’t move this Congress
They need help counting votes before it can move
It’s headed to markup soon, though the vote will be close
items.x: “Heavy lift” is usually a polite forecast that nothing will happen. Sometimes it’s an accurate read of the floor; sometimes it covers the office not wanting to try. Either way, don’t plan around passage.
items.ask: “What would make it lighter: a different vehicle, a narrower version, or more Republicans on board?”

items.q: “Happy to keep the lines of communication open.”
o: They want monthly check-ins
The meeting is over and nothing was committed
They want to be the lead office
They want you to testify
items.x: This is a goodbye. It keeps the relationship friendly without promising anything. A follow-up is fine, but don’t read this line as interest.

items.q: “We’d want to see who else is on before we commit.”
o: A polite brush-off, since they expect no one else will sign on
A real condition: they want other offices to sign on first
They want polling on how the bill plays in their state
A firm yes
items.x: One of the more useful lines you’ll hear. Offices want political cover, especially from the other party or their own state delegation. It’s a request for information you can actually meet.
items.ask: “Which offices’ support would matter most to the senator?”

items.q: “The boss has some concerns.”
o: A firm no
Real but unnamed objections, about policy or politics
They want a bigger, more ambitious version before signing on
The boss already supports it and is just being careful
items.x: Concerns can mean a fixable drafting problem or an in-district company lobbying against the bill. The office often won’t say which unless you ask, so your job is to find out.
items.ask: “Are the concerns about the policy itself, or about who’s opposing it?”

items.p: You ask a Hill staffer whether their boss will cosponsor a bill. Put these replies in order from coldest to warmest.
items: “We’re monitoring it.”
“The boss supports the goals.”
“We’d want to see who else is on.”
“Can you send the text and the cosponsor list?”
“Who should I talk to in the lead sponsor’s office?”
items.x: Roughly: watching, then praising the idea, then naming a condition, then asking for materials, then asking how to join. Treat this as a rule of thumb. A particular staffer’s habits can reshuffle the middle.

units.title: Process Words
units.desc: The vocabulary of how a bill actually moves.

items.p: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Committee session where members amend and vote on a bill
A bill likely to pass that other provisions can ride on
A spending cut or revenue that offsets a bill’s cost
CBO’s estimate of what a bill would cost
A letter one office sends to all offices, often seeking cosponsors
items.x: These five come up in almost every legislative meeting.

items.q: “Has it been scored?”
items.p: Why would a staffer ask this?
o: They want your organization’s scorecard rating of the member’s votes
They’re checking for a CBO cost estimate, a sign they’re thinking about passage
They want polling numbers showing how the bill plays back home
They’re asking about the vote count from the committee markup
items.x: Cost matters once a bill might actually move, so this question is usually a sign of real interest. If there’s no score yet, expect to hear the question again.

items.q: “We’d need to find a vehicle for this.”
o: The bill needs a new sponsor
It needs to ride on a must-pass bill instead of moving alone
They need a press event
It needs an identical companion bill introduced in the House before it can move
items.x: Most standalone bills never get floor time. Provisions often ride on bills that have to pass, like the NDAA (the annual defense authorization) or appropriations. A lot of AI policy has moved this way.
items.ask: “Which vehicle looks realistic, and when does that text get locked?”

items.q: “The Chair wants regular order on this.”
o: Leadership will write the final text behind closed doors
It should get hearings and markup before the floor
It should pass by unanimous consent
It should be attached to the budget and skip committee review
items.x: “Regular order” means the textbook process: hearings, markup, then the floor. Hearing it from committee staff means you’ll work through them, and the timeline will be slower.

items.p: A Senate staffer says, “We cannot hotline it while there is a hold.” What should you infer about the bill’s path?
o: A senator objects, so quick passage by unanimous consent is blocked for now.
A committee has rejected it, so the bill must be introduced again next Congress.
Cloture has already failed, so the Senate cannot consider it again this session.
The House must suspend its rules before the Senate can debate the bill.
ow: A hold does not tell you the committee rejected the bill.
A hold does not establish that a cloture vote occurred or failed.
House suspension procedure does not control the Senate.
items.x: A hold signals an objection to moving by unanimous consent. Leadership may negotiate it away or spend floor time using other procedures; cloture is one possible route and is not automatically required in every case.

items.q: “We could try to hotline it.”
o: Call the White House and ask it to weigh in on the bill
Pass it quickly in the Senate if no office objects
Push it through committee without a hearing
Move it to the House floor under suspension of the rules
items.x: Hotlining works for noncontroversial bills. A single hold stops it, which is why staff will ask whether anyone is likely to object.

items.q: “Honestly, it’s a messaging bill.”
o: A bill about telecommunications and media policy
A bill to make a point, not expected to pass
A bill drafted by the member’s press office staff
A bill that already passed by a quick voice vote
items.x: Messaging bills stake out a position for the party or a campaign. Cosponsoring one is cheap, so it tells you less about how the member would vote on a real deal.

items.q: “That’s a Byrd rule problem.”
o: It would violate the Senate’s ethics rules on member conduct
In reconciliation, provisions that aren’t mainly budgetary can be struck
It needs 67 votes to get through the Senate
It conflicts with a House rule on how bills are drafted
items.x: Reconciliation bills pass the Senate with a simple majority, but the Byrd rule lets senators strike provisions that aren’t mainly about the budget. In 2025, the proposed moratorium on state AI laws was rewritten around broadband funding to survive it; the Senate then voted 99-1 to remove it anyway.

units.title: Who’s Who
units.desc: Who you meet tells you how the office is treating your issue.

items.p: Match each title to the job.
pairs: Legislative Director: runs the policy staff and agenda
Legislative Assistant: covers a portfolio of issues
Legislative Correspondent: answers constituent mail, often junior
Runs the office and makes the political calls
Professional Staff Member: committee staffer who works on text
items.x: Personal offices have the LD, LAs and LCs. Committees have their own staff, who usually write the text.

items.p: You asked for a meeting on AI safety. The office books you with the LC instead of the tech LA. What’s the best read?
o: You’ve been snubbed and should escalate
Lower priority for now, but the LC may write the memo the LA reads
The office has no tech LA
The LC is the decision-maker
items.x: Junior staff often take first meetings. Take them seriously: LCs write memos, get promoted, and remember who was useful.
items.ask: “How does this usually get in front of the LA?”

items.q: “That’s really a question for committee staff.”
o: The office opposes the bill but won’t say so directly
The committee writes the text; this office won’t lead
You should take this to the Rules Committee staff instead
They want you to testify at an upcoming committee hearing
items.x: Offices whose member isn’t on the committee that handles the bill rarely shape its text. If they offer an introduction to committee staff, that’s a real step forward.
items.ask: “Would you be willing to connect me with the right person on the committee?”

items.q: “The boss is a yes, but she won’t lead on it.”
o: She’ll introduce it herself next month and look for cosponsors
She’ll vote yes or cosponsor, but won’t push for it
She opposes it
She’ll whip votes for it
items.x: Members have limited bandwidth to lead. A “yes but won’t lead” office gives you a cosponsor, not a champion. You still need a champion somewhere else.

items.p: A bill funds grants to state election offices. Which Senate committee handles election administration law?
o: Judiciary
Rules and Administration
Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
Commerce, Science, and Transportation
items.x: Senate Rules and Administration handles federal election law. In the House it’s the Committee on House Administration. The grant money itself runs through appropriations.

items.p: A bill requires frontier AI developers to report safety incidents. Where would it most likely go in the Senate?
o: Commerce
Rules and Administration
Finance
Agriculture
items.x: Commerce handles most tech regulation, though AI bills can also land in Judiciary, Homeland Security or Armed Services depending on how they’re written. Drafting choices can steer a bill toward a friendlier committee.

items.q: “Could we do this in report language instead?”
o: Put it in a press release
Put it in a spending bill’s committee report instead of in law
Ask CRS to write a report
Enter it into the Congressional Record during floor debate on the bill
items.x: Report language isn’t binding law, but agencies usually follow it because the same committee funds them next year. It’s a much easier ask than a statute and a common win for advocates.

items.q: “Leadership hasn’t weighed in yet.”
o: Leadership quietly opposes it but doesn’t want to say so publicly
Offices are waiting to see if leaders will back it or give it floor time
It’s already scheduled for a floor vote next week
It’s dead, since leadership never takes up bills like this
items.x: Leadership controls the floor. Many offices won’t commit before they know where leadership stands, especially on anything that splits the caucus.
items.ask: “Do you know who in leadership’s office is working on this?”

units.title: Real Interest
units.desc: The signals that mean an office is actually moving.

items.p: In a meeting, what kind of remark from a staffer is the strongest sign of real interest in your bill?
o: “Thanks so much for coming in.”
“This is really helpful context for us to have.”
“Can you send the bill text and who else has signed on?”
“We’ll keep it in mind as things move forward.”
items.x: Requests for specific materials mean someone is preparing to brief the member or make a decision. Thanks and praise are just good manners.

items.q: “What’s the strongest argument against this?”
items.p: A staffer asks you this. What’s the best read?
o: They’re hostile and looking for a reason to oppose the bill
A good sign: they’re preparing to brief the boss
They want to end the meeting and are signaling you should leave
They’re testing your loyalty to the coalition behind the bill
items.x: Staff who might recommend a yes need to know what the boss will be asked. Answer honestly. Spin here costs credibility fast.

items.q: “Could you help us with some language on this?”
o: A polite brush-off to end the meeting on a friendly note
A strong signal: they want drafting help
They want you to write a press statement for the boss
They want you to proofread a bill they’ve already finished
items.x: Small offices rely on outside groups for help with text (staff call this technical assistance, or “TA”). If they want your language, your idea may be going into a bill, though maybe not the bill you came to pitch.
items.ask: “Is this for something the boss is planning to introduce?”

items.q: “Send me a one-pager.”
o: Always a brush-off
Ambiguous: it depends on whether they asked anything specific
Always a strong signal
They want a longer memo
items.x: Sometimes it’s how staff end a meeting. Sometimes they really need something to forward. If they asked pointed questions during the meeting, it’s probably real.

items.p: After the meeting, which follow-up from the office means the most?
o: The staffer says they’ll pass your one-pager to the boss
A thank-you note
The staffer introduces you to committee staff on the issue
You get added to the office newsletter and its event invitation list
items.x: An introduction spends some of the staffer’s own credibility. When they make one, they’re betting your issue is worth the committee’s time.

items.q: “We’re hearing from a lot of stakeholders on this.”
o: There’s broad support for it from many outside groups
Other groups, often opponents, are lobbying too
They want you to bring more groups into the coalition
They’ve already decided and are just being polite
items.x: This usually means industry or other groups are making the opposite case. It’s an opening to find out what they’re hearing.
items.ask: “Who are you hearing from, and what are they saying?”

items.p: After you meet with a Hill office about a bill, put these follow-ups in order from weakest to strongest signal of interest.
items: You’re added to the office newsletter
“Thanks again, we’ll be in touch.”
An email asking two specific questions about the bill
An introduction to the committee staffer on the issue
A request for help drafting language
items.x: Effort is the signal. The more work the staffer does after the meeting, the more the issue is moving. Treat the exact order as a rule of thumb.

units.title: Ask the Next Question
units.desc: Decoding the phrase is half the job. The follow-up gets you the truth.

items.q: “The senator is very engaged on AI, and we’re looking at a range of approaches.”
items.p: What’s the best follow-up?
o: “Great. So will she sign on as a cosponsor of our bill?”
“Is she drafting her own bill on this?”
“I’ll send over a one-pager summarizing our bill.”
“Thanks for your time.”
items.x: Members who want to lead on an issue rarely cosponsor a rival bill. If she’s drafting her own, the realistic win is getting your language into hers.

items.q: “That’s a heavy lift.”
items.p: What’s the best follow-up?
o: “I understand. Thanks anyway for your time today.”
“What would make it lighter?”
“Other offices we’ve met with think it’s easy.”
“Can I meet with the senator directly about it?”
items.x: This turns a vague no into a list of specific obstacles, some of which you might be able to remove.

items.q: “The boss has some concerns.”
items.p: What’s the best follow-up?
o: “Understood, and thanks for flagging them. What are they?”
“Are they about the policy, or who’s opposing it?”
“Other members we’ve met with don’t have any concerns.”
“Can we deal with those later, after the boss signs on?”
items.x: “What are they?” is fine, but separating policy from politics gets you more. Drafting problems can be fixed with text. Political problems need validators or cover.

items.q: “We’ll get back to you.”
items.p: What’s the best follow-up?
o: “Great, thanks. I’ll wait to hear from you.”
“When should I check back, and who should I follow up with?”
“Can you commit now, before I leave the office?”
“I’ll just email your boss directly to follow up.”
items.x: Get a time and a name. It’s polite, and it makes silence informative: if they haven’t answered by then, you’ve learned something.

items.q: “We’d want to see who else is on.”
items.p: What’s the best follow-up?
o: “Don’t worry, everyone’s already on board with it.”
“Which offices matter most to the senator?”
“That’s not a good reason to hold off on signing.”
“OK, thanks. I’ll check back with you in a few weeks.”
items.x: Get specific names. Same-state colleagues, committee members and offices from the other party tend to matter most, but each office has its own list.

items.q: “We don’t usually take positions before markup.”
items.p: What’s the best follow-up?
o: “Could you make an exception, given how much is at stake?”
“Understood. Is the senator weighing any amendments?”
“Then I’ll check back with you after the markup is over.”
“That seems evasive.”
items.x: Committee members often avoid public positions before markup to keep room to negotiate. Amendments are where they actually shape the bill, so ask about those.

lingo.description: A playful, less-verified course on Hill jargon.
caveat: A playful, less-verified course on Hill jargon.
Meanings vary by chamber, party, office and individual staffer. Don’t rely on these answers as guidance; ask someone with relevant Hill experience.

proc.name: Procedure

units.title: The Basic Path
units.desc: How a bill gets from an idea to the floor.

items.p: Put the usual steps for a bill in order, from introduction to the floor.
items: A member introduces the bill
It’s referred to a committee
The committee holds a hearing
The committee marks it up
The committee reports it
The full chamber considers it
items.x: This is the textbook path, often called regular order. Many bills skip the hearing, and leadership sometimes skips committee entirely by bringing a bill straight to the floor.

items.p: Who can formally introduce a bill in the House?
o: Any member of the House
Any member, or the White House
Any registered lobbyist
Only committee chairs
items.x: Only members can introduce bills. Agencies, the White House and outside groups often write the text, but a member has to put it in. In the House that means dropping it in the “hopper,” a box on the floor.

items.p: Under the Constitution, which bills must start in the House?
o: Bills raising revenue
All bills over $1 billion
Treaties
Bills about elections
items.x: The Origination Clause (Article I, Section 7) requires revenue bills to start in the House, and by custom appropriations bills do too. The Senate works around this by taking a House-passed bill and replacing its text. The Affordable Care Act moved on H.R. 3590, which began as a tax bill about homeownership for service members.

items.p: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The member who introduces the bill and leads on it
A member who formally signs on in support
A matching bill introduced in the other chamber
Sending a bill to the committee with jurisdiction
The box on the House floor where new bills are dropped
items.x: A long cosponsor list shows support, but it doesn’t move a bill. The committee does.

items.p: Who usually decides whether a bill gets a hearing or a markup?
o: The chair of the committee
The bill’s sponsor
The minority leader
The chamber’s parliamentarian
items.x: The chair controls the committee’s agenda. A bill the chair won’t schedule usually goes nowhere, whatever its cosponsor count.

items.p: In the House, who refers a new bill to committee?
o: The Speaker, advised by the parliamentarian
The bill’s sponsor, who names a committee when introducing it
The Rules Committee
The Clerk, who assigns new bills to committees by lottery
items.x: Referral is formally the Speaker’s call, made in practice on the parliamentarian’s advice about jurisdiction. A bill can go to several committees, and each one becomes a place where it can stall.

items.q: “The chair is going to mark up her own substitute.”
items.p: What does that tell you?
o: The committee will mark up the chair’s rewrite instead of the original
The bill is dead and won’t get a markup at all
The chair is leaving the committee and naming a substitute
The bill skips markup and goes straight to the floor
items.x: Committees often mark up an “amendment in the nature of a substitute,” which replaces the whole bill. The substitute is the text that matters from then on, so get a copy as soon as it circulates.

items.p: Roughly what share of introduced bills become law in a typical recent Congress?
o: A few percent
About a tenth
About a third
Most of them
items.x: Only a few percent of bills become law, and most never get a committee vote. Many are introduced to stake out a position, with no real plan to pass them.

units.title: The House Floor
units.desc: The majority controls the House floor, mostly through the Rules Committee.

items.p: What does a “rule” from the Rules Committee do?
o: Sets debate time and allowed amendments for one bill
Permanently changes the House’s standing rules for all future bills
Decides whether a bill is constitutional
Schedules committee hearings
items.x: Most major bills reach the House floor under a special rule written for that bill. The House has to adopt the rule by majority vote before it can debate the bill.

items.p: Match each type of rule to what it allows.
pairs: Any germane amendment can be offered
Only amendments the Rules Committee lists
Adopting the rule automatically changes the bill’s text
items.x: Open rules have become rare. Most major bills now come up under structured or closed rules, which lets the majority avoid amendment votes it doesn’t want.

items.p: Why is Rules called “the Speaker’s committee”?
o: The majority holds 9 of its 13 seats, and the Speaker picks them
The Speaker chairs it
It only meets when the Speaker attends
It writes the Speaker’s floor schedule
items.x: The 9 to 4 split and the Speaker’s control over majority appointments make Rules an arm of leadership. That control can slip: as part of his 2023 deal to become Speaker, Kevin McCarthy put hardliners on the committee who could block rules.

news.h: Majority members vote down their own party’s rule

items.p: What happens when a rule fails on the floor?
o: Leadership needs a new rule or another route to bring the bill up
The bill passes automatically without a separate vote
The Senate takes up its own version of the bill instead
The Speaker is removed and a new one must be elected
items.x: Rule votes used to be party-line formalities. Since 2023, hardliners in the majority have sunk rules to protest leadership, which can stall a bill even when it has the votes to pass.

items.p: Under “suspension of the rules,” what does a bill need to pass?
o: Two-thirds of those voting
A simple majority of those voting
60 votes
Unanimous consent
items.x: Most bills the House passes go through suspension, usually noncontroversial ones like naming post offices. It skips the Rules Committee entirely, at the cost of a two-thirds threshold.

news.h: Petition to force a vote on releasing the Epstein files gets its 218th signature

items.p: What does reaching 218 signatures do?
o: After a waiting period, it can force a vote over leadership’s objection
It passes the bill without a recorded floor vote
It sends the bill straight to the Senate, skipping a House vote
It removes the committee chair who blocked the bill
items.x: A discharge petition lets a majority of the House pull a bill out of committee. It rarely succeeds, because majority members don’t like to cross their own leaders. This one reached 218 when newly sworn-in Rep. Adelita Grijalva signed, after a delay in seating her that critics said was meant to stall the vote.

items.p: What is the motion to recommit?
o: The minority’s last chance to send a bill back to committee
A motion to restart the bill from scratch
A Senate motion to reconsider a vote that the chamber already took
A vote to override a veto
items.x: It comes right before the final vote and almost always fails. Since 2021, House rules have barred attaching amendment instructions to it, which used to make it the minority’s favorite tool for forcing awkward votes.

items.p: Put a major House bill’s floor steps in order.
items: Rules Committee reports a rule
House adopts the rule
General debate
Amendments the rule allows
Motion to recommit
Final passage vote
items.x: If the rule fails at the second step, nothing after it happens.

units.title: The Senate Floor
units.desc: Unlimited debate means the Senate runs on agreement, and one senator can slow almost anything.

items.p: Why does the Senate do most of its business by unanimous consent?
o: Debate is nearly unlimited, so consent is much faster
The Constitution requires consent for most Senate business
Senate rules bar roll-call votes on routine matters
It makes votes easier to count
